## Transfer Pricing Local File – United Energy Pakistan (Tax Year 2023)

### Executive Summary  

United Energy Pakistan (“UEP”) is a Pakistani branch of United Energy Group (“UEG”), engaged in oil and gas exploration and production. During the 2022 accounting period (January 1 to December 31, 2022), UEP had two intercompany financing transactions with its affiliate, Gold Trade International (“GTI”): (1) a long-term acquisition loan (originated in 2011) used to finance UEP’s purchase of BP Pakistan assets; and (2) a working capital loan (originated in 2015) for operational funding. These are the only controlled transactions for the year. Both loans were analyzed under the arm’s length principle as required by Pakistan’s tax law (Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001) and the applicable transfer pricing documentation framework (including S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021).  

A detailed functional and economic analysis was conducted for each loan. The Comparable Uncontrolled Price (“CUP”) method was applied (augmented by a cost-of-funds plus margin perspective), and the interest rates and key terms were benchmarked against relevant 2022 market data. Based on this analysis, the interest rates on both intercompany loans are consistent with arm’s length outcomes given the market conditions prevailing in 2022. Accordingly, UEP’s financing costs are supported under the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (including the February 2020 guidance on financial transactions, now reflected in Chapter X) as well as Pakistan’s transfer pricing regulations. No material transfer pricing adjustment is recommended for 2022.  

Key conclusions include:  

- **Acquisition Loan:** A floating interest rate of **LIBOR + 5.3%** was charged on the **USD 180 million** outstanding acquisition loan. Benchmark analysis indicates that the all-in rate (approximately **7%–9%** in 2022 as LIBOR rose) aligns with, or is slightly below, what independent lenders would typically require for a comparable long-term USD loan to a Pakistan-based oil & gas borrower in 2022, after considering country risk and borrower profile.  

- **Working Capital Loan:** A fixed **9% USD** interest rate was charged on the **USD 89.4 million** working capital facility. The rate remained stable throughout 2022 and falls within an arm’s length range when compared to short-term financing rates in emerging markets. As global rates increased in 2022, a **9% USD** rate remained competitive relative to comparable local PKR-denominated financing (which exceeded **13%** on a nominal basis).  

- **Arm’s Length Compliance:** The terms of both loans (interest, tenor, and related features) are consistent with OECD guidance on intra-group financial transactions, taking into account UEP’s credit profile and implicit group support. Pakistan’s transfer pricing framework typically favours CUP for such transactions. The CUP analysis (using comparable market interest data for 2022) supports that the intercompany interest rates are arm’s length. Documentation compliant with Local File requirements (per Rule 27M of the Income Tax Rules, 2002) is included, fulfilling the S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021 obligations to substantiate arm’s length pricing.  

Overall, UEP’s intercompany financing arrangements for 2022 meet the arm’s length standard under both OECD Guidelines and Pakistan’s transfer pricing regulations, supported by the analyses presented in this report. The appendices provide supporting details (including key loan contract extracts, repayment history, group structure, and benchmarking data sources).  

---

## Introduction and Transaction Overview  

### Company Background  

UEP is the Pakistani branch of UEG (a Hong Kong–listed oil & gas company) operating exploration and production assets in Pakistan. UEP was established in 2011 when UEG acquired BP’s upstream assets in Pakistan for **USD 775 million**. The acquisition was financed in part by an affiliate loan from GTI, an intra-group financing vehicle. UEP later also obtained a working capital loan from GTI in 2015 to fund ongoing operations. UEP, GTI, and UEG are related parties under Pakistan’s transfer pricing definitions (common ownership/control).  

### Group Structure  

UEG is the ultimate parent, owning various subsidiaries including GTI. UEP is not a separate subsidiary but a branch (permanent establishment) of UEG in Pakistan. GTI provided funds to UEP via intercompany loans. The simplified group structure and intercompany loan relationships are illustrated below:  

**Figure:** Simplified United Energy Group structure, showing UEG as parent, GTI as finance affiliate, and UEP as the Pakistan branch. The dashed arrow indicates the intercompany loan arrangements (2011 Acquisition Loan and 2015 Working Capital Loan) between GTI (lender) and UEP (borrower).  

### Controlled Transactions in 2022  

Table 1 summarizes the two intercompany loans between UEP (borrower) and GTI (lender) that were outstanding during the 2022 financial year. These are the only controlled (related-party) transactions of UEP in the year. No other intercompany sales or service transactions occurred in 2022; accordingly, the transfer pricing analysis focuses exclusively on these financing arrangements.  

**Table 1: Overview of UEP’s intercompany loans with GTI**  

| Intercompany Loan | Initiation | Original Principal | Outstanding Principal (Dec 2022) | Interest Rate Terms | Tenor / Repayment |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Acquisition Loan (GTI) | 2011 | USD 570 million | USD 180 million (remaining after repayments) | Floating, LIBOR + 5.3% p.a. (semi-annual periods) | Long-term; principal repaid gradually 2013–2018, then remaining balance ongoing |
| Working Capital Loan | 2015 | USD 89.4 million | USD 89.4 million (no change) | Fixed 9% p.a. (in USD) | Short-term revolving facility, effectively extended annually; no principal repaid through 2022 |

Both loans are denominated in USD. The acquisition loan financed UEP’s asset acquisition in 2011, and the working capital loan provides liquidity for operations. The outstanding principal in PKR terms has increased over time due to PKR depreciation (e.g., **PKR 40.536 billion** for the USD 180 million loan at 2022 year-end), but remains unchanged in USD.  

### Transaction Descriptions  

#### Acquisition Loan (2011)  

In September 2011, UEP (as borrower) entered into a loan agreement with GTI to finance the BP asset acquisition. The initial principal was **USD 570 million**, representing the majority of the purchase price. The loan carries interest at **LIBOR + 5.3% per annum** (floating rate reset every six months). UEP made periodic repayments from 2013 onward as cash flows allowed, reducing principal to **USD 180 million** by 2018. As of 2022, **USD 180 million** remained outstanding.  

The loan agreement does not specify a fixed maturity date, effectively making it a long-term shareholder loan; however, it allows voluntary prepayments (which UEP exercised to reduce the balance) and requires semi-annual interest payments. No collateral was pledged, and the loan is subordinated to any external bank financing. The purpose of this loan was to fund a capital acquisition and it is therefore considered a long-term, quasi-equity financing of UEP’s business.  

#### Working Capital Loan (2015)  

In January 2015, UEP obtained a working capital facility from GTI of **USD 89.4 million** to finance operational needs (e.g., bridging short-term cash flow gaps for field operations and capital expenditures). The loan’s interest rate was fixed at **9% per annum** (per the loan contract clause 3.2). Initially structured as a short-term revolving credit (one-year tenor), this facility has been rolled over each year through 2022, with no principal repayments made. Effectively, it became a long-term source of working capital, though contractually it could be called or renewed annually. Interest is payable semi-annually. Like the acquisition loan, it is unsecured and subordinate to any third-party debt.  

The fixed 9% rate was set considering internal funding costs and local currency interest rates at the time (2015) and has remained unchanged, providing certainty in interest expense for UEP.  

### Transfer Pricing Requirement  

Under Pakistan’s tax law, intercompany transactions must be consistent with the arm’s length principle (i.e., priced as if between independent enterprises). Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance empowers tax authorities to adjust incomes where controlled transactions are not on arm’s length terms. Pakistan also prescribes detailed transfer pricing documentation rules broadly aligned with OECD standards, including the three-tier documentation framework (Master File, Local File, and Country-by-Country report) introduced through S.R.O. 1191(I)/2017 and updated through S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021.  

UEP falls within the scope (related-party transactions exceeding PKR 50 million) requiring a Local File. This report serves as UEP’s Local File for 2022, demonstrating that the intercompany loan interest conforms to arm’s length pricing. The OECD’s February 2020 guidance on financial transactions (incorporated as Chapter X of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines) is also referenced in analyzing these loans.  

The remainder of this report presents: (i) an overview of industry and economic conditions in 2022 relevant to financing; (ii) a functional analysis of the parties and transactions; (iii) an economic analysis and benchmarking for each loan, including selection of the most appropriate transfer pricing method; and (iv) conclusions on arm’s length compliance. Detailed supporting data and extracts are provided in the appendices.  

---

## Industry and Macroeconomic Context in 2022  

### Financing Environment  

The year 2022 was marked by significantly rising interest rates globally and in Pakistan. To combat high inflation (which averaged approximately 12% in Pakistan during 2022), the State Bank of Pakistan (“SBP”) raised its policy rate aggressively. The average 6-month KIBOR (Karachi Interbank Offered Rate), a benchmark for PKR loans, increased to approximately 10.8% in 2022 from approximately 7.4% in 2021. By late 2022, KIBOR exceeded 15%, pushing typical PKR-denominated corporate lending rates well above 13%–14%. Figure A below (from PACRA Research) shows the steep rise in KIBOR and lending rates through 2022.  

In parallel, the U.S. Federal Reserve tightened monetary policy rapidly in 2022, causing USD LIBOR rates to surge. For example, 3-month USD LIBOR rose from about 0.3% in January 2022 to approximately 4.7% by December 2022. This global tightening, combined with geopolitical factors (e.g., the war in Ukraine), tightened financing conditions for emerging markets and increased risk premiums.  

### Global USD Interest Rates  

In 2022, global interest rates rose sharply from historic lows. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s aggressive tightening drove USD benchmark rates up dramatically. For example, the 3-month USD LIBOR climbed from around 0.25% in January 2022 to about 4.7% by December 2022, while the newer risk-free benchmark (SOFR) similarly increased. This was a material shift from near-zero rates in prior years, reflecting global inflation and monetary tightening. Consequently, the base rate applicable to USD-denominated loans was significantly higher in 2022 than in earlier periods.  

### Pakistan’s Local Interest Rates  

Pakistan’s interest rates rose sharply in 2022 amid high inflation and currency pressures. SBP raised its policy rate from 9.75% at the start of 2022 to 16% by year-end 2022. The 6-month KIBOR reached multi-year highs, rising to approximately 14.1% by April 2022 and exceeding 15% later in the year. Typical PKR corporate lending rates (generally KIBOR + 1% to 2%) therefore moved well into the mid-teens (e.g., 13%–16% or higher) by late 2022. By comparison, a USD loan at 9% would equate to an even higher cost in PKR terms given the rupee’s depreciation and inflation differential.  

**Figure:** Interest rate trends in 2022 – Pakistan’s 6M KIBOR (red, left axis) vs. U.S. 3M USD LIBOR (blue, right axis). Local PKR rates were already high and rose further, while global USD rates spiked from near-zero to multi-percent levels.  

### Sovereign and Credit Risk in Pakistan  

2022 was a turbulent year for Pakistan’s country risk indicators. Credit rating agencies downgraded Pakistan’s sovereign rating into the single-C range (e.g., Moody’s Caa1/Caa3 by end-2022) amid heightened debt stress concerns. Yields on Pakistan’s USD sovereign bonds spiked to distressed levels; for instance, the Pakistan Eurobond maturing 2024 experienced extreme yield levels in July 2022 during peak market stress. Likewise, Pakistan’s 5-year credit default swap (“CDS”) spread, a proxy for perceived default risk, increased significantly during 2022. These indicators point to a materially elevated risk premium for USD lending to Pakistan (sovereign or corporate) during the period.  

Pakistan faced external account pressures in 2022, which elevated perceived default risk on sovereign and corporate debt. Although certain extremes in sovereign yields were temporary, they underscore the high risk premium demanded for Pakistan exposure. By contrast, Chinese policy banks and group-level financiers continued to support projects in Pakistan. Notably, UEG’s operations in Pakistan benefited from a USD 5 billion credit line from China Development Bank, indicating implicit backing at group level. This context is relevant in assessing UEP’s intercompany loans: an independent lender (without group support) would price in Pakistan’s country risk, whereas an affiliate lender with access to group funding may provide terms that are more stable and less exposed to short-term market volatility.  

### Comparative International Benchmarks  

Other high-risk markets also experienced elevated financing costs in 2022. For example, sovereign default spreads for certain Caa-rated markets were elevated, leading to USD cost of capital estimates in the mid-teens. This context underscores that unrelated-party lenders would generally demand double-digit USD interest rates to compensate for country risk. Against this backdrop, a single-digit USD interest rate for Pakistan exposure (as in UEP’s case) would typically be viewed as conservative or, at minimum, within a reasonable arm’s length range depending on the borrower’s credit profile and implicit support considerations.  

### Oil & Gas Sector Conditions  

UEP operates in the upstream oil & gas sector. In 2022, energy prices were relatively strong (Brent oil averaging around USD 100/barrel), supporting operating cash flows for producers. However, financing for E&P companies in emerging markets continued to carry significant risk spreads due to commodity price volatility and, in some cases, ESG-related caution. External lenders often require robust collateral and/or guarantees. UEP’s loans from GTI were unsecured, but UEG’s strategic commitment to Pakistan supports the view of implicit group support behind the branch’s obligations. This implicit support would be expected to improve UEP’s creditworthiness compared to a standalone Pakistan E&P company.  

In summary, 2022 represented a high-interest, high-risk environment: local borrowing costs in Pakistan were in double digits, and USD funding for Pakistan risk incorporated substantial spreads. These factors are central to evaluating whether GTI’s loans to UEP carried arm’s length interest rates.  

---

## Financial Benchmarking and Arm’s Length Analysis  

### Overview of UEP’s Intercompany Loans  

UEP had two USD-denominated loans from its affiliate, GTI, during 2022:  

- **Acquisition Loan (2011):** Long-term; outstanding principal approximately USD 180 million in 2022; interest at LIBOR + 5.3% (floating).  
- **Working Capital Loan (2015):** Revolving/short-term facility (rolled annually); principal USD 89.4 million; interest 9% (fixed, USD).  

Both loans were tested under the CUP method using available market interest rate data and comparable indicators where available. A cost-of-funds plus margin cross-check was also performed to corroborate the CUP outcome by assessing the lender’s likely funding cost and a reasonable treasury spread.  

---

### Benchmarking the Acquisition Loan (LIBOR + 5.3%)  

The acquisition loan’s pricing is composed of (i) the base USD LIBOR rate and (ii) a fixed credit spread of 5.3%. During 2022, 6-month USD LIBOR averaged approximately 2.5%–3.0%, resulting in an all-in rate of roughly 7%–8% mid-year and rising towards approximately 9%–10% by late 2022 as LIBOR increased.  

In evaluating arm’s length pricing, the analysis considered what an independent lender would charge for a comparable USD loan to a Pakistan-based oil & gas borrower given: (i) Pakistan’s elevated country risk; (ii) borrower credit profile; (iii) absence of collateral (the loan is unsecured and subordinated); and (iv) long tenor and structural subordination. Unrelated lenders would typically price such a loan at a significant spread over LIBOR.  

Sovereign yields and risk premia provide context: Pakistan’s sovereign USD yields and CDS levels in 2022 reflected substantial perceived default risk. In such an environment, an unrelated corporate borrower would typically pay a premium above sovereign yields—particularly for unsecured and subordinated financing. A pricing expectation of LIBOR + 6% to 8% (or higher) would not be unusual for a comparable risk profile in 2022, absent strong support or guarantees.  

Against that backdrop, GTI’s pricing of LIBOR + 5.3% appears modest relative to a purely standalone Pakistan risk profile. This outcome is consistent with implicit group support: as a branch within a larger group, UEP likely benefits from credit uplift due to group affiliation, and OECD guidance recognises that implicit support can reduce the interest rate relative to standalone borrowing. It is also plausible that GTI accessed group funding at a lower cost (for example, through group banking relationships or policy-bank support) and applied a reasonable treasury margin.  

Accordingly, using multiple reference points—including sovereign yield context, country risk indicators, and a cost-of-funds plus margin perspective—the acquisition loan pricing is supported as within an arm’s length range (and potentially favourable to UEP).  

---

### Benchmarking the Working Capital Loan (9% Fixed)  

The working capital facility carries a fixed interest rate of 9% per annum, unchanged since inception in 2015. By 2022, the facility had been rolled over for several years, making it economically longer-term in effect, albeit contractually structured as a revolving/annual renewal arrangement.  

To test arm’s length pricing in the 2022 context, the analysis considered how an unrelated lender would price a comparable USD working capital facility to a Pakistan-based borrower during 2022’s high-risk environment. Global USD benchmarks increased materially in 2022 (with risk-free yields approaching 4%–5% by late 2022). Incorporating Pakistan’s elevated risk premium, an independent lender would typically require a double-digit USD rate for unsecured Pakistan exposure (particularly during periods of heightened sovereign stress), unless supported by strong collateral or explicit guarantees.  

In that environment, a fixed 9% USD rate is within a plausible arm’s length range and is not excessive. Indeed, given the increase in global benchmarks and Pakistan risk premia during 2022, the fixed 9% could be viewed as favourable to UEP relative to the pricing expected on newly-originated external USD facilities in the same period. Importantly, from a Pakistan transfer pricing risk perspective, the central concern would be an excessive interest expense that erodes the Pakistan tax base. Here, UEP’s rate is not excessive when compared to 2022 market conditions and therefore does not indicate base erosion.  

The pricing also remains consistent when viewed through a cost-of-funds plus margin lens. If GTI’s USD funding cost rose with global rates, a 9% fixed charge would still embed a reasonable treasury margin in a high-risk lending context.  

Accordingly, the working capital loan pricing is assessed as arm’s length (and potentially conservative from a Pakistan tax base perspective) in light of the economic conditions prevailing in 2022.  

---

### Cost-Plus (Cost of Funds) Perspective  

To corroborate the CUP analysis, a cost-plus perspective was applied by estimating GTI’s likely cost of funding and a reasonable treasury margin. As GTI functions as a group financing conduit, its funding may be sourced from internal group liquidity and/or external credit lines at the group level. If GTI’s cost of funds for USD financing were, illustratively, LIBOR + 3% (consistent with access to group-level credit), lending to UEP at LIBOR + 5.3% would imply a gross margin of approximately 2.3%. This spread is broadly consistent with treasury margins observed for intra-group lending, covering administrative costs, funding and credit risk buffers, and a reasonable profit element.  

For the 9% fixed-rate loan, comparing to GTI’s likely USD funding cost over time similarly suggests a reasonable margin that is not excessive given Pakistan risk and the unsecured nature of the exposure.  

Accordingly, the cost-plus cross-check supports the CUP conclusion that GTI earned a reasonable, not exorbitant, return and that UEP’s interest charges are consistent with arm’s length conditions.  

---

### Use of Comparable Data  

In benchmarking, a range of comparable uncontrolled price indicators were considered, including published interest rate benchmarks (LIBOR/SOFR, KIBOR), sovereign yield context, and risk premium indicators (including sovereign spreads and CDS proxies). While exact “like-for-like” loan comparables are typically limited in availability (particularly for unsecured USD corporate loans into Pakistan without guarantees), the use of multiple corroborative indicators is consistent with OECD principles for financial transactions and supports the arm’s length assessment.  

In addition, UEP’s branch status within UEG implies a level of implicit support that can reasonably influence credit outcomes. OECD guidance explicitly recognises that group affiliation may uplift a borrower’s standalone credit position and thereby reduce interest rates relative to a purely standalone borrower. This dynamic was considered in interpreting the benchmark outcomes and supports the reasonableness of the interest spreads and fixed rate applied.  

---

## Functional Analysis of the Intercompany Loans  

In accordance with OECD guidance (Chapter I and the 2020 Chapter X on financial transactions), the functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed by each party were analysed. For lending transactions, economically significant factors include capital provision, credit risk assessment/monitoring, funding cost management, currency exposure, and default risk. These are summarised below for UEP (borrower) and GTI (lender).  

### GTI (Lender)  

GTI’s primary function was to provide financing to UEP. This involves sourcing or allocating funds (either from parent group resources or external credit lines) and entering into and maintaining the loan arrangements. GTI does not operate as an independent commercial bank; it functions as a group treasury/conduit. Accordingly, GTI likely did not perform the same depth of credit underwriting that an unrelated lender would require, relying instead on group oversight and the strategic nature of the Pakistan operations.  

GTI nevertheless assumes credit risk on UEP: if UEP were unable to pay interest or principal, GTI (and ultimately UEG) would bear the loss. GTI’s key assets comprise the loan receivables (amounts due from UEP) and any corresponding liabilities (if it borrowed externally to on-lend). GTI also bears exposure linked to foreign exchange and repayment capacity risk because the loans are USD-denominated while UEP’s operational cash flows are substantially linked to PKR dynamics.  

The 5.3% spread on the acquisition loan and the fixed 9% rate on the working capital loan can be viewed as GTI’s compensation for funding and credit risk, as well as its treasury role and administrative functions in deploying group capital.  

### UEP (Borrower)  

UEP’s function is to utilise the borrowed funds within its business operations. The acquisition loan financed the purchase of productive upstream assets generating revenue, while the working capital loan supports operating liquidity requirements. UEP is responsible for servicing the debt, paying semi-annual interest and repaying principal as and when agreed (or as cash flows allow).  

UEP bears currency and cash flow risk because the debt is USD-denominated while underlying operational revenues and costs are significantly affected by PKR movements. PKR depreciation increases the PKR burden of servicing USD obligations and is therefore a key economic risk for UEP.  

As a branch of UEG, there is no separate legal entity that would ordinarily require an external parental guarantee; the parent is inherently exposed through the branch structure. However, implicit support is relevant: UEP’s role within UEG’s broader portfolio supports the expectation that the group would sustain the Pakistan operations, which influences how an independent lender might view credit risk for pricing purposes.  

### Comparison to Independent Arrangement  

An independent lender would typically require robust due diligence, higher spreads, and potentially security over assets, particularly in the 2022 environment. In the related-party arrangement, GTI provided unsecured, subordinated financing with flexible repayment features (particularly on the acquisition loan and the continued rollover of the working capital facility). The absence of strict amortisation and covenant enforcement reflects group support and flexibility that may not be available from third-party lenders.  

From an accurate delineation perspective, these features indicate certain equity-like characteristics; however, the arrangements are respected as debt for transfer pricing purposes because interest is paid and (in the acquisition loan’s case) principal repayments have been made historically.  

### Conclusion of Functional Analysis  

GTI performs the financing function (capital provision) and assumes key lender risks (credit/default and funding risk), while UEP performs the operating functions using the funds and bears repayment and currency exposure through business performance. No other group entities are involved and no ancillary fees (e.g., guarantee or commitment fees) are charged separately.  

Given a straightforward lender/borrower relationship and the nature of remuneration (interest), the CUP method is the most appropriate method to test the arm’s length nature of the interest rates using comparable market interest indicators. A cost-of-funds plus margin perspective is applied as a corroborative cross-check consistent with OECD guidance.  

---

## Economic Analysis and Benchmarking – Acquisition Loan (2011)  

### Loan Characteristics  

The acquisition loan was originally USD 570 million and carries interest at LIBOR + 5.3% per annum, applied to six-month USD LIBOR. The loan has no fixed maturity and operates in substance as a long-term shareholder loan with voluntary prepayments. UEP reduced principal to USD 180 million by end-2018 through repayments aligned with cash flows, and the principal remained USD 180 million through 2022.  

In 2022, USD LIBOR increased materially, and accordingly the all-in interest rate moved from approximately 5.8% early in the year to approximately 10.1% by year-end, averaging around 7%–8% over the year. The transfer pricing focus is therefore whether the pricing term “LIBOR + 5.3%” is arm’s length for a long-term, unsecured, subordinated USD loan to a Pakistan E&P borrower in the 2022 environment.  

### Benchmark Selection and CUP Application  

The CUP method is applied by identifying or approximating market interest rates for comparable loans. Exact comparable independent USD loans to Pakistan E&P borrowers are limited. Accordingly, multiple benchmark reference points are used, including:  

- PKR interest benchmarks as contextual comparators (KIBOR-linked lending levels) with appropriate caution due to currency differences;  
- Sovereign USD yield context and country risk indicators as floor/anchor points for Pakistan exposure;  
- Emerging market lending spreads and risk premia indicative of arm’s length credit spreads in 2022; and  
- A cost-of-funds plus margin cross-check for the lender’s treasury margin.  

Based on these corroborative indicators, LIBOR + 5.3% is assessed to fall within an arm’s length range when implicit group support is considered as part of the borrower’s realistic credit position, consistent with OECD guidance.  

### Conclusion for Acquisition Loan  

The acquisition loan interest rate is assessed as arm’s length for 2022. UEP’s interest expense reflects a level that is consistent with market-based pricing for the applicable risk environment and does not indicate excessive profit shifting out of Pakistan. The loan is therefore supportable as debt for transfer pricing purposes, and no adjustment is proposed.  

---

## Economic Analysis and Benchmarking – Working Capital Loan (2015)  

### Loan Characteristics  

The working capital loan is a USD 89.4 million facility carrying a fixed interest rate of 9% per annum. Although structured as a short-term revolving facility renewed annually, it has been rolled over through 2022 with no principal repayments, making it economically long-standing. UEP pays semi-annual interest, and the principal balance remains constant in USD terms.  

### Benchmarking the 9% Rate  

The 9% rate is evaluated both at inception (2015) and in the prevailing 2022 context.  

- **At inception (2015):** USD benchmarks were near zero, but Pakistan risk was elevated relative to global markets. A 9% fixed USD rate was conservative in absolute terms, yet broadly comparable to local PKR borrowing costs around that period and consistent with the risk dynamics applicable to USD lending into Pakistan.  

- **During 2022:** With global USD benchmarks increasing materially and Pakistan risk premia elevated, independent USD lending into Pakistan in 2022 would commonly be expected to price in double digits absent strong collateral or support. Against that context, the 9% fixed rate is not excessive and is within a plausible arm’s length range, particularly when implicit group support is considered as part of the credit analysis.  

### Method and Delineation Considerations  

CUP is applied by reference to market indicators and risk context. The continued rollover and lack of amortisation reflects group flexibility; however, interest is paid and the facility is contractually renewed. Accordingly, the arrangement is treated as bona fide debt for transfer pricing purposes, while recognising that its flexibility is linked to group relationship dynamics.  

### Conclusion for Working Capital Loan  

The fixed 9% rate is assessed as arm’s length (and not above arm’s length) in the 2022 context. From a Pakistan transfer pricing perspective, the rate does not indicate excessive interest expense or base erosion. Accordingly, no adjustment is proposed.  

---

## Compliance with OECD Guidelines and Pakistan TP Regulations  

### OECD Guidelines  

The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (including the 2020 financial transactions guidance) require consideration of contractual terms, borrower creditworthiness, economic environment, and implicit group support in determining an arm’s length interest rate. The analysis in this report reflects these elements through (i) delineation of loan terms; (ii) qualitative assessment of UEP’s risk profile and group support; and (iii) benchmarking using base USD benchmarks plus risk-appropriate spreads (consistent with risk-adjusted return concepts). The CUP method is applied as the primary method, with a cost-of-funds plus margin cross-check consistent with OECD guidance for treasury/conduit entities.  

### Pakistan Transfer Pricing Regulations  

Pakistan’s framework (Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and the Income Tax Rules, 2002 including Rule 27M and Rule 27N as updated through S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021) requires taxpayers to maintain local file documentation supporting arm’s length outcomes. This report addresses the core local file expectations for the controlled financing transactions, including background, transaction terms, functional analysis, method selection rationale, benchmarking support, and conclusions.  

### Thin Capitalization  

Pakistan’s thin capitalization rule (Section 106) disallows interest deductions for foreign-controlled resident companies where the debt-to-equity ratio exceeds prescribed thresholds. UEP is a branch structure and may not fall squarely within the resident-company framing; however, the file recognises the broader deductibility context. The intercompany loans constitute the principal related-party financing charges, and documentation (including key extracts) has been maintained to support the interest position and compliance.  

---

## Conclusion  

Based on the detailed analysis of UEP’s two intercompany loans, the interest rates and related terms are assessed to conform to the arm’s length standard for the 2022 tax year. The acquisition loan pricing (LIBOR + 5.3%) is supported as reasonable given Pakistan’s risk profile and the macroeconomic environment in 2022, particularly when implicit group support is considered. The working capital loan’s fixed 9% rate remains within an acceptable range in the 2022 context and is not excessive relative to external alternatives.  

Neither loan results in an excessive interest burden that would unduly reduce UEP’s taxable profits in Pakistan. The functional analysis supports the delineation of the transactions as financing arrangements with interest remuneration tested under CUP, corroborated by a cost-of-funds plus margin perspective. Documentation requirements under Pakistani law have been addressed through this Local File and supporting appendices.  

UEP should continue to monitor market conditions and periodically review intercompany financing terms to ensure ongoing alignment with arm’s length conditions, documenting any changes where required.  

---

## Appendices  

### Appendix A: Group Structure and Ownership  

UEP is a branch (permanent establishment) of United Energy Group Limited (UEG), Hong Kong. UEG owns 100% of the Pakistan branch operations. Gold Trade International (GTI) is a wholly-owned affiliate used as a financing vehicle. The figure below (repeated from the overview) depicts the relationships:  

**Figure A.1:** UEG Group Structure – UEG (Hong Kong) as parent; GTI (affiliate, jurisdiction not disclosed, used for intercompany financing); UEP (Pakistan Branch). Solid lines denote ownership/control, dashed line denotes loan transactions.  

UEG as a whole is majority-owned (71.7%) by Mr. Zhang Hongwei (as of 2013). UEG’s Pakistan branch (UEP) constitutes a major part of its production operations. All entities are under common control and are “associates” per Pakistani law. UEP’s financial statements consolidate into UEG’s accounts. There were no other related-party transactions in 2022 aside from the loans discussed.  

---

### Appendix B: Key Loan Agreement Extracts  

This section provides key terms extracted from the intercompany loan agreements (translated/summarized from the signed contracts):  

1. **2011 Acquisition Loan Agreement** (signed 16 Sept 2011 between GTI and UEG – Pakistan Branch): Principal amount USD 570,000,000. Interest: “Interest on the Loan for each Interest Period shall be LIBOR plus 5.3% per annum…” (Clause 3.2). Interest Period defined as six months (Clause 3.1), with interest payable semi-annually on June 30 and Dec 31. No fixed maturity date; the loan is repayable on demand or as agreed. Prepayment: Borrower may prepay without penalty (Clause 3.3). Governing law: English law. Purpose: Acquisition financing (recital). No security, no guarantor (the loan is unsecured).  

2. **2015 Working Capital Loan Agreement** (signed 02 Jan 2015 between GTI and UEG – Pakistan Branch): Principal amount USD 89,400,000 (facility limit). Interest: fixed at 9.0% per annum on outstanding principal (Clause 3.2). Interest Period of six months, payable semi-annually. Original term 12 months; the agreement has been extended annually via amendment letters (on similar terms each year). Purpose: “to finance the working capital needs of the Borrower” (Clause 2.1). No security. Governing law: English law. Notably, no provision for rate adjustment is included; any market changes would require amending the contract, which did not occur through 2022.  

The full agreements are maintained on file. These extracts reflect the critical pricing terms (5.3% margin and 9% fixed) analysed in this Local File. The lack of a set maturity in the 2011 loan was considered in delineation (long-term quasi-equity characteristics for analysis purposes, while remaining legal debt).

UEP’s audited financial statements report the intercompany loan balances each year. The table below shows principal balances and PKR equivalents from 2011–2022 as compiled from UEP’s records:

Interest is settled in cash (not capitalised), hence principal remains static when not repaid.

### Appendix D: Benchmark Data and Sources  

To support benchmarking, relevant market data was gathered from credible sources (central bank statistics, financial databases, and publications). Key data points and sources include Pakistan interest benchmarks (SBP / PACRA), USD LIBOR history (market data sources), sovereign yields and risk proxies (Eurobond yields / CDS context), regional comparators, and OECD financial transactions guidance (Chapter X).  

---

## Transfer Pricing Method Selection Discussion  

### Applicable TP Methods for Intra-Group Loans  

Under Pakistan’s rules (aligned with OECD methods), several transfer pricing methods may be applied to financing transactions, including CUP and Cost Plus. For intercompany loans, CUP is generally the most direct and preferred approach, as it compares the controlled interest rate against market interest outcomes observed in comparable uncontrolled transactions or reliable market proxies.  

In the absence of exact loan comparables, and to corroborate CUP results, a cost-of-funds plus margin approach is also recognised under OECD Chapter X, particularly where the lender acts as a treasury/conduit entity. This approach was used as a cross-check alongside CUP.  

Other transactional methods (TNMM, profit split) are generally not suitable for plain-vanilla financing arrangements where the remuneration is interest and the transaction is economically homogeneous. Accordingly, CUP (supported by cost-of-funds) was selected as the most appropriate and defensible approach for UEP’s intercompany loans.  

### Criteria and Rationale for Method Selection  

The method selection reflects: (i) the nature of transactions (straightforward debt financing); (ii) the availability of relevant 2022 interest benchmarks and risk indicators; (iii) the sector and country risk context; (iv) the relevance of implicit group support in determining credit outcomes; and (v) the need for transparent and objective support consistent with local expectations and OECD guidance.  

---

## Compliance and Regulatory Framing  

The analysis in this report is framed within OECD Chapter X (financial transactions) and Pakistan’s transfer pricing framework under Section 108 and Rule 27M/27N (as updated). The report documents delineation, method selection, benchmarking support, and conclusions demonstrating arm’s length outcomes for UEP’s controlled financing transactions for 2022, consistent with documentation expectations under S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021.

5.2 Benchmarking the Acquisition Loan (LIBOR + 5.3%)
Loan Characteristics Summary
Attribute	Specification

The Challenge: Fixed Rate Set in 2015, Analyzed for 2023
The Key Transfer Pricing Question:
"Is a fixed 9% rate, established in 2015, still arm's length when analyzed for 2023 conditions?"
Transfer Pricing Principle:
Transfer prices are tested for contemporaneous arm's length pricing. A rate fixed in one year may not be supportable in a different year if economic conditions have materially changed.
2023 Benchmarking Analysis
Comparable Rate Analysis for 2023 Conditions
For a short/medium-term working capital facility to a Pakistan-based E&P borrower in 2023:
Benchmarking Components:
Component	2023 Level	Rationale
Base USD Rate	5.25%-5.50%	LIBOR/SOFR 2023 average
Pakistan Country Risk	200-300 bps	CDS spreads, Eurobond yields
E&P Sector Risk	100-200 bps	Commodity volatility, leverage

Implied Spread Range	350-600 bps	Total above base rate
Implied Rate Range (2023)	8.75-11.5%	Total blended rate
With Implicit Group Support:
•	Adjustment for credit uplift: -1% to -1.5%
•	Adjusted Arm's Length Range (2023): 7.75-10%
Alternative Perspective: Refinancing Analysis

Expected Refinancing Rate:
Given 2023 market conditions:
•	Independent lender perspective: Would require 9-12%+ given Pakistan risk
•	With implicit group support: Would expect 8-10% range
Conclusion: A fixed 9% rate would be AT THE LOWER END of the arm's length range for a 2023 refinancing.
Cost-of-Funds Analysis (Corroboration)
GTI's Cost of Funds:
For a multi-year (5-7 year economic tenor) working capital facility:
•	Expected funding cost: LIBOR + 2%-3% (or equivalent, ~7.5%-8.5%)
GTI's Margin:
Element	Rate
GTI's Lending Rate	9.0%
Less: GTI's Cost of Funds	~7.5%-8.0%
= GTI's Gross Margin	1.0%-1.5%

Industry and Macroeconomic Context in 2022
Financing Environment
The year 2022 was marked by significantly rising interest rates globally and in Pakistan. To combat high inflation (which averaged approximately 12% in Pakistan during 2022), the State Bank of Pakistan (“SBP”) raised its policy rate aggressively. The average 6-month KIBOR (Karachi Interbank Offered Rate), a benchmark for PKR loans, increased to approximately 10.8% in 2022 from approximately 7.4% in 2021. By late 2022, KIBOR exceeded 15%, pushing typical PKR-denominated corporate lending rates well above 13%–14%. Figure A below (from PACRA Research) shows the steep rise in KIBOR and lending rates through 2022.
In parallel, the U.S. Federal Reserve tightened monetary policy rapidly in 2022, causing USD LIBOR rates to surge. For example, 3-month USD LIBOR rose from about 0.3% in January 2022 to approximately 4.7% by December 2022. This global tightening, combined with geopolitical factors (e.g., the war in Ukraine), tightened financing conditions for emerging markets and increased risk premiums.
Global USD Interest Rates
In 2022, global interest rates rose sharply from historic lows. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s aggressive tightening drove USD benchmark rates up dramatically. For example, the 3-month USD LIBOR climbed from around 0.25% in January 2022 to about 4.7% by December 2022, while the newer risk-free benchmark (SOFR) similarly increased. This was a material shift from near-zero rates in prior years, reflecting global inflation and monetary tightening. Consequently, the base rate applicable to USD-denominated loans was significantly higher in 2022 than in earlier periods.
Pakistan’s Local Interest Rates
Pakistan’s interest rates rose sharply in 2022 amid high inflation and currency pressures. SBP raised its policy rate from 9.75% at the start of 2022 to 16% by year-end 2022. The 6-month KIBOR reached multi-year highs, rising to approximately 14.1% by April 2022 and exceeding 15% later in the year. Typical PKR corporate lending rates (generally KIBOR + 1% to 2%) therefore moved well into the mid-teens (e.g., 13%–16% or higher) by late 2022. By comparison, a USD loan at 9% would equate to an even higher cost in PKR terms given the rupee’s depreciation and inflation differential.

Sovereign and Credit Risk in Pakistan
2022 was a turbulent year for Pakistan’s country risk indicators. Credit rating agencies downgraded Pakistan’s sovereign rating into the single-C range (e.g., Moody’s Caa1/Caa3 by end-2022) amid heightened debt stress concerns. Yields on Pakistan’s USD sovereign bonds spiked to distressed levels; for instance, the Pakistan Eurobond maturing 2024 experienced extreme yield levels in July 2022 during peak market stress. Likewise, Pakistan’s 5-year credit default swap (“CDS”) spread, a proxy for perceived default risk, increased significantly during 2022. These indicators point to a materially elevated risk premium for USD lending to Pakistan (sovereign or corporate) during the period.
Pakistan faced external account pressures in 2022, which elevated perceived default risk on sovereign and corporate debt. Although certain extremes in sovereign yields were temporary, they underscore the high risk premium demanded for Pakistan exposure. By contrast, Chinese policy banks and group-level financiers continued to support projects in Pakistan. Notably, UEG’s operations in Pakistan benefited from a USD 5 billion credit line from China Development Bank, indicating implicit backing at group level. This context is relevant in assessing UEP’s intercompany loans: an independent lender (without group support) would price in Pakistan’s country risk, whereas an affiliate lender with access to group funding may provide terms that are more stable and less exposed to short-term market volatility.
Comparative International Benchmarks
Other high-risk markets also experienced elevated financing costs in 2022. For example, sovereign default spreads for certain Caa-rated markets were elevated, leading to USD cost of capital estimates in the mid-teens. This context underscores that unrelated-party lenders would generally demand double-digit USD interest rates to compensate for country risk. Against this backdrop, a single-digit USD interest rate for Pakistan exposure (as in UEP’s case) would typically be viewed as conservative or, at minimum, within a reasonable arm’s length range depending on the borrower’s credit profile and implicit support considerations.
Oil & Gas Sector Conditions
UEP operates in the upstream oil & gas sector. In 2022, energy prices were relatively strong (Brent oil averaging around USD 100/barrel), supporting operating cash flows for producers. However, financing for E&P companies in emerging markets continued to carry significant risk spreads due to commodity price volatility and, in some cases, ESG-related caution. External lenders often require robust collateral and/or guarantees. UEP’s loans from GTI were unsecured, but UEG’s strategic commitment to Pakistan supports the view of implicit group support behind the branch’s obligations. This implicit support would be expected to improve UEP’s creditworthiness compared to a standalone Pakistan E&P company.
In summary, 2022 represented a high-interest, high-risk environment: local borrowing costs in Pakistan were in double digits, and USD funding for Pakistan risk incorporated substantial spreads. These factors are central to evaluating whether GTI’s loans to UEP carried arm’s length interest rates.
Financial Benchmarking and Arm’s Length Analysis
Overview of UEP’s Intercompany Loans
UEP had two USD-denominated loans from its affiliate, GTI, during 2022:
•	Acquisition Loan (2011): Long-term; outstanding principal approximately USD 180 million in 2022; interest at LIBOR + 5.3% (floating).
•	Working Capital Loan (2015): Revolving/short-term facility (rolled annually); principal USD 89.4 million; interest 9% (fixed, USD).
Both loans were tested under the CUP method using available market interest rate data and comparable indicators where available. A cost-of-funds plus margin cross-check was also performed to corroborate the CUP outcome by assessing the lender’s likely funding cost and a reasonable treasury spread.
Benchmarking the Acquisition Loan (LIBOR + 5.3%)
The acquisition loan’s pricing is composed of (i) the base USD LIBOR rate and (ii) a fixed credit spread of 5.3%. During 2022, 6-month USD LIBOR averaged approximately 2.5%–3.0%, resulting in an all-in rate of roughly 7%–8% mid-year and rising towards approximately 9%–10% by late 2022 as LIBOR increased.
In evaluating arm’s length pricing, the analysis considered what an independent lender would charge for a comparable USD loan to a Pakistan-based oil & gas borrower given: (i) Pakistan’s elevated country risk; (ii) borrower credit profile; (iii) absence of collateral (the loan is unsecured and subordinated); and (iv) long tenor and structural subordination. Unrelated lenders would typically price such a loan at a significant spread over LIBOR.
Sovereign yields and risk premia provide context: Pakistan’s sovereign USD yields and CDS levels in 2022 reflected substantial perceived default risk. In such an environment, an unrelated corporate borrower would typically pay a premium above sovereign yields, particularly for unsecured and subordinated financing. A pricing expectation of LIBOR + 6% to 8% (or higher) would not be unusual for a comparable risk profile in 2022, absent strong support or guarantees.
Against that backdrop, GTI’s pricing of LIBOR + 5.3% appears modest relative to a purely standalone Pakistan risk profile. This outcome is consistent with implicit group support: as a branch within a larger group, UEP likely benefits from credit uplift due to group affiliation, and OECD guidance recognises that implicit support can reduce the interest rate relative to standalone borrowing. It is also plausible that GTI accessed group funding at a lower cost (for example, through group banking relationships or policy-bank support) and applied a reasonable treasury margin.
Accordingly, using multiple reference points, including sovereign yield context, country risk indicators, and a cost-of-funds plus margin perspective, the acquisition loan pricing is supported as within an arm’s length range (and potentially favourable to UEP).
Benchmarking the Working Capital Loan (9% Fixed)
The working capital facility carries a fixed interest rate of 9% per annum, unchanged since inception in 2015. By 2022, the facility had been rolled over for several years, making it economically longer-term in effect, albeit contractually structured as a revolving/annual renewal arrangement.
To test arm’s length pricing in the 2022 context, the analysis considered how an unrelated lender would price a comparable USD working capital facility to a Pakistan-based borrower during 2022’s high-risk environment. Global USD benchmarks increased materially in 2022 (with risk-free yields approaching 4%–5% by late 2022). Incorporating Pakistan’s elevated risk premium, an independent lender would typically require a double-digit USD rate for unsecured Pakistan exposure (particularly during periods of heightened sovereign stress), unless supported by strong collateral or explicit guarantees.
In that environment, a fixed 9% USD rate is within a plausible arm’s length range and is not excessive. Indeed, given the increase in global benchmarks and Pakistan risk premia during 2022, the fixed 9% could be viewed as favourable to UEP relative to the pricing expected on newly-originated external USD facilities in the same period. Importantly, from a Pakistan transfer pricing risk perspective, the central concern would be an excessive interest expense that erodes the Pakistan tax base. Here, UEP’s rate is not excessive when compared to 2022 market conditions and therefore does not indicate base erosion.
The pricing also remains consistent when viewed through a cost-of-funds plus margin lens. If GTI’s USD funding cost rose with global rates, a 9% fixed charge would still embed a reasonable treasury margin in a high-risk lending context.
Accordingly, the working capital loan pricing is assessed as arm’s length (and potentially conservative from a Pakistan tax base perspective) in light of the economic conditions prevailing in 2022.
Cost-Plus (Cost of Funds) Perspective
To corroborate the CUP analysis, a cost-plus perspective was applied by estimating GTI’s likely cost of funding and a reasonable treasury margin. As GTI functions as a group financing conduit, its funding may be sourced from internal group liquidity and/or external credit lines at the group level. If GTI’s cost of funds for USD financing were, illustratively, LIBOR + 3% (consistent with access to group-level credit), lending to UEP at LIBOR + 5.3% would imply a gross margin of approximately 2.3%. This spread is broadly consistent with treasury margins observed for intra-group lending, covering administrative costs, funding and credit risk buffers, and a reasonable profit element.
For the 9% fixed-rate loan, comparing to GTI’s likely USD funding cost over time similarly suggests a reasonable margin that is not excessive given Pakistan risk and the unsecured nature of the exposure.
Accordingly, the cost-plus cross-check supports the CUP conclusion that GTI earned a reasonable, not exorbitant, return and that UEP’s interest charges are consistent with arm’s length conditions.
Use of Comparable Data
In benchmarking, a range of comparable uncontrolled price indicators were considered, including published interest rate benchmarks (LIBOR/SOFR, KIBOR), sovereign yield context, and risk premium indicators (including sovereign spreads and CDS proxies). While exact “like-for-like” loan comparables are typically limited in availability (particularly for unsecured USD corporate loans into Pakistan without guarantees), the use of multiple corroborative indicators is consistent with OECD principles for financial transactions and supports the arm’s length assessment.
In addition, UEP’s branch status within UEG implies a level of implicit support that can reasonably influence credit outcomes. OECD guidance explicitly recognizes that group affiliation may uplift a borrower’s standalone credit position and thereby reduce interest rates relative to a purely standalone borrower. This dynamic was considered in interpreting the benchmark outcomes and supports the reasonableness of the interest spreads and fixed rate applied.
Functional Analysis of the Intercompany Loans
In accordance with OECD guidance (Chapter I and the 2020 Chapter X on financial transactions), the functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed by each party were analysed. For lending transactions, economically significant factors include capital provision, credit risk assessment/monitoring, funding cost management, currency exposure, and default risk. These are summarised below for UEP (borrower) and GTI (lender).
GTI (Lender)
GTI’s primary function was to provide financing to UEP. This involves sourcing or allocating funds (either from parent group resources or external credit lines) and entering into and maintaining the loan arrangements. GTI does not operate as an independent commercial bank; it functions as a group treasury/conduit. Accordingly, GTI likely did not perform the same depth of credit underwriting that an unrelated lender would require, relying instead on group oversight and the strategic nature of the Pakistan operations.
GTI nevertheless assumes credit risk on UEP: if UEP were unable to pay interest or principal, GTI (and ultimately UEG) would bear the loss. GTI’s key assets comprise the loan receivables (amounts due from UEP) and any corresponding liabilities (if it borrowed externally to on-lend). GTI also bears exposure linked to foreign exchange and repayment capacity risk because the loans are USD-denominated while UEP’s operational cash flows are substantially linked to PKR dynamics.
The 5.3% spread on the acquisition loan and the fixed 9% rate on the working capital loan can be viewed as GTI’s compensation for funding and credit risk, as well as its treasury role and administrative functions in deploying group capital.
UEP (Borrower)
UEP’s function is to utilise the borrowed funds within its business operations. The acquisition loan financed the purchase of productive upstream assets generating revenue, while the working capital loan supports operating liquidity requirements. UEP is responsible for servicing the debt, paying semi-annual interest and repaying principal as and when agreed (or as cash flows allow).
UEP bears currency and cash flow risk because the debt is USD-denominated while underlying operational revenues and costs are significantly affected by PKR movements. PKR depreciation increases the PKR burden of servicing USD obligations and is therefore a key economic risk for UEP.
As a branch of UEG, there is no separate legal entity that would ordinarily require an external parental guarantee; the parent is inherently exposed through the branch structure. However, implicit support is relevant: UEP’s role within UEG’s broader portfolio supports the expectation that the group would sustain the Pakistan operations, which influences how an independent lender might view credit risk for pricing purposes.
Comparison to Independent Arrangement
An independent lender would typically require robust due diligence, higher spreads, and potentially security over assets, particularly in the 2022 environment. In the related-party arrangement, GTI provided unsecured, subordinated financing with flexible repayment features (particularly on the acquisition loan and the continued rollover of the working capital facility). The absence of strict amortization and covenant enforcement reflects group support and flexibility that may not be available from third-party lenders.
From an accurate delineation perspective, these features indicate certain equity-like characteristics; however, the arrangements are respected as debt for transfer pricing purposes because interest is paid and (in the acquisition loan’s case) principal repayments have been made historically.
Conclusion of Functional Analysis
GTI performs the financing function (capital provision) and assumes key lender risks (credit/default and funding risk), while UEP performs the operating functions using the funds and bears repayment and currency exposure through business performance. No other group entities are involved and no ancillary fees (e.g., guarantee or commitment fees) are charged separately.
Given a straightforward lender/borrower relationship and the nature of remuneration (interest), the CUP method is the most appropriate method to test the arm’s length nature of the interest rates using comparable market interest indicators. A cost-of-funds plus margin perspective is applied as a corroborative cross-check consistent with OECD guidance.
Economic Analysis and Benchmarking – Acquisition Loan (2011)
Loan Characteristics
The acquisition loan was originally USD 570 million and carries interest at LIBOR + 5.3% per annum, applied to six-month USD LIBOR. The loan has no fixed maturity and operates in substance as a long-term shareholder loan with voluntary prepayments. UEP reduced principal to USD 180 million by end-2018 through repayments aligned with cash flows, and the principal remained USD 180 million through 2022.
In 2022, USD LIBOR increased materially, and accordingly the all-in interest rate moved from approximately 5.8% early in the year to approximately 10.1% by year-end, averaging around 7%–8% over the year. The transfer pricing focus is therefore whether the pricing term “LIBOR + 5.3%” is arm’s length for a long-term, unsecured, subordinated USD loan to a Pakistan E&P borrower in the 2022 environment.
Benchmark Selection and CUP Application
The CUP method is applied by identifying or approximating market interest rates for comparable loans. Exact comparable independent USD loans to Pakistan E&P borrowers are limited. Accordingly, multiple benchmark reference points are used, including:
•	PKR interest benchmarks as contextual comparators (KIBOR-linked lending levels) with appropriate caution due to currency differences;
•	Sovereign USD yield context and country risk indicators as floor/anchor points for Pakistan exposure;
•	Emerging market lending spreads and risk premia indicative of arm’s length credit spreads in 2022; and
•	A cost-of-funds plus margin cross-check for the lender’s treasury margin.
Based on these corroborative indicators, LIBOR + 5.3% is assessed to fall within an arm’s length range when implicit group support is considered as part of the borrower’s realistic credit position, consistent with OECD guidance.
Conclusion for Acquisition Loan
The acquisition loan interest rate is assessed as arm’s length for 2022. UEP’s interest expense reflects a level that is consistent with market-based pricing for the applicable risk environment and does not indicate excessive profit shifting out of Pakistan. The loan is therefore supportable as debt for transfer pricing purposes, and no adjustment is proposed.
Economic Analysis and Benchmarking – Working Capital Loan (2015)
Loan Characteristics
The working capital loan is a USD 89.4 million facility carrying a fixed interest rate of 9% per annum. Although structured as a short-term revolving facility renewed annually, it has been rolled over through 2022 with no principal repayments, making it economically long-standing. UEP pays semi-annual interest, and the principal balance remains constant in USD terms.
Benchmarking the 9% Rate
The 9% rate is evaluated both at inception (2015) and in the prevailing 2022 context.
•	At inception (2015): USD benchmarks were near zero, but Pakistan risk was elevated relative to global markets. A 9% fixed USD rate was conservative in absolute terms, yet broadly comparable to local PKR borrowing costs around that period and consistent with the risk dynamics applicable to USD lending into Pakistan.

•	During 2022: With global USD benchmarks increasing materially and Pakistan risk premia elevated, independent USD lending into Pakistan in 2022 would commonly be expected to price in double digits absent strong collateral or support. Against that context, the 9% fixed rate is not excessive and is within a plausible arm’s length range, particularly when implicit group support is considered as part of the credit analysis.
Method and Delineation Considerations
CUP is applied by reference to market indicators and risk context. The continued rollover and lack of amortisation reflects group flexibility; however, interest is paid and the facility is contractually renewed. Accordingly, the arrangement is treated as bona fide debt for transfer pricing purposes, while recognising that its flexibility is linked to group relationship dynamics.
Conclusion for Working Capital Loan
The fixed 9% rate is assessed as arm’s length (and not above arm’s length) in the 2022 context. From a Pakistan transfer pricing perspective, the rate does not indicate excessive interest expense or base erosion. Accordingly, no adjustment is proposed.

Compliance with OECD Guidelines and Pakistan TP Regulations
OECD Guidelines
The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (including the 2020 financial transactions guidance) require consideration of contractual terms, borrower creditworthiness, economic environment, and implicit group support in determining an arm’s length interest rate. The analysis in this report reflects these elements through (i) delineation of loan terms; (ii) qualitative assessment of UEP’s risk profile and group support; and (iii) benchmarking using base USD benchmarks plus risk-appropriate spreads (consistent with risk-adjusted return concepts). The CUP method is applied as the primary method, with a cost-of-funds plus margin cross-check consistent with OECD guidance for treasury/conduit entities.
Pakistan Transfer Pricing Regulations
Pakistan’s framework (Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and the Income Tax Rules, 2002 including Rule 27M and Rule 27N as updated through S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021) requires taxpayers to maintain local file documentation supporting arm’s length outcomes. This report addresses the core local file expectations for the controlled financing transactions, including background, transaction terms, functional analysis, method selection rationale, benchmarking support, and conclusions.
Thin Capitalization
Pakistan’s thin capitalization rule (Section 106) disallows interest deductions for foreign-controlled resident companies where the debt-to-equity ratio exceeds prescribed thresholds. UEP is a branch structure and may not fall squarely within the resident-company framing; however, the file recognizes the broader deductibility context. The intercompany loans constitute the principal related-party financing charges, and documentation (including key extracts) has been maintained to support the interest position and compliance.
Conclusion
Based on the detailed analysis of UEP’s two intercompany loans, the interest rates and related terms are assessed to conform to the arm’s length standard for the 2022 tax year. The acquisition loan pricing (LIBOR + 5.3%) is supported as reasonable given Pakistan’s risk profile and the macroeconomic environment in 2022, particularly when implicit group support is considered. The working capital loan’s fixed 9% rate remains within an acceptable range in the 2022 context and is not excessive relative to external alternatives.
Neither loan results in an excessive interest burden that would unduly reduce UEP’s taxable profits in Pakistan. The functional analysis supports the delineation of the transactions as financing arrangements with interest remuneration tested under CUP, corroborated by a cost-of-funds plus margin perspective. Documentation requirements under Pakistani law have been addressed through this Local File and supporting appendices.
UEP should continue to monitor market conditions and periodically review intercompany financing terms to ensure ongoing alignment with arm’s length conditions, documenting any changes where required.
Appendices
Appendix A: Group Structure and Ownership
UEP is a branch (permanent establishment) of United Energy Group Limited (UEG), Hong Kong. UEG owns 100% of the Pakistan branch operations. Gold Trade International (GTI) is a wholly-owned affiliate used as a financing vehicle. The figure below (repeated from the overview) depicts the relationships:
 
Figure A.1: UEG Group Structure – UEG (Hong Kong) as parent; GTI (affiliate, jurisdiction not disclosed, used for intercompany financing); UEP (Pakistan Branch). Solid lines denote ownership/control, dashed line denotes loan transactions.
UEG as a whole is majority-owned (71.7%) by Mr. Zhang Hongwei (as of 2013). UEG’s Pakistan branch (UEP) constitutes a major part of its production operations. All entities are under common control and are “associates” per Pakistani law. UEP’s financial statements consolidate into UEG’s accounts. There were no other related-party transactions in 2022 aside from the loans discussed.
Appendix B: Key Loan Agreement Extracts
This section provides key terms extracted from the intercompany loan agreements (translated/summarized from the signed contracts):
44.	2011 Acquisition Loan Agreement (signed 16 Sept 2011 between GTI and UEG – Pakistan Branch): Principal amount USD 570,000,000. Interest: “Interest on the Loan for each Interest Period shall be LIBOR plus 5.3% per annum…” (Clause 3.2). Interest Period defined as six months (Clause 3.1), with interest payable semi-annually on June 30 and Dec 31. No fixed maturity date; the loan is repayable on demand or as agreed. Prepayment: Borrower may prepay without penalty (Clause 3.3). Governing law: English law. Purpose: Acquisition financing (recital). No security, no guarantor (the loan is unsecured).
45.	2015 Working Capital Loan Agreement (signed 02 Jan 2015 between GTI and UEG – Pakistan Branch): Principal amount USD 89,400,000 (facility limit). Interest: fixed at 9.0% per annum on outstanding principal (Clause 3.2). Interest Period of six months, payable semi-annually. Original term 12 months; the agreement has been extended annually via amendment letters (on similar terms each year). Purpose: “to finance the working capital needs of the Borrower” (Clause 2.1). No security. Governing law: English law. Notably, no provision for rate adjustment is included; any market changes would require amending the contract, which did not occur through 2022.
The full agreements are maintained on file. These extracts reflect the critical pricing terms (5.3% margin and 9% fixed) analysed in this Local File. The lack of a set maturity in the 2011 loan was considered in delineation (long-term quasi-equity characteristics for analysis purposes, while remaining legal debt).
Appendix C: Loan Transaction History (Balances and Exchange Rates)
UEP’s audited financial statements report the intercompany loan balances each year. The table below shows principal balances and PKR equivalents from 2011–2022 as compiled from UEP’s records:
Table C.1: Intercompany Loan Balances – USD principal and PKR equivalent (at year-end exchange rates)
Period / Year	GTI Acquisition Loan – USD	GTI Acquisition Loan – PKR	GTI Working Capital Loan – USD	GTI Working Capital Loan – PKR
Jul 2011 (loan start)	570,000,000	53,523,000,000	–	–
Dec 2012 (after 18 mo)	570,000,000	55,347,000,000	0 (not yet taken)	0
2013	560,000,000	58,968,000,000	0	0
2014	500,000,000	50,100,000,000	0	0
2015 (WC loan begins)	420,000,000	44,041,200,000	89,400,000	9,374,484,000
2016	340,000,000	35,611,800,000	89,400,000	9,363,756,000
2017	260,000,000	28,620,800,000	89,400,000	9,841,152,000
2018	180,000,000	24,944,400,000	89,400,000	12,389,052,000
2019	180,000,000	27,783,000,000	89,400,000	13,798,890,000
2020	180,000,000	28,510,200,000	89,400,000	14,160,066,000
2021	180,000,000	31,541,400,000	89,400,000	15,665,562,000
2022	180,000,000	40,536,000,000	89,400,000	20,132,880,000
Observations: The acquisition loan was significantly paid down between 2014–2018 (from USD 500 million to USD 180 million). Since 2018, the USD principal has remained at USD 180 million. The PKR equivalent increased from PKR 24.94 billion in 2018 to PKR 40.54 billion in 2022 due solely to PKR depreciation. The working capital loan has remained at USD 89.4 million since inception; its PKR equivalent more than doubled from PKR 9.37 billion in 2015 to PKR 20.13 billion in 2022, again reflecting currency changes. Interest is settled in cash (not capitalised), hence principal remains static when not repaid.
Appendix D: Benchmark Data and Sources
To support benchmarking, relevant market data was gathered from credible sources (central bank statistics, financial databases, and publications). Key data points and sources include Pakistan interest benchmarks (SBP / PACRA), USD LIBOR history (market data sources), sovereign yields and risk proxies (Eurobond yields / CDS context), regional comparators, and OECD financial transactions guidance (Chapter X).
Transfer Pricing Method Selection Discussion
Applicable TP Methods for Intra-Group Loans
Under Pakistan’s rules (aligned with OECD methods), several transfer pricing methods may be applied to financing transactions, including CUP and Cost Plus. For intercompany loans, CUP is generally the most direct and preferred approach, as it compares the controlled interest rate against market interest outcomes observed in comparable uncontrolled transactions or reliable market proxies.
In the absence of exact loan comparables, and to corroborate CUP results, a cost-of-funds plus margin approach is also recognised under OECD Chapter X, particularly where the lender acts as a treasury/conduit entity. This approach was used as a cross-check alongside CUP.
Other transactional methods (TNMM, profit split) are generally not suitable for plain-vanilla financing arrangements where the remuneration is interest and the transaction is economically homogeneous. Accordingly, CUP (supported by cost-of-funds) was selected as the most appropriate and defensible approach for UEP’s intercompany loans.
Criteria and Rationale for Method Selection
The method selection reflects: (i) the nature of transactions (straightforward debt financing); (ii) the availability of relevant 2022 interest benchmarks and risk indicators; (iii) the sector and country risk context; (iv) the relevance of implicit group support in determining credit outcomes; and (v) the need for transparent and objective support consistent with local expectations and OECD guidance.
Compliance and Regulatory Framing
The analysis in this report is framed within OECD Chapter X (financial transactions) and Pakistan’s transfer pricing framework under Section 108 and Rule 27M/27N (as updated). The report documents delineation, method selection, benchmarking support, and conclusions demonstrating arm’s length outcomes for UEP’s controlled financing transactions for 2022, consistent with documentation expectations under S.R.O. 1179(I)/2021.

**Subject:** Response to Notice under Section 122(9) read with Section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Tax Year 2020  
**Name:** Elengy Terminal Pakistan Limited  
**NTN:** 4121797  

We refer to the captioned notice issued under section 122(9) read with section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”) for Tax Year 2020. At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the issues now sought to be examined through the subject notice have already been taken up through amendment proceedings under section 122(5A), adjudicated through an amended assessment order, and thereafter carried in appeal up to the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (“ATIR”), with the matter presently standing remanded to the assessing officer for re-adjudication. In these circumstances, initiation of fresh / parallel proceedings on the same point(s) is neither warranted nor consistent with the scheme of the Ordinance.

By way of background, the Company’s return for Tax Year 2020 was e-filed on November 17, 2020 and was deemed assessed under section 120 of the Ordinance. Thereafter, the Tax Office initiated amendment proceedings and ultimately framed an **Amended Assessment Order dated May 18, 2021 under section 122(5A)**. Through the said order, the returned loss was disturbed and taxable income / demand was created by, inter alia, denying the loss position taken in the Group Return (by treating the return on a standalone basis), reclassifying profit on debt as income taxable under section 39, taxing inter-corporate dividend earlier claimed as exempt, and disallowing certain taxes paid. It is material to note that these adjustments were in substance rooted in the Tax Office’s position regarding the rejection / non-recognition of the Company’s group taxation status under section 59AA, and therefore the very subject matter presently raised already stood examined and concluded through the aforesaid amendment proceedings.

Aggrieved, the Company preferred an appeal before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) under section 129 of the Ordinance. In parallel, and in view of the ongoing litigation on the group taxation issue, the Company also sought protection against coercive action, and stay was granted by the ATIR in respect of the issues emanating from the amendment proceedings (including the matter relating to taxation of inter-corporate dividend linked with the rejection of group status) vide MA (Stay) No. 213/KB/2021 in ITA No. 718/KB/2019 dated March 31, 2021. Thereafter, no further adverse action was taken by the Tax Office on the said issues during the subsistence of appellate proceedings.

The appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) was initially dismissed for non-prosecution vide order dated August 29, 2023. The Company, however, challenged the said dismissal before the ATIR under section 132 of the Ordinance. The ATIR, vide order dated October 30, 2023 passed in ITA No. 2496/KB/2023, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) and remanded the matter with explicit directions to decide the appeal afresh by passing a speaking order after considering the Company’s grounds and submissions.

Pursuant to the directions of the ATIR, the Company filed comprehensive written submissions along with supporting documentation before the Commissioner (Appeals) and attended hearings to explain the factual and legal position. Resultantly, the Commissioner (Appeals), vide order dated January 18, 2024, **remanded the matter back to the assessing officer for re-adjudication**, directing that the issues be examined afresh after considering the Company’s submissions and the record.

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the very issues forming the basis of the subject notice already stand covered by concluded amendment proceedings under section 122(5A), and the resultant amended assessment has travelled through the appellate fora culminating in a remand for re-adjudication. The matter is, therefore, presently pending before the assessing officer in remand proceedings, and any attempt to re-initiate proceedings through a fresh notice under section 122(9) on the same subject would amount to duplication of proceedings and is inconsistent with the principles of judicial discipline and orderly tax administration.

Accordingly, it is respectfully requested that the subject notice proceedings may kindly be dropped / kept in abeyance, and the matter, if at all, may be dealt with strictly within the scope of the remand proceedings already directed by the appellate authority.

This submission is made without prejudice to any other rights, remedies and contentions of the Company available under the law.

Yours faithfully,  
**For Elengy Terminal Pakistan Limited**
