# Transfer Pricing Local File – Financial Environment for FY2019 and FY2023 ## FY2019 (Tax Year 2020): Economic and Financial Conditions **USD Interest Rates (LIBOR):** U.S. dollar interest rates eased during 2019. The 3-month USD LIBOR opened the year near **2.8%** and fell to about **1.9%** by December 2019【9†L977-L985】【9†L986-L989】. This decline reflected the U.S. Federal Reserve’s pivot to rate cuts in mid-2019 – the Fed reduced its benchmark rate from ~2.5% to ~1.75% over the year, easing global dollar funding costs. Lower USD LIBOR meant the base rate for the acquisition loan (LIBOR + 5.3%) also fell, with UEP’s floating interest margin added on top. For example, a LIBOR of ~2.5% in early 2019 implied about a 7.8% all-in rate, whereas by late 2019 the all-in rate had dropped to ~7.2%, all else equal. **PKR Interest Rates (KIBOR & Lending):** In contrast, Pakistani rupee interest rates **rose sharply** in 2019 as the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) tightened monetary policy to counter high inflation. SBP hiked its benchmark rate to **13.25%** (an 8-year high) by July 2019【12†L188-L196】. Consequently, the 6-month KIBOR (Karachi Interbank Offered Rate) climbed into the **13–14%** range by late 2019 (up from single digits in 2018). Local PKR lending rates for corporations (typically KIBOR plus a credit spread) moved well into the mid-teens. In early 2019, KIBOR was still in the 10–11% range, but by Q4 2019 it exceeded 13%, meaning typical PKR-denominated working capital loans were charging on the order of **14–15%** interest. These high local rates underscore Pakistan’s tight monetary conditions in 2019, against which UEP’s USD loan rates (around 7–8% in 2019) were significantly lower on a nominal basis. **Pakistan Sovereign Credit Risk:** Pakistan’s sovereign risk profile in 2019 was strained but saw **some improvement** after a mid-year IMF bailout. The country’s credit ratings remained in the single-**B** speculative grade (Moody’s **B3**, S&P **B-**)【27†L83-L91】【27†L95-L100】. Yields on Pakistan’s USD bonds, which had spiked in 2018, stabilized in 2019. By late 2019, Pakistan’s Eurobond spread over U.S. Treasuries (EMBI Global index) had narrowed to around **420 basis points**, down from ~582 bps at end-2018 as investor confidence tentatively improved with the IMF program【27†L83-L91】. While still high, this spread moderation indicated a slightly lower perceived default risk than the prior year. No sovereign rating upgrades occurred (Moody’s maintained a negative outlook through 2019), but the successful IMF agreement and fiscal tightening helped contain further deterioration. Overall, Pakistan was viewed as a high-risk borrower in 2019, requiring significant risk premiums on any new debt, though outright default fears were not as acute as in later years. **Domestic Macroeconomic Indicators:** 2019 was a year of **macroeconomic adjustment** for Pakistan. GDP growth slowed to around **3%** (and would fall below 2% in FY2020) amid fiscal austerity and high interest rates. Inflation surged into double digits – averaging about **10–11%** in 2019 and reaching ~12.6% year-on-year by Dec 2019【57†L69-L77】 – driven by a steep rupee depreciation and energy tariff hikes. To counter price pressures, the SBP kept real interest rates positive, holding the policy rate at 13.25% into year-end 2019【57†L75-L83】. The Pakistani rupee was moved to a market-determined exchange rate under the IMF program, resulting in a sharp drop in its value. The PKR fell from ~PKR 139 per USD in January to about **PKR 155 per USD** by December 2019【17†L1-L4】. (In June 2019 it briefly hit a low around PKR 163 before stabilizing【16†L1-L4】.) This ~11% annual depreciation (and ~30% cumulative drop from early 2018 levels) increased the local-currency burden of UEP’s USD loans. Pakistan’s external imbalances showed improvement by late 2019 – the current account deficit narrowed substantially and foreign reserves stabilized with IMF support. However, the combination of high inflation, a weakened currency, and tight monetary policy underscored the **elevated country risk** facing any lender to a Pakistan-based borrower in 2019. **Global Financing Environment:** The global credit environment in 2019 was relatively benign. Major central banks turned dovish – notably, the U.S. Fed’s rate cuts eased global liquidity and improved emerging-market sentiment【18†L57-L62】. By late 2019, global interest rates and yields were on a downtrend. U.S. 10-year Treasury yields fell below 2% (from ~2.7% in January 2019), and U.S. high-yield credit spreads narrowed as recession fears abated. This accommodative backdrop meant **lower base rates** for USD financing and plenty of investor appetite for emerging-market debt, which likely helped Pakistan roll over its external funding in 2019. Indeed, Pakistan’s successful Eurobond/Sukuk issuances around that time (e.g. a 5-year Sukuk at ~6.75% in late 2018) benefited from the global hunt for yield. In summary, 2019 saw **easier global financial conditions** compared to 2018, partially offsetting Pakistan’s country-specific risks. For transfer pricing purposes, the global low-interest environment in 2019 would tend to keep USD loan rates (like LIBOR + 5.3%) on the lower side of historical ranges. **Oil & Gas Industry Context:** The upstream oil & gas sector in 2019 experienced stable but subdued conditions. Brent crude oil prices averaged about **$64/barrel** for the year【48†L607-L614】, fluctuating roughly between $55 and $75. There were no extreme spikes in 2019 – prices were lower than in 2018 (which averaged $71) amid adequate global supply. This moderate price level provided **steady cash flows** for oil producers, though not windfall profits. Industry investment was recovering from the mid-2010s downturn but remained cautious. Global upstream capital expenditures in 2019 were on the order of ~$500 billion, still below the pre-2014 peak levels【54†L115-L123】【55†L78-L86】. Many oil majors continued to prioritize capital discipline, focusing on shareholder returns over aggressive expansion. For a Pakistan E&P business like UEP, the stable oil price meant its operational cash generation in 2019 was decent, though the company faced local challenges (e.g. security costs, regulatory issues). Upstream investment in Pakistan itself was limited in 2019, with few new fields being developed. Overall, the oil market environment in 2019 was **neutral**: it did not create additional stress for UEP (as prices were not crashing), but it also did not provide a significantly higher revenue that might have improved UEP’s credit profile. A **summary of key 2019 indicators** is provided below:
Indicator (2019)Value / Trend
**3M USD LIBOR** (Jan→Dec 2019)Dropped from ~2.8% to ~1.9%【9†L977-L985】【9†L986-L989】 as Fed cut rates
**6M KIBOR** (PKR)Rose to ~13.5% by late 2019 (from ~10% in 2018) as SBP hiked policy rate to 13.25%【12†L188-L196】
**SBP Policy Interest Rate**13.25% (July–Dec 2019), up 750 bps since Jan 2018【12†L208-L216】
**Inflation (CPI)**~11% average in 2019; ~12.6% YoY in Dec 2019【57†L69-L77】 (multi-year high)
**PKR/USD Exchange Rate**PKR ~139 → 155 over 2019 (≈11% depreciation)【17†L1-L4】; flexible exchange rate adopted【12†L231-L239】
**Sovereign Credit Rating**B3 (Moody’s); B- (S&P) – highly speculative grade【27†L95-L100】
**Sovereign Yield Spread**~420 bps EMBI spread by late 2019 (narrowed from ~582 bps in 2018)【27†L83-L91】
**Brent Crude Oil Price**Avg ~$64/bbl【48†L607-L614】; range ~$55–$75; stable demand/supply
*Insight:* In 2019, UEP’s intercompany loans (at ~7–9% USD interest) were incurred in a period of **low global USD rates but high local PKR rates and country risk**. An arm’s length lender to a Pakistan entity would demand a hefty country risk spread (given double-digit local rates and B3/B- credit rating), which supports the **LIBOR + 5.3%** margin on the long-term loan. The working capital loan’s fixed 9% USD rate in 2019 was also reasonable relative to PKR borrowing costs (teens) and Pakistan’s sovereign yields (which were 8–10% on USD bonds) – indicating it was not excessive from a transfer pricing standpoint. --- ## FY2023 (Tax Year 2024): Economic and Financial Conditions **USD Interest Rates (LIBOR):** By 2023 the interest rate picture had reversed, with global rates at their highest in over a decade. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s fight against inflation in 2022–2023 drove USD benchmarks sharply upward. The 3-month USD LIBOR surged from around **0.3% in early 2022** to about **5.5% by mid-2023**【9†L1085-L1093】【9†L1101-L1108】. During calendar 2023, 3M LIBOR fluctuated roughly in the **4.8%–5.5%** range – for instance, averaging ~5.3% in H1 2023【9†L1101-L1108】. (LIBOR was phased out after June 2023, with SOFR as its successor, but the legacy loan still formally referenced LIBOR.) This steep rise in base rates meant UEP’s floating acquisition loan carried a **much higher all-in interest rate** in 2023 (LIBOR + 5.3% = roughly 10.5%–11% by mid-year) compared to prior years. Even the fixed-rate working capital loan at 9% became relatively cheap in USD terms given that 6-month US dollar SOFR was around 5.5%. In summary, **2023’s global interest rate environment was tight**, putting upward pressure on arm’s length interest expectations for USD loans. **PKR Interest Rates (KIBOR & Lending):** Domestic interest rates in Pakistan **spiked to record levels** in 2023 amid severe inflation and monetary tightening. The SBP raised its policy rate to an all-time high of **21% by April 2023** and further to **22% by June 2023**【59†L51-L58】【61†L81-L89】. As a result, 6-month KIBOR soared above **22%** (from ~11% just two years prior【5†L1-L9】). By late 2023, 6M KIBOR hovered in the 22–23% range, and even short-term PKR T-bill yields were ~20–22%. **Corporate borrowing rates in PKR** routinely exceeded **+24% nominal** (e.g. a typical loan at KIBOR + 2% would be ~24% or more). These are extraordinarily high financing costs, reflecting the acute domestic conditions. For context, Pakistan’s inflation-adjusted **real interest rate** was barely positive despite the high nominal rates, given inflation running 25–35%. Such expensive local credit made UEP’s USD-denominated funding even more critical. The intercompany loans at single-digit USD rates (9–11%) were a **bargain** relative to any PKR alternatives in 2023 (which were double that in percentage terms). In arm’s length analysis, one must consider that an independent lender to a Pakistani borrower in 2023 would likely price a USD loan with a substantial risk premium – easily pushing all-in rates into the teens – consistent with the distressed local credit environment. **Pakistan Sovereign Credit Risk:** Pakistan’s sovereign risk in 2023 deteriorated to **extremely high levels**, approaching default territory. Amid a balance-of-payments crisis and stalled IMF program, credit rating agencies sharply downgraded Pakistan. In February 2023, Moody’s cut Pakistan’s rating two notches to **Caa3**, citing “increasingly fragile liquidity” and elevated default risk【34†L180-L188】【34†L199-L207】 – the lowest rating Pakistan had seen in decades. S&P and Fitch around the same time kept Pakistan in the CCC range (around CCC+/CCC), also indicating imminent default risk. Sovereign bond markets reflected this distress: Pakistan’s international bonds traded at deep discounts. For example, a US$1 billion Eurobond due April 2024 traded around **46 cents on the dollar** in March 2023, implying a yield over **100%**【37†L48-L56】【37†L66-L74】. Earlier, in late 2022, a 2025 maturity bond had even implied yields of 70–80+%. Five-year credit default swap (CDS) spreads spiked above **5,000 basis points** (50% upfront insurance cost) during 2022, and remained extremely high in H1 2023 – only easing after mid-2023 when a last-minute IMF deal was secured. By mid-2023, Pakistan was widely seen as at risk of defaulting on external debt absent urgent refinancing. (Indeed, in July 2023 Pakistan narrowly avoided default by securing a new IMF Stand-By Arrangement.) **Country risk premiums were thus extraordinarily high** during 2023: any arm’s length USD lending to a Pakistani obligor would have demanded a very large spread. This validates that an interest margin of +5.3% (as on UEP’s acquisition loan) was, if anything, on the low end given Pakistan’s **Caa3/CCC credit** profile in 2023. The sovereign’s own US$ bonds traded at yields in the ~20–30% range for medium-term tenors, whereas UEP was paying roughly 11% – consistent with implicit parent support mitigating some risk, but still within a plausible arm’s length range considering security and tenure differences. By late 2023, there were glimmers of stabilization – Pakistan averted default and even saw its 5-year CDS fall below 3,000 bps after IMF disbursement, with rating outlooks stabilizing【35†L102-L110】. However, throughout the 2023 year in review, Pakistan remained one of the **riskiest sovereign credits** globally, an essential factor in benchmarking intercompany loan rates. **Domestic Macroeconomic Indicators:** The Pakistani economy in 2023 was in **crisis mode**, markedly worse than in 2019. Inflation hit its highest levels on record – consumer prices were up **36.4% year-on-year in April 2023** (and nearly 38% in May), the steepest inflation in Pakistan’s history【59†L38-L46】. Average CPI inflation for full-year 2023 is estimated around 29–30%, compared to ~10% in 2019. This surge was driven by subsidy removals, supply shocks (flood impacts, import restrictions), and the massive rupee depreciation. The Pakistani rupee lost about **28% of its value against the dollar in FY23** alone【61†L53-L61】. The USD/PKR rate, which was ~175 at end-2021 and ~226 at end-2022, collapsed to around **PKR 285 per USD by June 2023**【61†L61-L69】 (briefly trading above PKR 300 in the open market in Q3 2023). By Dec 2023, the rupee was near 280 (having recovered slightly from all-time lows after currency controls were tightened). This depreciation drastically inflated the PKR equivalent of UEP’s USD debt – for instance, each $1 of loan translated to ~PKR 280+ by 2023, double the rupee cost compared to a few years prior. GDP growth turned negative: Pakistan’s real GDP growth for FY2023 was around **0%** (officially +0.3%【61†L71-L79】, essentially stagnation), a sharp drop from ~6% just a year earlier. The country was forced to curtail imports severely due to dollar shortages, causing an industrial slowdown. Interest rate hikes to 22% helped cool domestic demand but at the cost of private sector credit and investment. Unemployment and poverty metrics worsened under the stress. In summary, **macroeconomic stability eroded in 2023** – inflation was out of control, the currency was in free-fall for much of the year, and policy tightening reached extremes. Any lender would view a Pakistan borrower in 2023 as facing acute macro risks (exchange risk, policy risk, etc.), justifying high risk premiums or conservative loan terms. **Global Financing Environment:** Globally, 2023 was characterized by **tight monetary policy and cautious credit markets**. The U.S. Federal Reserve had rapidly raised the Fed Funds rate from near zero in 2021 to ~5.25% by May 2023 – the fastest hiking cycle in decades – in order to tame inflation. This pushed up base rates worldwide: USD SOFR and LIBOR were in the 5%+ range, Eurozone and UK rates were also climbing, and global bond yields rose. By 2023, financing costs in hard currency had increased substantially for all borrowers. Moreover, 2022’s geopolitical shocks (e.g. the Russia-Ukraine war) had led to wider credit spreads, especially for lower-rated issuers. Early in 2023, **global credit spreads** remained elevated (reflecting recession fears and risk aversion), and investors demanded extra yield to hold emerging-market debt. Frontier market issuers like Pakistan found themselves effectively shut out of capital markets during this period. However, later in 2023, there was some improvement in global risk sentiment: U.S. inflation began cooling and the Fed paused rate hikes, prompting hopes that global rates had peaked. By Q4 2023, many emerging market bonds saw spreads tighten and prices rally from distressed levels【35†L98-L107】. For example, some of the riskiest sovereign bonds (Pakistan included) saw significant price gains in late 2023 as default risk perceptions ebbed slightly and investors speculated on recovery value【35†L56-L64】【35†L90-L99】. Nonetheless, the **global environment in 2023 was challenging for borrowers**: interest rates were high and liquidity was more selective than in the late-2010s. In transfer pricing terms, the high global rate environment would increase arm’s length interest rates even for intercompany loans – the risk-free component (e.g. U.S. Treasury yield) was much higher in 2023 (~4% for 5-year UST) than in 2019 (~1.5% for 5-year UST). Thus, a fair market rate for a USD loan in 2023 would naturally be higher, even before adding risk spreads, simply due to this shift in global benchmarks. **Oil & Gas Industry Context:** The oil market in 2023 was volatile but favorable overall for producers, which provides important sector context for UEP. Brent crude prices averaged approximately **$82 per barrel** in 2023【52†L330-L338】 – significantly higher than in 2019, though lower than the extraordinary levels of 2022 (which averaged ~$100 due to the post-pandemic surge and the Ukraine war). In the first half of 2023, Brent traded in the $70–85 range as global demand concerns (and Chinese economic softness) kept prices in check. Later in the year, OPEC+ production cuts and war-related supply risks pushed Brent to a peak around the **mid-$90s** in September 2023, before retreating. For upstream companies, 2023’s price level still meant **strong cash flows** – oil firms globally were coming off record 2022 profits and remained generally flush. **Upstream investment** ticked upward accordingly. Industry reports show global upstream oil & gas capital expenditure rose about **10–15% in 2023**, on top of a 39% jump in 2022, reaching around $530–550 billion (near pre-2015 levels)【55†L78-L86】【54†L115-L123】. However, much of the increase went to offset cost inflation (drilling and service costs climbed) and to short-cycle projects; companies remained cautious on mega-projects given price volatility and energy transition uncertainties【54†L125-L134】. In Pakistan, the oil/gas sector faced additional headwinds: companies struggled with payment delays from the government and regulatory hurdles, dampening local upstream investment despite high global oil prices. For UEP as an E&P operator, the high oil price in 2023 was a **positive factor** for its operating performance (increasing revenue in PKR terms especially with a weak rupee). A strong sector outlook generally improves a borrower’s creditworthiness – independent lenders might view an oil company more favorably when oil prices are robust, assuming the company can export or sell at international parity. That said, in Pakistan’s case, currency and repatriation issues partly impeded full benefit. Overall, the **upstream industry outlook in 2023 was relatively strong**, which supports that a 9–11% USD interest rate on intra-group loans would not be out of line – oil sector borrowers globally could secure financing thanks to healthy commodity prices (albeit Pakistan’s country risk would heavily influence the rate). Key economic and market indicators for 2023 are summarized below:
Indicator (2023)Value / Trend
**3M USD LIBOR** (Jan→Jun 2023)Rose from ~4.8% in Jan to ~5.5% by June【9†L1101-L1108】 (highest since 2007)
**6M KIBOR** (PKR)Around 22–23% by late 2023 (up from ~11% in 2021), reflecting SBP policy rate 21–22%【59†L51-L58】【61†L81-L89】
**SBP Policy Interest Rate**22% (June 2023)【61†L81-L89】 – record high, vs. 9% in early 2022
**Inflation (CPI)**~29% avg in 2023; peaked at 36.4% YoY in Apr 2023【59†L38-L46】 (all-time high)
**PKR/USD Exchange Rate**PKR ~226 → 285 in 2023 (≈26% depreciation); hit ~PKR 299/US$ in May 2023【61†L61-L69】【61†L63-L71】
**Sovereign Credit Rating**Caa3 (Moody’s Feb 2023)【34†L180-L188】; CCC+/CCC (S&P/Fitch) – extremely speculative
**Eurobond Yields (2023)**April 2024 bond at ~46¢ (yield ~106%) in Mar 2023【37†L48-L56】【37†L66-L74】; 5-year CDS > 30% p.a.
**Brent Crude Oil Price**Avg ~$82/bbl【52†L330-L338】; range ~$70–95; OPEC+ cuts supported prices
*Insight:* In 2023, Pakistan’s risk profile was extremely high, yet UEP’s intercompany loans were **priced at fixed 9% (USD)** and **floating ~LIBOR+5.3% (~10–11%)**. Given that local interest benchmarks exceeded 20% and sovereign debt was trading at distressed yields, these intra-group rates appear **moderate**. A third-party lender would have likely charged a double-digit USD rate or required collateral/short tenor under such conditions. The fact that UEP continued to pay ~9–11% on USD funding in 2023 suggests the rates were **in line with (or even below) market** expectations for an unsecured, long-term loan to a Pakistan oil & gas borrower (benefiting from group support). This supports the arm’s length nature of the loans: despite the turmoil, the pricing remained within a range that independent lenders might consider (especially since UEP’s oil sector and affiliate backing mitigate some risk). The comprehensive data above demonstrate that the **economic factors of 2019 vs 2023 differ greatly**, but in both cases the intercompany loan rates can be justified as reasonable given prevailing LIBOR, country risk premiums, and industry outlook in each year.

Below is a **drafted response limited strictly to Point Nos. 5 and 9** of the notice issued under section 122(9) for Tax Year 2020. The language is aligned with assessment-stage pleadings and squarely addresses factual errors, legal position, and jurisdictional defects, with clear rebuttal of proposed additions.

---

### **Response to Point No. 5 – Alleged Long-Term Loan under Section 39(3)**

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the figure as well as the very **nature of the liability confronted in Point No. 5 is factually incorrect and misconceived**.

It is clarified that **no long-term loan appears in the audited financial statements** of the Company for the year ended **December 31, 2019**. Contrary to the assertion contained in the notice, the audited accounts reflect the following positions under **current liabilities** only:

- A **loan from a related party amounting to Rs. 315,000,000**, and  
- A **short-term secured borrowing of Rs. 110,000,000**, already explained to your good office in response to **Point No. 4** of the same show cause notice.

Accordingly, the premise that a **long-term loan of Rs. 242,137,524** exists is incorrect, unsupported by the audited accounts, and not borne out from the record.

Without prejudice, it is further submitted that the **closing balance of Rs. 315,000,000** appearing under current liabilities represents a duly explained movement during the year. The **opening balance stood at Rs. 285,000,000**, while **only Rs. 30,000,000 was received during the year**, resulting in the stated closing balance. This reconciliation is fully verifiable from the audited financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2019.

For complete clarity and ready reference, a **copy of the relevant bank statement** evidencing receipt of **Rs. 30,000,000 through proper banking channels** has been enclosed herewith. There is, therefore, **no unexplained credit**, concealment, or unaccounted receipt so as to invoke section 39(3) of the Ordinance.

In view of the above factual clarity and documentary substantiation, the proposed addition under section 39(3) is **wholly unwarranted, legally unsustainable, and liable to be dropped**.

---

### **Response to Point No. 9 – Alleged Unreconciled Bank Receipts under Sections 111 and 39**

At the outset, it is submitted that the approach adopted in Point No. 9 proceeds on an **erroneous legal assumption** that **bank credits, per se, constitute taxable revenue**, which is contrary to settled law.

It is well established through a **consistent line of decisions of higher appellate authorities** that **mere receipts or credits in bank accounts do not automatically represent income**, unless the nature of such receipts is independently established as taxable income. Bank statements are only **movement records** and cannot substitute for income determination under the charging provisions of the Ordinance.

Furthermore, the reliance placed on **section 111(1)(a)** is legally flawed. It is respectfully pointed out that, as settled by the **Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan**, an addition under section 111 cannot be sustained **without initiating independent proceedings under the said provision**, supported by specific confrontation, opportunity, and findings. In the present case, **no separate proceedings under section 111 were ever initiated**, rendering the proposed addition jurisdictionally defective and void.

Without prejudice to the above, the reconciliation prepared in the notice itself suffers from **a fundamental factual error**. The notice incorrectly assumes that the **opening balance of trade receivables is “Nil”**, whereas, as per the **audited financial statements**, the Company had an **opening trade receivable balance of Rs. 91,000,117**, which is clearly disclosed and verifiable from the audited accounts.

This incorrect assumption vitiates the entire reconciliation exercise, and the so-called “unreconciled receipts” figure is therefore **mathematically and conceptually flawed**.

In view of the above legal position, factual inaccuracies, and absence of lawful proceedings under section 111, it is respectfully submitted that **no addition is permissible on account of bank receipts**, and the proposed adjustment under sections 111 and 39 is liable to be **dropped in entirety**.

---

Please find the attached notice and prepare a response relating Point 5 and 9. 

With respect to Point No. 5: Please highlight that the figure and nature confronted in the notice are incorrect. Please note that there is no long-term loan appearing in the audited accounts for the period ended December 31, 2019. However, a loan from a related party of Rs 315,000,000 appears as current liabilities.  Furthermore, a short-term borrowing secured of Rs 110,000,000 also appears as a current liability, which was already explained to your good office vide replying to Point No. 4 of said show cause notice. 

Furthermore, the opening balance of loan from a related party of Rs 285,000,000 was received, and only Rs 30,000,000 was received during the period, resulting in a closing balance of Rs 315,000,000 duly verified from audited accounts for the period ended December 31, 2019. For your ready reference, we enclosed a copy of the relevant bank statement to establish that the loan amount of Rs 30,000,000 was received from the bank channel. Therefore, an addition under section 39(3) is warranted. 

With respect to Point No. 9. Please highlight in the various decision from higher authorities that receipts from bank accounts can't constitute revenue. Furthermore, also highlight that in the Supreme Court of Pakistan decision on section 111 of the Ordinance, no separate proceedings were initiated; therefore, an addition on account of 111 can't be made in the instant case.  

Please highlight an error that there is an alleged reconciliation as well, i.e., the opening balance of trade receivable is 0. However, as per audited accounts, our client have received an opening of Rs 91,000,117, which is duly verifiable from audited accounts.

Below is a **more detailed, refined, and tightly reasoned response**, structured **in continuous paragraphs under clear main headings**, suitable for direct placement in a reply to the notice under section 122(9). The tone, sequencing, and articulation are aligned with assessment-stage litigation standards and appellate defensibility.

---

## **Response to Point No. 5 – Alleged Long-Term Loan and Proposed Addition under Section 39(3)**

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the allegation contained in Point No. 5 of the notice is based on an **incorrect appreciation of both the facts and the audited financial statements** of the Company for the year ended December 31, 2019. The notice proceeds on the assumption that a **long-term loan amounting to Rs. 242,137,524** exists in the accounts, whereas **no such long-term liability appears in the audited accounts for the relevant period**.

It is clarified that, as per the audited financial statements, the Company has disclosed only **current liabilities**, comprising (i) a **loan from a related party amounting to Rs. 315,000,000**, and (ii) a **short-term secured borrowing of Rs. 110,000,000**. There is **no classification of any long-term loan whatsoever**, and therefore the very basis of the confrontation in Point No. 5 is factually misconceived. The short-term secured borrowing of Rs. 110,000,000 has already been duly explained to your good office in response to **Point No. 4** of the same show cause notice, along with its nature and source.

Without prejudice to the above, it is further submitted that the **loan from the related party of Rs. 315,000,000 is fully explained and reconciled**. The opening balance of this loan as at January 1, 2019 stood at **Rs. 285,000,000**, while only **Rs. 30,000,000 was received during the year**, resulting in the closing balance of **Rs. 315,000,000** as reflected in the audited accounts for the period ended December 31, 2019. This movement is clearly disclosed in the financial statements and is fully traceable.

For the sake of completeness and to remove any residual doubt, a **copy of the relevant bank statement** is enclosed, evidencing that the amount of **Rs. 30,000,000 was received through proper banking channels**. There is thus **no unexplained receipt, no anonymous credit, and no element of concealment** that could justify invocation of section 39(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

In these circumstances, where the alleged long-term loan does not exist, and the actual current liabilities are fully explained, reconciled, and supported by audited accounts and bank evidence, any proposed addition under section 39(3) would be **without factual foundation, contrary to record, and legally unsustainable**, and therefore liable to be dropped.

---

## **Response to Point No. 9 – Alleged Unreconciled Bank Credits and Proposed Addition under Sections 111 and 39**

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the approach adopted in Point No. 9 reflects a **fundamental legal misconception**, namely that **aggregate bank credits can, by themselves, be equated with taxable revenue**. It is a settled principle, consistently affirmed by higher appellate fora, that **bank receipts are not synonymous with income**, and that every credit appearing in a bank statement does not automatically assume the character of taxable receipts unless its **nature as income is independently established** under the charging provisions of the Ordinance.

The reliance placed on section 111(1)(a), read with section 39, is equally misplaced. It is respectfully pointed out that the **Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan**, while interpreting section 111 of the Ordinance, has categorically held that an addition under this provision cannot be sustained **unless independent proceedings under section 111 are initiated**, accompanied by proper confrontation, opportunity of explanation, and specific findings. In the present case, **no separate proceedings under section 111 were ever initiated**, and the provision is sought to be invoked merely as a consequential adjustment, which is **impermissible in law**.

Without prejudice to the above legal infirmities, it is further submitted that the **reconciliation prepared in the notice itself is factually erroneous and internally inconsistent**. The notice assumes that the **opening balance of trade receivables is “Nil”**, whereas, as per the audited financial statements, the Company had an **opening trade receivable balance of Rs. 91,000,117**. This figure is clearly disclosed in the audited accounts and is verifiable from the record already available with the Department.

This incorrect assumption materially distorts the entire reconciliation exercise, rendering the resulting figure of alleged “unreconciled receipts” unreliable and unsustainable. Once the correct opening balance of trade receivables is taken into account, the computational basis adopted in the notice collapses, and the proposed difference ceases to exist in its confronted form.

In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that **bank credits, without establishing their revenue nature, cannot be brought to tax**, and that in the absence of independent proceedings under section 111, no addition can lawfully be made on this account. Coupled with the factual errors in the reconciliation itself, the proposed addition under sections 111 and 39 is **devoid of legal authority, contrary to settled jurisprudence, and liable to be dropped in entirety**.

---

In this regard, Rule 27AA read with Rule 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 clearly provides that a Master File is required only where the taxpayer forms part of a multinational enterprise group meeting the **prescribed consolidated group revenue thresholds** and other qualifying conditions for the relevant accounting period.

Based on:
- the taxpayer’s factual profile for the subject tax year,
- the scale and nature of controlled transactions undertaken, and
- the disclosures duly made in the prescribed transfer pricing supplementary form,

the taxpayer **does not fall within the category of persons required to prepare or furnish a Master File for Tax Year 2023**.

To evidence the above position, we enclose the duly completed **Supplementary Transfer Pricing Form (S2)**, which forms an integral part of the return and statutorily captures the determination regarding applicability of Master File and related documentation requirements fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file2.

Accordingly, in terms of the governing statutory framework, **the requirement of submission of a Master File does not arise in the present case**.

---

### 2. **Local File – Compliance**

Without prejudice to the above, and in full compliance with section 108(3) of the Ordinance read with Rule 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002, we enclose herewith the **Transfer Pricing Local File for Tax Year 2023**.

The Local File has been prepared in accordance with the prescribed contents and documentation requirements and contains, inter alia:
- details of the associated enterprises and controlled transactions,
- functional and economic analysis,
- selection and application of the most appropriate transfer pricing method, and
- benchmarking analysis supporting arm’s length outcomes.

---

### 3. **Conclusion**

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that:
- the taxpayer has duly complied with the **Local File documentation and furnishing requirements** under the Ordinance; and
- the **Master File requirement is not applicable** for the subject tax year in terms of the statutory thresholds and rules.

The above submissions are made in good faith and in strict conformity with the applicable provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and the Income Tax Rules, 2002.

:::writing{id="73425" variant="email" subject="Section 161(1) Order – Specific Breakdown of Tax Demand and Targeted Appellate Strategy | Tax Year 2020"}
Dear [Client Name],

Further to our earlier emails, we set out below a **more specific and transaction-level discussion of the tax demand created under the order passed u/s 161(1) for Tax Year 2020**, together with our **focused course of action to contest the same before the Commissioner (Appeals)** fileciteturn1file0.

---

### 1. Statutory Basis of the Demand

The impugned order has been passed under **section 161(1)** by treating the Company as an *assessee in default* on the premise that tax was allegedly **not deducted / not deposited at source** on certain payments made during the year. Consequential **default surcharge** has also been levied up to the date of the order.

It is important to note that section 161 proceedings are **not charging provisions**; they are *purely consequential* and can only survive if:
- a clear withholding obligation exists under a specific section,
- the nature of payment squarely falls within that section, and
- non-deduction is established on facts.

Our position is that these essential conditions have not been satisfied in the present case.

---

### 2. Specific Components of the Tax Demand

Based on our review of the order, the demand broadly emanates from the following areas:

#### (a) **Salary, Wages and Employee-Related Costs**

A substantial portion of the demand has been raised by treating **gross salary and wage expense** as a withholding default. This approach is fundamentally flawed.

The Company operates a **payroll-based taxation mechanism**, where:
- tax on salaries is deducted under section 149 at the time of payment,
- annual salary tax workings are prepared,
- withholding is deposited through CPRs, and
- salaries are reported through prescribed withholding statements.

The order does not identify **any specific employee, payment, or shortfall**. Instead, it relies on aggregate expense figures extracted from IRIS and proceeds on a presumption of non-compliance. Such an approach is contrary to law and repeatedly disapproved by appellate fora.

**Appellate focus:**  
We will demonstrate full payroll compliance through salary tax workings, CPRs, and reconciliation with audited accounts, establishing that section 161 cannot be invoked on a gross or presumptive basis.

---

#### (b) **Manufacturing Expenses**

Manufacturing expenses have been treated as a homogeneous block and subjected to withholding assumptions under section 153, without appreciating their **composite nature**.

These expenses typically include:
- raw material consumption,
- utilities,
- in-house labor,
- repairs and maintenance,
- consumables, and
- internal allocations.

Many of these items **do not constitute “payments for services”**, nor do they involve third-party service providers triggering withholding obligations. The order fails to segregate:
- service vs. non-service components,
- third-party payments vs. internal costs, and
- taxable vs. non-taxable heads.

**Appellate focus:**  
We will establish that withholding provisions cannot be applied to manufacturing expenses in gross and that only **identifiable, qualifying service payments** (if any) can be examined — not aggregated ledger balances.

---

#### (c) **Selling, Distribution and Administrative Expenses**

The order proceeds on the assumption that selling and administrative expenses are automatically subject to withholding, without:
- identifying the nature of individual payments,
- specifying the applicable withholding section,
- addressing thresholds, exemptions, or exclusions.

Expenses such as freight reimbursements, statutory payments, utilities, marketing costs, and routine administrative outlays have been lumped together and treated as withholding defaults, which is legally untenable.

**Appellate focus:**  
We will demonstrate that:
- many payments fall outside the scope of withholding altogether,
- others are either exempt or below thresholds, and
- several items represent reimbursements or non-service payments.

---

#### (d) **Mechanical Levy of Default Surcharge**

Default surcharge has been levied **automatically and consequentially**, without examining:
- whether a valid withholding default exists in the first place,
- whether the alleged non-deduction arose from a bona fide legal interpretation, and
- whether the demand itself is sustainable.

Since surcharge is **accessory to the principal demand**, it cannot survive independently.

**Appellate focus:**  
Deletion of principal demand will automatically nullify surcharge; alternatively, surcharge is not leviable where no willful default is established.

---

### 3. Core Legal Weakness in the Order

At its heart, the order suffers from a **structural legal defect**:  
It attempts to convert **accounting disclosures and IRIS-based summaries** into withholding defaults, without first establishing the statutory trigger for deduction.

Settled jurisprudence holds that:
- withholding tax cannot be imposed by inference or approximation,
- section 161 cannot be invoked on aggregated expense figures, and
- the burden lies on the department to demonstrate a **specific, identifiable default**.

---

### 4. Targeted Course of Action

In light of the above, our proposed course of action is as follows:

1. **File a detailed appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals)** within limitation, challenging the order both on jurisdiction and merits.
2. **Issue-wise rebuttal**, addressing each expense category separately rather than on an aggregated basis.
3. **Document-driven defence**, including payroll records, CPRs, audited schedules, and nature-of-expense explanations.
4. **Seek recovery protection**, if required, once the recovery posture of the department becomes clear.
5. **No voluntary payment recommended** at this stage, given the strength of the case and arguable legal position.

---

### 5. Way Forward

We are in the process of structuring the appeal to directly address the weaknesses identified above and to position the case for full relief at the first appellate stage. Draft grounds and a statement of facts will be shared shortly for your review.

This demand is **contestable on strong legal and factual footing**, and the appellate remedy is both appropriate and proportionate in the circumstances.

Warm regards,  
Zuhair

Dear [Client Name],

We write to apprise you that the tax authorities have now passed the **order under section 122(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2020**, a copy of which is enclosed for your reference fileciteturn0file0.

At the outset, we are pleased to confirm that **the proceedings have been concluded in full alignment with the originally filed return**, and no adverse adjustment, disallowance, or addition has been made. This outcome has been achieved **after rigorous and sustained representation**, particularly in light of several technical and presentational issues that arose during the course of the audit and amendment proceedings.

By way of background, the case originated from audit proceedings under section 177, followed by a show-cause notice under section 122(9), wherein multiple issues were confronted. A recurring theme across these issues was that **certain figures appearing in the IRIS return did not fully align, line-by-line, with the audited financial statements**, largely due to system-driven classifications, aggregation mechanics, and limitations within the IRIS reporting framework. These mismatches, if viewed in isolation, had the potential to give rise to adverse inferences despite there being no underlying tax exposure.

Through detailed submissions, reconciliations, and documentary evidence, each of the key issues was addressed and resolved as under:

First, with respect to **purchases, cost of sales, and operating expenses**, the tax authorities examined the allowability and substantiation of major expense heads. After reviewing the audited accounts, supporting schedules, and explanations furnished, it was accepted that the expenditures were **wholly and exclusively incurred for business purposes**, duly recorded, and verifiable. Consequently, **no disallowance was made**, notwithstanding the initial concern arising from presentation differences between IRIS disclosures and the audited accounts.

Second, regarding **trade payables and other liabilities**, concerns were raised under section 34(5) on the basis of figures extracted from IRIS that did not precisely match the audited financial statements. We demonstrated that the apparent differences were attributable to classification and aggregation variances, and that the liabilities were genuine, duly disclosed, and supported by movement and payment evidence. The tax authorities accepted this position and **no addition under section 34(5) was made**.

Third, in relation to **short-term and long-term borrowings**, which were initially proposed to be treated as income under section 39(3), comprehensive evidence was furnished to establish that these represented bona fide banking facilities and properly documented related-party financing arrangements, received through verifiable banking channels. The explanation was accepted in full, and **all proposed additions on this account were dropped**.

Fourth, with respect to **income from other sources**, including items classified under the Final Tax Regime, the authorities examined the nature and taxability of such receipts. After reviewing the supporting documentation and legal position, it was accepted that the income had been **correctly classified and taxed**, and that no recharacterization under sections 18 or 39 was warranted.

Fifth, concerning **depreciation, gratuity contributions, and other admissible deductions**, the claims were examined against the audited records and statutory provisions. It was confirmed that depreciation had been computed in accordance with the Ordinance, that no impermissible initial allowance had been claimed, and that employee-related contributions were duly paid and allowable. Accordingly, **all claims were allowed as filed**.

Finally, one of the most critical areas involved **bank reconciliations and turnover matching**, where gross bank credits appearing in IRIS initially appeared significantly higher than declared revenues. Through detailed reconciliations, it was demonstrated that the apparent differences arose from non-revenue items such as financing inflows, sweep movements, and internal transfers. Upon verification, the authorities expressly recorded that **there was no difference between bank credits and declared revenue**, and no adverse inference was drawn.

In view of the above, the tax authorities have expressly concluded that the assessment is to stand **in the same position as per the originally filed return**, with no enhancement of income and no additional tax liability. Importantly, this outcome was achieved **despite multiple procedural and presentational inconsistencies in IRIS**, which were successfully contextualized and neutralized through careful explanation and evidence-based advocacy.

Accordingly, as the order merely upholds the return position and does not give rise to any tax demand or further compliance requirement, **no further action is required at this stage**. The proceedings stand concluded for Tax Year 2020.

We will retain the order on record and continue to monitor the matter from a risk-management perspective. Should you wish to discuss any specific aspect of the order or its implications in more detail, we would be pleased to do so.

Warm regards,  
Zuhair

Dear [Client Name],

Further to our earlier communication, we set out below a **detailed discussion of the tax demand created through the order passed under section 161(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2020**, along with our **recommended course of action** fileciteturn1file0.

**1. Nature and Composition of the Tax Demand**

The order treats the Company as an *assessee in default* on the allegation that tax was not deducted and/or deposited at source on certain expense heads. Based on this premise, the tax office has raised:

– **Principal tax demand** under section 161(1); and  
– **Default surcharge** on the alleged non-deduction/non-payment, computed mechanically up to the date of the order.

The demand is substantial and has been computed by aggregating various expense categories, including salaries, manufacturing expenses, selling and distribution expenses, and certain other operational costs, by broadly assuming that these were subject to withholding under different provisions of section 153 and allied withholding sections.

**2. Key Weaknesses in the Order**

From a technical and legal standpoint, the order suffers from multiple infirmities, which materially weaken the sustainability of the demand:

First, the conclusions are **largely driven by IRIS-based extractions and classifications**, without proper reconciliation with the audited financial statements and detailed schedules. Several expense heads have been picked up in gross, without appreciating their underlying nature, break-up, or tax treatment.

Second, the order **does not adequately distinguish between payments that are inherently subject to withholding and those that fall outside the withholding regime**, such as pure reimbursements, internal cost allocations, employee-related costs already taxed through payroll, or payments not constituting “services” within the meaning of the Ordinance.

Third, in a number of instances, the tax office has **applied withholding provisions in an expansive and mechanical manner**, without identifying the correct charging section, rate, threshold, or the factual trigger for deduction. This approach runs contrary to settled law that withholding obligations must be construed strictly and cannot be imposed by implication or assumption.

Fourth, the **default surcharge has been levied automatically**, without considering that the Company had taken a bona fide and legally supportable position, supported by audited accounts and disclosures, and that there was no deliberate failure or concealment involved.

**3. Our Position on Merits**

On merits, the case is **strongly arguable**. The demand does not arise from any undisclosed transaction or unrecorded payment; rather, it stems from differences in interpretation and presentation. The underlying expenses are duly recorded, audited, and form part of the Company’s normal manufacturing and business operations.

Importantly, the law is well settled that:
– section 161 proceedings are **consequential in nature** and must be based on a clear, identifiable withholding obligation;  
– the burden lies on the tax authority to demonstrate *how* and *under which provision* tax was deductible; and  
– mere availability of expenditure figures in IRIS does not, by itself, justify treating a taxpayer as an assessee in default.

These principles provide a solid foundation for appellate relief.

**4. Proposed Course of Action**

In view of the above, our recommended course of action is as follows:

– **Filing of appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals):**  
  The order is appealable, and we will file a comprehensive appeal within the statutory limitation period, supported by a detailed statement of facts, grounds of appeal, and legal arguments.

– **Focus of appellate challenge:**  
  The appeal will primarily challenge (i) the jurisdictional and legal basis of invoking section 161(1), (ii) incorrect application of withholding provisions, (iii) failure to appreciate the factual record and audited accounts, and (iv) unjustified levy of default surcharge.

– **Recovery protection / stay:**  
  Concurrently, we will assess and advise on the most appropriate strategy to **protect against coercive recovery**, whether through a stay application before the Commissioner (Appeals) or through administrative engagement with the tax office, depending on the recovery posture adopted by the department.

– **No immediate payment recommended at this stage:**  
  Given the arguable nature of the issues and the availability of an effective appellate remedy, we do not recommend making payment merely on the basis of the impugned order, unless required as part of a specific stay or risk-mitigation strategy.

**5. Way Forward**

We will now proceed to prepare the appeal documentation and will share the draft grounds and statement of facts for your review shortly. The objective will be to comprehensively place the factual and legal position on record at the first appellate stage and seek deletion of the entire demand.

We remain available to discuss any specific component of the demand or the appellate strategy in more detail, should you wish to do so.

Warm regards,  
Zuhair

We have carefully reviewed the order in detail, including the annexures and tabulations forming part of the demand, and set out below a **specific discussion of the disallowances giving rise to the tax demand**, together with the **documentation required** to effectively contest the same before the Commissioner (Appeals).

At the outset, it is important to note that the demand has not been raised on the basis of any single, identified transaction. Rather, the tax office has proceeded by extracting **aggregate expense figures from the IRIS system and audited accounts**, and has then assumed, in a broad and mechanical manner, that withholding tax ought to have been deducted on such amounts. This methodology itself is legally flawed; nevertheless, for appellate purposes, each component of the demand must be addressed on facts.

The **largest component of the demand relates to salaries, wages, and other employee-related benefits**. The order acknowledges that salary expense has been claimed in the audited accounts; however, it proceeds to treat a portion of the salary cost as a withholding default without identifying any specific employee, payment, or shortfall. No reconciliation has been carried out between payroll records and tax actually deducted under section 149. Instead, the conclusion is drawn on the basis of gross figures appearing in IRIS. To rebut this allegation, we will require complete **salary tax workings for the year**, month-wise payroll summaries, **withholding statements filed for salaries**, CPRs evidencing deposit of salary tax, and a reconciliation linking the audited salary expense with payroll records and tax deposits.

The **second major disallowance arises from manufacturing expenses**, which the tax office has broadly subjected to withholding assumptions under section 153. The order treats manufacturing expenses as a single block and presumes that these represent payments to suppliers or service providers attracting withholding obligations. This approach ignores the composite nature of manufacturing costs, which include raw material consumption, utilities, in-house labour, consumables, repairs, and internal allocations—many of which do not involve any third-party payment at all. For appellate purposes, we will need a **detailed break-up of manufacturing expenses**, vendor-wise listings where third-party payments are involved, copies of major invoices, and a clear segregation between service payments, supply of goods, utilities, and internal costs. This will allow us to demonstrate that withholding provisions cannot be applied on an aggregated basis.

The order also raises a demand in respect of **selling, distribution, and administrative expenses**, again by assuming that such expenses are automatically subject to withholding tax. The order does not identify the applicable withholding section for each category, nor does it examine thresholds, exemptions, or the actual nature of payments. Items such as freight, utilities, statutory payments, marketing expenses, office overheads, and reimbursements have been lumped together and treated as withholding defaults. To address this, we will require a **general ledger extract of selling and administrative expenses**, vendor-wise payment details, copies of significant contracts (if any), and identification of expenses that represent reimbursements, utilities, or statutory levies falling outside the withholding regime.

In addition to the principal tax demand, the order has **levied default surcharge mechanically**, treating it as an automatic consequence of the alleged non-deduction. Since default surcharge is purely accessory in nature, its sustainability is entirely dependent on the validity of the principal demand. Once the underlying withholding assumptions are rebutted, the surcharge will not survive. No separate documentation is required for surcharge, beyond establishing that no withholding default exists.

In summary, the tax demand has been created due to a **presumptive and IRIS-driven approach**, rather than any concrete finding of non-compliance. For purposes of appeal, our focus will be to convert the discussion from aggregated figures to **transaction-level facts**, supported by documentary evidence. Accordingly, we request you to please arrange the following, on a priority basis: payroll and salary tax records for the year; detailed break-up of manufacturing expenses with supporting schedules; vendor-wise details of selling and administrative expenses; and copies of major invoices and contracts where services were procured.

Once the above documentation is available, we will be in a strong position to file a comprehensive appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), supported by factual reconciliations and settled legal principles. We will guide you on the format and level of detail required for each set of documents to ensure consistency with the appellate strategy.

Please let us know if you would like to discuss any specific component of the demand or documentation requirement in further detail.

Warm regards,  
Zuhair

## 🚨 Advance Tax Recovery Is *Not* a Free-for-All  
### Lahore High Court Draws Clear Legal Lines for FBR

**Tax Insight | Important Judgment**

The Lahore High Court has delivered a significant ruling clarifying **how and when advance tax can be recovered by FBR**. The decision reinforces that **tax recovery must follow due process—step by step, not shortcut by shortcut**.

---

### ⚖️ What Was the Issue?
FBR issued a **recovery notice under section 138(1)** to recover advance tax **without first giving a proper notice under section 137** and without allowing reasonable time to respond. The taxpayer challenged this action as unlawful.

---

### 🧠 What the Court Clarified
The Court made two critical points:

1. **Advance tax unpaid after the due date can be treated as “deemed assessed” under section 147(7)**  
   ➜ No *separate* assessment order under sections 120 or 122 is required for recovery.

2. **But recovery cannot start abruptly**  
   ➜ **A mandatory notice under section 137 must be issued first**, clearly stating:
   - the amount payable  
   - the basis of liability  
   - a future due date for payment  

Skipping this step violates **due process and Article 4 of the Constitution**.

---

### ❌ What the Court Rejected
The Court firmly rejected the idea that:
- FBR can jump directly to coercive recovery, or  
- section 138 can be used **without complying with section 137 first**.

Tax recovery, the Court emphasized, **is not meant to be a “grab-and-go” process**.

---

### ✅ Final Outcome
- The recovery notice issued directly under section 138(1) was **declared unlawful**.
- FBR was allowed to **restart the recovery process**, but **only by following the correct legal sequence**.

---

### 📌 Why This Matters for Taxpayers
This judgment is a strong reminder that:
- **Even where tax is legally due, procedure matters**  
- **Notices, timelines, and the right to respond are not optional**  
- Any recovery action taken in haste can be challenged and struck down

---

### 🧾 Practical Takeaway
If you receive a **recovery notice for advance tax**, always check:
- Was a **proper section 137 notice** issued first?
- Were you given **reasonable time to respond**?
- Does the notice clearly explain **how the amount was computed**?

If not, the recovery may be **legally vulnerable**.

---

**To:** Management of Engro Vopak & Elengy Terminals Ltd. (EVTL)  
**From:** [Your Tax Advisor’s Firm]  
**Date:** January 5, 2026  
**Subject:** Withholding Tax on Upfront Concession Fee Paid to Port Qasim Authority (PQA)  

## Background and Issue  
EVTL has paid an upfront concession fee to Port Qasim Authority – a statutory government authority – in consideration for 30-year BOT concession rights to build, operate, and transfer a terminal at Port Qasim. We are asked to determine whether this one-time concession fee is subject to withholding tax under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”), and if so, under which provision (e.g. section 153, 155, etc.). We must characterize the nature of the payment (royalty, service fee, rent/lease, or capital outlay) and assess the corresponding withholding obligations. We also outline the consequences of non-compliance (e.g. penalties or disallowances). 

## Relevant Tax Provisions Overview  
- **Section 153 (Payments for Goods, Services, and Contracts):** Section 153(1) obligates every prescribed withholding agent (including companies) to deduct income tax from payments to residents for: **(a)** sale of goods, **(b)** rendering of services, or **(c)** execution of a contract (other than goods/services)【22†L6003-L6011】. The tax is deducted from the gross amount at specified rates. EVTL, as a company, is a prescribed person for these purposes.  
- **Section 155 (Rent of Immovable Property):** Requires withholding on rent paid for use of land, buildings, furniture or fittings. Companies paying rent to any person must deduct tax at source (15% for Active Taxpayers, or higher for non-filers) on the gross rent【33†L1151-L1160】. “Rent” is defined as any amount received by an owner as consideration for use or occupation of land or a building【58†L119-L127】. This includes lease or license payments for property rights.  
- **“Royalty” Definition:** The Ordinance defines “royalty” broadly as any amount (periodic or lump sum) paid as consideration for the use of, or right to use, intellectual property, copyrights, patents, designs, secret processes, **“or other like property or right”**【53†L933-L942】, as well as for technical know-how, use of industrial/commercial equipment, etc. Notably, withholding on royalty is explicitly required when paying **non-residents** (Section 152)【13†L13-L19】. There is **no parallel provision requiring tax withholding on royalties paid to resident persons** – such income for a resident payee is generally taxable to them directly, absent a specific withholding clause.  
- **Other Potential Provisions:** Section 233 covers brokerage and commission (not applicable here). Various Section 236 provisions impose advance tax on specific transactions; e.g. **Section 236A** requires the seller (here, PQA if considered “selling” lease rights via auction/tender) to collect advance tax at 10% on the gross auction/concession price. This would be an advance tax on EVTL (as bidder) rather than a withholding on PQA’s income. We will discuss this if relevant.  

## Characterization of the Concession Fee  

**1. As a Royalty:**  If the upfront fee were characterized as consideration for use of a “property or right” of the government, one might ask if it constitutes a **“royalty”**. A royalty can include payments for the use of intellectual property or proprietary rights【53†L933-L942】. However, the concession rights in question pertain to operating a port terminal – essentially a license to use physical infrastructure/land and to run a commercial facility. These rights are not in the nature of patents, copyrights or industrial know-how; nor is this a payment for the use of industrial equipment in the ordinary sense (the terminal is to be built/operated by EVTL itself). In substance, the fee secures a long-term **franchise or license** to use government-owned premises and to conduct business there. This is more akin to leasing rights than to a royalty on intellectual property.  

*Tax Treatment:* Even if one were to call it a “royalty,” **no withholding tax is prescribed on royalties paid to resident persons** under the Ordinance. Withholding on royalties applies when paying non-residents (under Section 152)【13†L13-L19】, which is not the case here since PQA is a Pakistani statutory authority. Thus, classifying the concession fee as a royalty would **not trigger any withholding requirement** by EVTL under the law. (PQA would simply include the amount in its taxable income, unless exempt). 

**2. As a Fee for Services:** Another angle is whether PQA is providing any “services” to EVTL in return for this upfront fee, such that Section 153(1)(b) might apply. In a typical services arrangement, the payee renders some service (professional, technical, or other) and the payer withholds tax on the fee【22†L6003-L6011】. Here, PQA is not performing any direct service; rather, PQA is granting EVTL the concession rights and access to land/port infrastructure. EVTL will itself build, operate, and maintain the terminal. PQA’s role is largely regulatory/contractual (oversight, allowing use of port land, etc.) rather than a service provider. There may be ancillary services from PQA (e.g. navigational aids, harbor dredging, security) but those are typically covered by separate port charges, not by the concession fee. 

On balance, the **upfront concession fee is not a payment “for the rendering of services” by PQA**, but for permission to use property and operate a facility. It does **not** squarely fall under Section 153(1)(b). Therefore, treating it as a service fee requiring withholding would be a stretch of Section 153’s intent. (No known FBR circular extends “services” to cover such concession arrangements, and in practice concession fees to government authorities have not been treated as services). 

**3. As Lease/ Rent of Property:** The concession agreement effectively gives EVTL the right to occupy and use port land/berths and perhaps existing installations, for 30 years, in return for consideration. This has the hallmarks of a lease or license of immovable property. Pakistani tax law treats amounts paid for the use of land or a facility as “rent,” even if termed “license fee” or “concession fee.” In a Sindh High Court case, for example, the court described payments made for operating from portions of a property as **“license fee… or rent for occupying”** those premises【58†L119-L127】, indicating that such license payments are considered rent in substance. 

Under the Ordinance, **rent** is any consideration for use or occupation of land or a building, paid to the owner (Section 15) – whether paid periodically or upfront (even a non-refundable lease premium is effectively rent or an advance against rent)【58†L119-L127】. Here, PQA as landowner/licensor granted EVTL the right to use port land/space. Accordingly, the ₹[X] upfront concession fee can be viewed as an advance lease/rent payment for the 30-year term. 

*Tax Treatment:* If characterized as rent, Section 155 squarely applies. EVTL was required to deduct withholding tax at the time of payment of the concession fee【33†L1151-L1160】. The rate applicable at the time would depend on PQA’s tax status (since PQA is a government entity, it is on the Active Taxpayers List; the rate for companies’ rent is generally 15% for ATL payees【33†L1151-L1160】). The tax so withheld would be adjustable against PQA’s final tax liability (not a final tax). We are not aware of any exemption in the law that spares government authorities from withholding on rent; unless PQA had obtained a specific exemption certificate from FBR under Section 159, EVTL had a legal obligation to deduct tax on this payment. 

It is worth noting that some BOT/project concession fees can have a dual nature (partly for use of land (rent) and partly for intangible franchise rights). However, Pakistani tax practice tends to treat the entire concession/lease payment as income from property or business income for the authority, with **Section 155 withholding** as the compliance mechanism for the payer. We have not found a published case directly on a port concession fee’s withholding, but the closest analogy – lease/license of public property – has been treated as rent subject to withholding【58†L119-L127】. 

**4. As Capital Expenditure (No Withholding):** EVTL will capitalize this concession fee as an intangible asset (a “right to operate a port terminal”) on its books, amortizable over 30 years. One might argue that since this is a one-time capital expense and not an ongoing expense, it falls outside the scope of routine withholding provisions (which predominantly target recurring payments for goods, services, contracts, or rent). There is precedent in some industries: for instance, telecom companies paying a lump-sum license fee to PTA for spectrum licenses generally did not treat those payments as subject to withholding – they were considered capital regulatory fees rather than payments for services or rent. 

However, **the tax law does not explicitly exempt capital payments from withholding if they otherwise fall into a taxable category**. The characterization for withholding is based on the nature of the payment **from the payee’s perspective**. In this case, from PQA’s perspective the concession fee is a form of business/property income. The fact that EVTL capitalizes it does not change PQA’s receipt into a non-taxable category. Unless we could successfully argue that the concession right is neither goods, nor services, nor property use – essentially a sui generis intangible right – EVTL would not be relieved from withholding obligations. Given the broad definition of “rent” and “contract” in the Ordinance, it is safer to conclude that **the payment is within scope of withholding (as rent/consideration for use of property)** rather than outside it. In short, treating it as a capital outlay **does not automatically exempt EVTL from withholding** in the eyes of tax law. 

**5. Advance Tax on Auction (Section 236A):** It is worth mentioning Section 236A, which requires the seller/lessor (in this case PQA) to collect **advance income tax at 10%** from the lessee on any premium or fee paid as a result of an auction or tender of rights. If the concession was awarded through a competitive bidding or public tender, PQA may have collected 10% of the concession fee as advance tax from EVTL. (For example, recent LNG terminal bids required a $10 million concession fee, on which 10% advance tax would be collected under 236A)【23†L5-L13】. **This advance tax is separate from the withholding tax regime** – it is an upfront tax paid by EVTL (the bidder) which can be adjusted against EVTL’s own income tax. It does **not** replace the withholding that EVTL must deduct on PQA’s income. In practice, there has been confusion on this point in some cases, but legally the two are parallel mechanisms. If both applied, EVTL would pay 10% (as advance tax under 236A) *and* withhold (say 15%) on the payment to PQA – though PQA could then claim credit for the tax withheld. Ideally, FBR would clarify or avoid such double collection. In absence of a specific exclusion, EVTL faced exposure on both fronts. 

## Conclusion – Withholding Obligation and Rationale  
After evaluating all characterizations, **our opinion is that the upfront concession fee is best viewed as a payment for lease/license of property (i.e. “rent”)**, which does attract withholding under Section 155. It is not merely a royalty or a service fee in the conventional sense, and treating it as a non-taxable capital payment would likely not withstand scrutiny given the nature of the rights acquired. Therefore, EVTL **was required to deduct income tax at source on the payment to PQA**, and remit it to the government. 

In numeric terms, if the concession fee was PKR __ million, EVTL should have withheld 15% (assuming PQA is an ATL taxpayer) and remitted PKR __ million to FBR, paying the net __ to PQA. PQA would then receive a withholding tax certificate and adjust that PKR __ million against its own tax payable (if any). If, on the other hand, PQA provided an exemption certificate or if there is a specific exemption for PQA in the Second Schedule (none is apparent for concession income), EVTL could have been relieved from withholding. Absent such exemption, the law obligated EVTL to deduct the tax. 

## Consequences of Incorrect Treatment  
If EVTL **failed to withhold** on this payment, several consequences arise under the Ordinance: 

- **Recovery of Tax Not Withheld (Sec. 161):** EVTL can be treated as an “assessee in default.” The tax that should have been deducted can be demanded from EVTL, even though PQA received the gross amount. FBR can recover the principal amount of tax that went un-withheld from EVTL【60†L108-L117】. (If PQA has meanwhile paid its own taxes on this income, EVTL may seek to defend against recovery to that extent, but that involves a detailed procedure and is not automatic). 

- **Default Surcharge:** Under Section 161(1A) and 205, a **default surcharge** (interest) accrues on the non-deducted tax, typically at 12% per annum (or a monthly rate) from the date it was due to be paid to government【60†L108-L117】. This can substantially increase the liability over time. 

- **Penalties:** Separately, Section 182 authorizes a penalty up to the amount of tax that was required to be deducted (potentially 100% of the shortfall) for failure to withhold. The exact penalty can vary – often a minimum penalty of Rs. 40,000 or higher (or such proportion of tax) is imposed. The tax authorities have discretion to reduce the penalty if there was reasonable cause, but generally non-compliance with withholding is penalized strictly to encourage compliance. 

- **Disallowance of Expense (Sec. 21(c)):** The tax law also “punishes” non-compliance by disallowing the related expense for income tax deduction. Section 21(c) disallows any business expense for which tax was required to be withheld but was not deducted/deposited【60†L108-L117】. In EVTL’s case, the concession fee is a capital expenditure, not a P&L deduction in one year. However, EVTL likely amortizes this concession right (for example, claiming amortization deductions under section 24 or via depreciation on intangibles). The tax authorities could invoke Section 21(c) to deny the amortization or any deduction related to the concession fee on the grounds that EVTL failed to deduct the required withholding tax. This effectively increases EVTL’s taxable income each year by the amount of amortization disallowed. (Notably, if EVTL later pays the missing tax under Section 161, the disallowance can be reversed – the law allows the expense deduction in the year the tax is paid or made good). 

In summary, **non-compliance with withholding obligations can result in EVTL having to pay the tax itself, plus interest and penalties, and potentially losing tax benefits of the expenditure【60†L108-L117】.** These outcomes underscore the importance of correctly identifying withholding duties on such payments. 

## References and Supporting Authorities  
- Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Section 153(1) (withholding on payments for goods, services, contracts)【22†L6003-L6011】.  
- ITO 2001 – Section 155 and Division V of Part III of First Schedule (withholding on rent of immovable property)【33†L1151-L1160】.  
- ITO 2001 – Section 2(54) definition of “royalty” (covers payments for use of intellectual property and similar rights)【53†L933-L942】.  
- ITO 2001 – Section 152(1) (withholding on royalty/fees paid to non-residents, highlighting no equivalent for residents)【13†L13-L19】.  
- Sindh High Court in *KSE v. Commissioner* (2016) – characterized license fees for use of property space as akin to rent for occupying property【58†L119-L127】.  
- Section 21(c) of ITO / FBR Circular 07 of 2016 – disallows deductions for payments where withholding tax was not deducted (covers salary, rent, brokerage, services, etc.)【60†L108-L117】.  

**Conclusion:** EVTL’s upfront concession fee to PQA falls within the ambit of taxable payments on which EVTL was obliged to withhold tax – most plausibly under Section 155 as rent/lease payment for use of PQA’s property. EVTL should ensure compliance by depositing any due withholding to avoid the financial and tax consequences outlined. If there was uncertainty in the law’s interpretation, EVTL could have sought a ruling from FBR in advance; however, based on the Ordinance and relevant interpretations, the conservative and correct approach was to treat the concession fee as a withholding-applicable payment. Please let us know if you need further clarification or assistance with any remedial steps.
