Please read the below advice: 

Mr. Hassam ullah Ullah Khan						                                      November 14, 2025
Senior Manger Business Finance & Commercial
Oxford University Press Pakistan (SMC-Pvt) Limited					DTA 000
Korangi Industrial Area
Karachi


Dear Sir 


INCOME TAX AND SALES TAX IMPLICATIONS: DIGITAL PRODUCTS


We refer to your e-mails and subsequent discussions held with our Partner Muhammad Shaheryar Khan in the context of the ‘e-product’ offered by Oxford University Press Pakistan (SMC-Private) Limited [OUP SMC]. 

2.	UNDERSTANDING 

2.1	A brief understanding  of the products is given in the ensuing paragraphs: 

(i)	The Oxford Reading Buddy [ORB]  platform, developed by Oxford University Press [OUP], serves a global audience. It provides associates, including OUP SMC, with access to a shared publishing platform and personalized lockers, enabling them to manage digital publications independently while benefiting from global resources. The platform supports the seamless flow of rights, money, and data between associates and the central system. OUP SMC is authorized to enter sub-rights licenses for distributing electronic rights. Customers purchase digital content via access tokens, and OUP SMC manage the financial transactions, ensuring revenue flows back to the central platform. Platform usage fees cover access to global content and locker maintenance, striking a balance between branch autonomy and global integration.

(ii)	The Oxford My E-Mate platform , powered by Magic-box, operates as a third-party digital reader, facilitating content distribution for OUP associates at both local and global levels. Authors grant electronic rights to OUP, which licenses these rights to associates for further distribution. The platform supports flexible access through school subscriptions or access codes and ensures online and offline availability via secure, encrypted apps. An annual licensing fee funds platform operations, enabling the smooth transfer of rights, revenue, and data. 

(iii)	The Oxford Extend platform  serves as a comprehensive learning and content management system [LMS/CMS], designed for schools to access educational materials through subscriptions. E-books, licensed by OUP in collaboration with authors, are uploaded to the platform and made accessible via secure apps for both online and offline use, ensuring uninterrupted access even without internet connectivity. Schools subscribe to the platform and e-books, generating revenue through royalties on branch net receipts and service charges for access and maintenance. Additionally, schools pay annual fees for platform updates and ongoing support. Oxford Extend ensures smooth integration through robust onboarding and training programs, allowing schools to maximize its potential. 


3.	Our opinion has been sought on the implications of income tax and sales tax on the above products of the OUP SMC. 


4.	INCOME TAX IMPLICATION 

4.1	The Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] does not define the term goods. Nevertheless, section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 defines goods to include 'every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money, stocks, shares, and securities.' Likewise, Article 260(1) of the Constitution of Pakistan defines goods to encompass all materials, commodities, and articles. Intangible digital offerings such as online access rights, e-subscriptions, and digital learning content do not fall within the traditional concept of movable property or commodities. 

4.2	On the other hand, services, as defined under provincial sales tax statutes and by the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), broadly include all activities other than the supply of goods, encompassing facilities, advantages, or amenities provided for consideration. Accordingly, where no tangible movable property is transferred, the underlying transaction is regarded as a service for tax purposes.

4.3	In the absence of explicit judicial precedent concerning digital platforms, the most defensible interpretation is that online digital platforms represent the provision of services rather than the sale of goods. These platforms provide users with access to content or functionalities, an advantage, without transferring ownership of a tangible item. Consequently, payments received by OUP SMC for platforms such as Oxford Reading Buddy, My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend represent consideration for services within the meaning of section 153(1)(b) of the Ordinance. Corporate customers making such payments are therefore required to withhold tax at the applicable rate for services.

4.4	Prior to the Finance Act 2025, the Ordinance contained no dedicated framework addressing the taxation of the digital economy. Accordingly, income derived by OUP SMC from its e-learning platforms was treated as ordinary business income, taxable under the normal regime. The Finance Act 2025, however, introduced a significant policy shift through the insertion of section 6A into the Ordinance and the inclusion of new statutory definitions for 'digitally delivered services' and 'e-commerce.' These provisions collectively brought digital transactions within the ambit of a final tax regime. 

4.5	Section 6A imposes tax on the gross receipts arising from the supply of digitally ordered goods or services made from within Pakistan through locally operated online platforms, including websites and digital marketplaces. For ready reference, the relevant statutory definitions and charging provision are reproduced below for ease of understanding:

(17C) “digitally delivered services” means any service delivered over the internet or electronic networks, where the delivery is automated and requires minimal or no human intervention including music, audio and video streaming services, cloud services, online software applications services, services delivered through online inter-personal interaction i.e., tele medicines, e-learning etc., online banking services, architectural design services, research and consultancy reports, accounting services in the form of digital files or any other online facility;

(19AA) “e-commerce” means sale or purchase of goods and services conducted over computer networks by methods specifically designed for the purpose of receiving or placing of orders either through websites, mobile applications or online marketplace having digital ordering features by using either mobile phone, iPad, Tablet or automated computer-to-computer ordering system

6A. Tax on payments for digital transactions in e-commerce platforms.– (1) Subject to this Ordinance, a tax shall be imposed, at the rate specified in Division IVA of Part I of the First Schedule, on every person who receives payment for supply of digitally ordered goods or services which are delivered from within Pakistan using locally operated online platforms including online marketplace or websites: 

Provided that the export proceeds subjected to withholding under section 154 and 154A shall not fall within the ambit of this section. 

(2) The tax imposed under sub-section (1) shall be computed by applying the relevant rate of tax to the gross amounts of receipts mentioned in sub-section (1).

4.6	The key feature of section 6A is that it taxes the gross receipts (including sales tax) arising from the supply of digitally ordered goods or services made from within Pakistan through online or digital platforms. The digital platforms operated by OUP SMC (being a locally operated platform) exhibit all essential elements of this regime. In each case, educational content is ordered, delivered, and accessed electronically, whether through personalized lockers, encrypted applications, or subscription-based portals, without the transfer of any tangible property. 

4.7	Customers, primarily schools and individual learners, purchase access tokens or annual subscriptions to use digital learning materials hosted on OUP servers. The substance of these transactions is therefore the provision of 'digitally delivered services', access to and use of an online system, rather than the sale of a physical good.

4.8	Revenue arising from such access fees, subscriptions, and platform-maintenance charges represents gross receipts derived from within Pakistan, as OUP SMC locally manages user access, licensing rights, and financial settlements with customers. The platforms also provide continuous digital support, maintenance, and content management, reinforcing that the income originates from an ongoing service relationship. Although the underlying infrastructure is globally developed , its operation in Pakistan through OUP SMC’s authorized management of rights, payments, and delivery constitutes a local digital presence for income-tax purposes.

4.9	Taken together, these features align precisely with the statutory definitions of 'digitally delivered services' and 'e-commerce' introduced through the Finance Act 2025. Accordingly, the income derived by OUP SMC from Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend qualifies as gross receipts chargeable to tax  under section 6A which is treated as final discharge of tax liability under section 8 of the Ordinance, with corresponding withholding obligations resting on payment intermediaries or digital platforms that facilitate the transactions.

4.10	Division IVA of the First Schedule prescribes tax at 1 percent on payments made through digital channels (such as bank transfers or credit/debit cards) and 2 percent on cash-on-delivery transactions. The proviso excludes transactions already treated as exports under sections 154 or 154A. Consequently, all domestic digital sales, including subscriptions, digital learning content, and e-books, are now subject to final tax on gross receipts (including sales tax) under section 6A read with section 153(2A) of the Ordinance.

4.11	The new regime also introduces a withholding framework for payment intermediaries and courier service providers facilitating digital transactions. Where payments are processed through an electronic gateway or intermediary, such entities must withhold and deposit tax at 1 percent for digital payments or 2 percent for cash-on-delivery before remitting net proceeds to the seller. By broadening the definitions of 'digitally delivered services', 'e-commerce', and 'online marketplace', the Finance Act 2025 ensures that automated and internet-based offerings, including online courses, subscription portals, and software-access services, are comprehensively covered. Accordingly, OUP SMC’s e-learning and content-delivery platforms clearly fall within the scope of this regime.

4.12	It may also be noted that the initial draft of the Finance Act 2025 had imposed a 5 percent 'digital presence tax' on foreign e-retailers earning income from Pakistan without a physical presence. Nevertheless, subsequent notifications exempted goods and services supplied from outside Pakistan  from this levy. As OUP SMC operates as a resident entity providing digital products locally, this provision is not applicable.

4.13	In summary, whether the customer is an individual subscriber or an educational institution, any supply of digital content or access made through an online platform now falls under section 6A of the Ordinance. OUP SMC, as the service provider, is not required to withhold tax on its own receipts; rather, the obligation lies with intermediaries  such as banks, payment gateways, or courier companies to collect and deposit the applicable tax. OUP SMC should ensure close coordination with these intermediaries to verify accurate deduction, timely deposit, and reconciliation of taxes withheld under section 6A of the Ordinance. All such transactions are to be reported as income subject to final tax under the newly introduced digital economy regime.

4.14	Please note that after promulgation of new provisions, no explicit exclusion has been provided for non-withholding of income tax under section 153(1)(a) and 153(1)(b) of the Ordinance. It means that buyer (where withholding agent) under section 153 is also  required to observe the withholding at the applicable rates. Resultantly, the withholding observed under normal provisions would become refundable to OUP SMC.

5.	FEDERAL SALES TAX IMPLICATION 

5.1	As discussed above, section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 defines goods as ‘every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money, stocks, shares and securities.’ This definition, focused on tangible movables, has traditionally been interpreted to include physical articles, merchandise, and electricity (which was expressly added by amendment). Intangible products, rights, or digital content are not encompassed. An access code or online subscription represents a contractual right to access, a chose in action, and is not a tangible article. It also lacks classification under the Pakistan Customs tariff, as no Harmonized System (HS) code exists for purely online services. Accordingly, digital platform access does not qualify as goods for purposes of the Sales Tax Act.

5.2	Where OUP SMC sells a physical item (for instance, a printed card or USB containing an access key), a nominal tangible element may be involved. Nevertheless, tax authorities typically assess the substance of the transaction. The intrinsic value of platforms such as Oxford Reading Buddy or Oxford My E-Mate lies in the content or service, not in the medium used to convey access credentials. Thus, even if a code is printed on paper, the transaction would be treated as a service rather than a sale of goods. Although there is no specific ruling on e-learning subscriptions, similar reasoning has been applied to electronically delivered software, which has consistently been classified as a service.

5.3	It is pertinent to highlight here that through the Finance (Supplementary) Act, 2022, the long-standing exemption on the import or supply of books was curtailed to cover only educational textbooks, thereby excluding other categories of books that were previously exempt. Subsequently, the Finance Act, 2022 reinstated the earlier position, restoring exemption for the import and supply of all kinds of books under the Sixth Schedule to the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

5.4	Accordingly, printed books, including educational textbooks, remain exempt from sales tax under the Sixth Schedule. The relevant entry (previously serial 53 and now consolidated at serial 32 pursuant to the Finance Act, 2022) encompasses ‘newsprint and books (excluding directories, brochures, and leaflets)’. It is important to note that this exemption is confined to printed material falling within the specified HS codes and does not extend to electronic or digital publications. Consequently, digital subscriptions, e-books, and similar electronic formats, lacking a defined tariff classification, lie outside the scope of the statutory exemption.

5.5	Moreover, legislative reforms have explicitly confined the exemption to printed books and newsprint, as digital books and equivalents do not fall under the ambit of ‘goods’. Consequently, access to OUP SMC’s digital platforms does not come under the scope of Sales Tax Act, 1990. Even if digital books are treated as ‘service’, it falls outside the purview of federal sales tax altogether.

5.6	Accordingly, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend do not qualify as goods under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Revenue derived from these platforms is not subject to the federal sales tax regime, except to the extent of any ancillary supply of physical media. OUP SMC should, however, ensure that invoices for digital access are segregated from those for printed books to preserve the exemption applicable to printed textbooks and prevent inadvertent mixing of taxable and exempt supplies.


6.	PROVINCIAL SALES TAX IMPLICATION 

6.1	Sindh 

6.1.1	Following the Finance Act 2025 Sindh’s adoption of CPC Version 2.1 for classification, the specific category for Oxford SMC’s digital learning products is now clearly identifiable under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SST Act).

6.1.2	Under section 2(79) of SST Act, ‘service’ now encompasses anything that is not good, including facilities, advantages, and rights supplied for consideration. The Second Schedule, updated through the Finance Act, 2025, links every taxable service to its CPC heading. Among these, CPC 843 - On-line content, particularly sub-class 84311 On-line books, newspapers and periodicals supplied electronically, specifically targets digital publishing and e-content distribution. The explanatory notes confirm that 84311 covers books, newspapers and periodicals supplied electronically through the internet. For ready reference, the relevant explanation is reproduced below for ease of understanding:

843 On-line content 

8431 On-line text based information 

84311 On-line books 

This sub-class includes: 
-on-line books, including school textbooks, general reference books, such as atlases and other books of maps or charts, dictionaries and encyclopedias

6.1.3	In substance, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate and Oxford Extend provide controlled access to digital publications and educational materials hosted on secure servers. The user purchases electronic rights to read, interact with, and store those materials on-line. No tangible property or software copy is transferred; the value lies in the delivery of information content. This business model precisely matches the statutory language of CPC 843, sub-class 84311. 

6.1.4	Having concluded that the services primarily fall under CPC 84311 (a subclass of CPC 843), reference is invited to Serial No. 20 of Part-II of the Second Schedule to the SST Act. Under this entry, services classified under CPC 843 are subject to a reduced rate of 3% SST, provided that OUP SMC exercises the option for such reduced rate in accordance with Rule 42I of the SST on Services Rules, 2011. If the option is not filed, these services will attract the standard SST rate of 15%.  It is further noted that Serial No. 20 of the First Schedule provides an exemption for ‘library and archive services’ falling under CPC 845. Nevertheless, based on the nature of activities, the services rendered by OUP SMC do not fall within this exempt category.

6.2	Punjab 

6.2.1	Following the Finance Act, 2025, the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012 (PST Act) retained its PSIC-based classification framework, which is functionally mapped to the UN Central Product Classification (CPC) Version 2.1. Each service listed in the Schedule continues to carry numeric classification headings (for example, 98.12, 9857.0000, 9858.0000) derived from the Pakistan Standard Industrial Classification (PSIC), which in turn draws from the international CPC structure. Thus, while the Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) has not expressly cited CPC Version 2.1 in its legislation, it operates on the same classification logic and coding principles.

6.2.2	Section 2(38) defines service to include anything which is not good, including facilities, utilities, and advantages provided for consideration. Section 3, as amended, imposes tax on all services unless specifically exempted in the First Schedule. Oxford SMC’s digital learning platforms, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend, constitute the provision of an electronic facility granting access to digital content, rather than the supply of goods. The user acquires an intangible right to view and interact with online publications, not ownership of any physical or downloadable copy.

6.2.3	Consequently, such transactions fall within Punjab’s corresponding to CPC 84311 (On-line books, newspapers and periodicals supplied electronically). Please note that S. No. 8 of First Schedule to PST Act inter alia provides exemption for services relating to libraries, which we understand is not relevant in the instant case as specific online content is being provided by OUP SMC and hence it is not a library in general meaning. Therefore, in absence of a specific exemption for educational e-publications, these supplies attract Punjab sales tax at 16 percent. 

6.3	Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 

6.3.1	Through the Finance Act, 2025, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa formally codified the adoption of CPC and HS Codes by inserting express language in section 3(4) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act, 2022. The Act empowers the Management Committee to specify or amend CPC Codes, HS Codes, or any other code for classification of services, while clarifying that inclusion or exclusion of a code does not affect the underlying taxability.

6.3.2	This amendment aligns KPK’s framework with the UN CPC Version 2.1 structure adopted by Sindh, ensuring that all digital, online, or electronically delivered services can be consistently classified. The broad definition of service under section 2(aaa) includes any advantage or facility provided electronically, making digital platforms taxable by their very nature.

6.3.3	Applying the CPC classification, Oxford SMC’s subscription-based access to digital learning materials squarely falls within CPC 84311 – On-line books and periodicals supplied electronically. Since KPK explicitly recognizes CPC Codes for classification, the receipts from these platforms are taxable as online content services at the general 15 percent KPK sales tax rate. 

6.4	Balochistan 

6.4.1	The Finance Act, 2025 introduced a structural reform in the Balochistan Sales Tax on Services Act, 2015 through the insertion of section 78B - Classification of services. This new provision authorizes the Balochistan Revenue Authority (BRA) to specify, by notification, classification codes for services including CPC Codes, HS Codes, or any other international classification system, and clarifies that such codes are adopted for purposes of administration, analysis, and facilitation. This reform brings Balochistan in line with Sindh and KPK, both of which have formally incorporated CPC systems into their provincial tax laws.

6.4.2	Section 78B therefore establishes a clear legal foundation for the use of CPC Version 2.1 within Balochistan’s service-tax framework. When read together with section 2(147), which defines service as anything that is not goods and includes facilities, advantages, and rights rendered for consideration, it is evident that access to online educational material qualifies as a taxable service.

6.4.3	Oxford SMC’s digital platforms, providing interactive reading, electronic content, and access rights to e-publications, fall squarely under CPC 84311, covering online books and digital periodicals supplied electronically. Accordingly, under BRA’s CPC-linked classification, these supplies constitute taxable online content services at the standard 15 percent rate unless an educational exemption is later notified. 

7.	CONCLUSION

7.1	In view of the foregoing analysis, it is concluded that the digital platforms operated by Oxford OUP SMC, namely Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend, constitute the provision of digitally delivered services rather than the sale of goods. Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, income derived from these platforms represents gross receipts from digital transactions squarely falling within the ambit of the newly inserted section 6A, introduced through the Finance Act, 2025. Accordingly, such receipts are now subject to final tax on a gross basis at the prescribed rates, with corresponding withholding responsibilities resting on payment intermediaries or courier entities facilitating the collection of subscription proceeds.

7.2	For federal sales tax purposes, access to digital content does not qualify as a supply of goods within the meaning of section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, nor does it fall under any exempt category of the Sixth Schedule, which is confined to printed publications. Consequently, digital subscriptions and e-learning services are excluded from the scope of federal sales tax.

7.3	At the provincial level, however, the services are squarely covered   within the taxable classification CPC 84311 – On-line books, newspapers, and periodicals supplied electronically, as adopted by the Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan revenue authorities   through the respective Finance Acts 2025. In each jurisdiction, such online content services are taxable at the general rate (15 percent in Sindh, KPK, and Balochistan; 16 percent in Punjab), unless a specific exemption is later notified for educational e-publications.



8.	We hope the above appropriately responds to the issue raised. If you have any queries, kindly let us know. 


9.	CAVEAT

9.1	Our opinion is based on the facts and assumptions stated above. Any inaccuracy therein could have a material impact on our recommendation and should, therefore, be intimated to us immediately.

9.2	Also, our opinion is based on the law as of todate. Tax laws are subject to changes from time to time and as such any changes may affect the advice contained in our opinion. We have no responsibility to update our advice for events and circumstances occurring after the date of this opinion, unless specifically requested by you.

9.3	Further, tax advice is a matter of interpretation of law and is based on our experience with the tax authorities. Accordingly, it cannot be said with certainty that the opinion expressed above will be accepted by the tax authorities.


9.4	We do not, in giving this opinion, accept or assume responsibility for any other purpose or to any other person to whom this opinion is shown or in whose hands it may come, unless expressly agreed by us in writing.


Yours truly

Hi Hassam, hope you are doing well. 
Thank you for sharing the additional commercial details for Oxford Reading Buddy (ORB), Oxford My E Mate and Oxford Extend along with some queries largely relating to withholding of income taxes.   
UNDERSTANDING ON ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
In this respect, we would to inform you that section 6A of the Ordinance provides that tax is imposed “on every person who receives payment for supply of digitally ordered goods or services which are delivered from within Pakistan using locally operated online platforms including online marketplace or websites,” and is chargeable “on the gross amounts of receipts” at the rates in Division IVA of the First Schedule (1% for digital payments, 2% for COD). 
In your case, all three platforms now stand clearly within each element of this charging provision: orders are placed online, content is delivered electronically to users located in Pakistan, and payments are received by OUP SMC as the local operator of the Pakistani instance of these platforms. Accordingly, subscription fees and e book access receipts from ORB, My E Mate and Extend continue to qualify as receipts from “digitally ordered…services…delivered from within Pakistan” and remain taxable on a gross receipts basis under section 6A at 1% (digital modes) or 2% (COD), in line with the earlier advice.
The fact that certain platforms are hosted on servers outside Pakistan does not dislodge this conclusion. Section 6A looks to where the goods or services are delivered from in a commercial and legal sense and whether they are supplied “using locally operated online platforms,” rather than the physical location of hardware. Here, contracts with schools are entered into by OUP SMC, access is provisioned and managed locally, and revenue is recognized in Pakistan, so the economically relevant nexus of the supply, and therefore the source of the gross receipts, lies in Pakistan notwithstanding offshore infrastructure. On this basis, the new hosting details confirm that OUP SMC remains the “person who receives payment” for in Pakistan digital supplies within the scope of section 6A and is correctly subject to final tax on the prescribed percentages of its gross receipts.
WITHHOLDING OF INCOME TAX QUERIES 
Q1. Who is the withholding agent for digital transactions, the customer or the payment intermediary/courier? Who should not be withholding tax?
Section 6A, read together with the special collection mechanism in section 153(2A), is designed so that the withholding responsibility for digitally ordered goods and services rests primarily on payment intermediaries and courier companies, not on the customer or the seller. Payment intermediaries (banks, gateways, wallets, etc.) are to deduct 1% on digital payments, while courier companies handling COD are to deduct 2% on the gross amount they collect. In this framework, OUP SMC is not a withholding agent on its own receipts, and ordinary customers (schools) are not withholding agents under section 6A as such; their only potential role as withholding agents arises under the general provisions of section 153(1), which were enacted earlier for services and other payments.
Q2. Can there be more than one withholding agent (customer and intermediary)? Which tax is final in such cases?
As the law currently stands, there is a technical risk that two parties could be treated as withholding agents on the same payment:
•	Section 153(2A) begins with a “notwithstanding” clause, creating a special rule for digital transactions through intermediaries and couriers, but it does not expressly state that section 153(1) no longer applies to those payments.
•	The negative list in section 153(5), which sets out payments on which the general withholding under section 153(1) does not apply, has not yet been updated to exclude transactions that fall within section 6A / 153(2A).
On a literal reading, this means that a prescribed buyer could still consider itself obliged to withhold under section 153(1)(b) on payments for digital services, even where the intermediary/courier is already withholding under section 6A via section 153(2A), resulting in double withholding. In such a scenario, the tax collected under section 6A remains the final tax on the digital transaction income, whereas any additional tax deducted under section 153(1)(b) would, in principle, be refundable/adjustable in OUP’s hands rather than altering the “final tax” nature of section 6A.
Q3. How should this double withholding risk be managed in practice?
To mitigate the risk of two separate withholdings on the same payment, it is advisable to make the intended hierarchy explicit in your invoice. The logic is that, because section 153(2A) opens with “notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1),” the special digital transaction mechanism should override the general rule for those specific payments. Accordingly, your invoice can include a clear caveat along the following lines:
•	For any transaction where a payment intermediary or courier company is acting as the withholding agent under section 6A read with section 153(2A), the buyer (customer) should not simultaneously treat itself as a withholding agent under section 153(1) in respect of the same payment.
This approach aligns with the policy intent of the digital regime (to centralize withholding at the intermediary/courier level and avoid unnecessary duplication) and provides OUP SMC with a defensible basis to resist double withholding in day to day operations. 
Q4. Does this mean there should be no withholding under section 153(1) where an intermediary/courier is already deducting under section 6A?
For digital transactions that clearly fall within section 6A and are processed through payment intermediaries or couriers who are performing their statutory withholding obligations, the recommended position is that no parallel withholding under section 153(1) should be applied by the buyer on the same payment.
In other words, in those specific cases, the only operative withholding mechanism should be that of the intermediary/courier under section 6A / 153(2A), and any attempt by the buyer to deduct again under section 153(1)(b) would effectively create double withholding and an avoidable refund situation for OUP SMC. Until the law is clarified through an amendment to the negative list, this contractual and procedural safeguard is the most practical way to preserve the intended single, final tax collection under section 6A. 
Q5 As also mentioned above, need clarity what if an intermediary doesn’t fulfill its obligations, will the final tax regime not apply on OUP?
If a payment intermediary or courier fails to withhold and deposit the tax, the underlying receipts of OUP SMC still fall within the scope of section 6A in terms of their nature (digitally ordered services delivered from within Pakistan).  In this regard, it is important to distinguish between the chargeability of income, and the procedural obligation to withhold.
Section 6A taxes the income by its nature, i.e., digitally ordered and digitally delivered services supplied from within Pakistan through a locally operated platform. The applicability of the final tax regime is therefore not contingent upon actual deduction at source, but on the character of the receipt.
Where a withholding agent fails to withhold tax, the legal exposure primarily rests with that agent under sections 161 and 205 of the Ordinance, including recovery of tax not withheld, default surcharge, and penalty. OUP Pakistan does not lose the benefit of the final tax regime merely because of a withholding lapse by an intermediary.
Q6 It is expected from Customer to WHT on invoice value (including provincial sales tax). What value should the payment intermediary deduct tax on whether the invoice value or the net of tax receipts?
For purposes of section 6A, the payment intermediary should withhold on the gross amount of receipts corresponding to the invoice value, including provincial sales tax, and not on a net of tax or net of charges basis. Section 6A expressly applies to the “gross amounts of receipts” for digitally ordered goods or services, and our earlier opinion already mention that the 1%/2% is to be computed on gross receipts inclusive of sales tax, so both the customer (for section 153) and the intermediary/courier (for section 6A) should apply withholding on the same full invoice value rather than on a reduced net amount. 
PROVINCIAL SALES TAX QUERIES
Q1 Need a comparison of pros and cons of the two different rates i.e., reduced rate vs standard rate (such as option to claim input tax).
Pros
Applying 3% on gross value of taxable supplies materially reduces the tax burden compared to 15%/16%, which is particularly beneficial where your customer base (schools) cannot fully recover input tax. Lower output tax makes it easier to keep subscription prices attractive in a price sensitive education market, without eroding your net margins as much as standard rate taxation would.
Cons
Reduced rate schemes typically come with limitations on claiming or carrying forward input tax, or treat the reduced rate as a kind of turnover tax, so you may not be able to fully offset provincial input tax on your own costs (e.g. local service providers, infrastructure). 
Q2 This does not clarify the question arising on the applicable jurisdiction in case of provincial sales tax authorities. We need clarity on which jurisdiction should apply and for what reasons.
As discussed with you, from a practical and risk management perspective, the most defensible approach is to treat Sindh as the primary place of taxation for your digital platform supplies, on the basis that the place of business, contract administration and invoicing functions are all situated in Karachi. OUP SMC’s registered office, management, billing systems and website administration are effectively operated from Sindh, so the “place of business from which the service is supplied” is Sindh, even though customers may access the platforms from other provinces.
On this footing, charging and reporting Sindh sales tax on your digital platform invoices aligns the tax treatment with the location of the supplying establishment and the jurisdiction that is actually exercising administrative control over the business, thereby simplifying compliance and reducing the risk of overlapping claims by multiple provincial authorities.
Q3 Applicability of the laws enacted / adopted by independent / autonomous territories such as AJK, GB etc. is not included here. Clarity is required on income derived from such regions. Further, jurisdiction question also requires clarity. Also, above analysis should also be expanded to include sale is made to customers based in such autonomous regions.
For sales tax purposes, the operational and administrative functions of the digital platforms are centrally managed from Karachi, including contracting, invoicing, and overall platform administration. On this basis, Sindh is the relevant province of supply, and Sindh Sales Tax should be applied; consequently, sales tax implications of other provincial jurisdictions would not arise on these transactions.
 For income tax purposes, the position remains unchanged from the earlier advice, namely that receipts from the digital platforms are taxable under section 6A of the Ordinance as gross receipts from digitally delivered services, subject to final tax at the prescribed rates. 
Q4 What is meant by service supply from outside Pakistan in the context of digital platforms (such as hosting on servers outside Pakistan)?
No. Through the Finance Act, 2025, the FBR initially sought to tax digital transactions in both scenarios: (i) supplies of goods and services delivered from outside Pakistan, and (ii) supplies made through locally operated online platforms. Nevertheless, following subsequent amendments / notifications, the scope relating to goods and services delivered from outside Pakistan was withdrawn.
In the present case, the taxability arises because the customer interface and commercial presence is created and operated by OUP SMC, which manages the subscriptions, access rights, billing, and collection locally. Accordingly, the transactions are treated as supplies made from within Pakistan through a locally operated platform. Conversely, had the digital goods or services been supplied directly by OUP UK from outside Pakistan, without any involvement, facilitation, or local interface by OUP SMC, the above domestic digital-platform tax implications would generally not arise.

### **Super Tax Under Section 4C Challenged as “Unconstitutional” Before Federal Court**

The Federal Constitutional Court is hearing appeals relating to the levy of super tax under Section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Taxpayers have argued that this provision is legally defective, unconstitutional, and does not meet the standards expected of valid federal legislation. The case is significant because if the court agrees with these arguments, it could impact not only future super tax demands, but also the legal sustainability of super tax already collected or enforced in past years.

### **Key Question Raised: Does FBR Have the Legal Standing to Challenge Tax Law in Court?**

In a notable procedural argument, taxpayers questioned what “legal right” or “pecuniary interest” the FBR has to challenge statutory provisions before High Courts. The argument is that FBR is a department within the Revenue Division and litigation must be carried out on behalf of the Federation through proper constitutional and administrative authorization. If the court accepts this objection, it could affect how tax authorities initiate and maintain litigation—especially cases where appeals are filed without clear, competent authorization.

---

### **PEMRA’s 5% Advertisement Levy Under Scrutiny — IHC Summons Attorney General**

### **6) What the Notification Also Emphasises: Faster Decisions + Written Reasons**

**Explanation:**  
The notification also lays down the process: taxpayers must apply with reasons for delay; the Commissioner should decide within **30 days** if no additional information is needed, or within **45 days** if further documents are required. The Commissioner must decide on merit and **record reasons** for approval or rejection. In everyday terms: **less time for late relief, and decisions must be documented properly**. fileciteturn0file0

### **7) President vs FTO: “Ombudsman Can’t Act Like a Parallel Tax Authority”**

**Explanation:**  
The President issued another ruling stating that the **Federal Tax Ombudsman (FTO)** is not meant to take up broad matters like policy questions, legal interpretation, or issues already covered under tax laws through existing forums. The ruling stresses that the FTO’s role is mainly to address **maladministration**—such as unfair treatment, unnecessary delay, or improper handling—rather than stepping into areas meant for FBR/Finance Ministry or courts. fileciteturn0file0

**Explanation:**  
APTMA asked FBR to withdraw video analytics monitoring at the **spinning stage**, arguing the real problem—undocumented cotton movement (“golmaal”)—starts at the **ginning stage**, where cotton is first processed and enters the supply chain. APTMA cited large differences between reported cotton production and cotton arriving at ginneries, suggesting leakages happen earlier in the chain. They proposed that enforcement and traceability should begin at ginning to be truly effective. fileciteturn0file0

**Explanation:**

---

### 1) **FBR Tightens the Net: Customs and Law-Enforcement Join Hands Against Smuggling**
**Explanation:**  
FBR’s senior customs leadership visited Quetta and held detailed sessions with customs formations and law-enforcement agencies (FC, Coast Guards, etc.) to improve border control and intelligence sharing. The message is clear: enforcement will be more coordinated and more aggressive, especially in high-risk border areas. At the same time, FBR also engaged the business community (Quetta Chamber) and issued on-the-spot directions to resolve legitimate trade issues—so the policy aim appears to be *“stop illegal trade, facilitate genuine traders.”*

---

### 2) **LHC Clarifies a Key Tax Rule: “Brand / Goodwill” Costs Can’t Be Claimed 100% in One Year**
**Explanation:**  
The Lahore High Court held that where an expense creates a long-term benefit—like brand building, goodwill, trademark value, or similar intangibles—the taxpayer cannot take the full tax deduction in a single year just to reduce taxable income for that year. Instead, the cost must generally be spread over multiple years through amortization, in line with Section 24. The Court also supported the tax department’s power to amend an assessment under Section 122(5A) *as long as the taxpayer is given a proper opportunity of hearing*—which is a major due-process point.

---

### 3) **Super Tax vs Petroleum Concession Agreements: “If You Cross the Cap, Investors May Go to Arbitration”**
**Explanation:**  
PPEPCA warned that many oil & gas investors have concession agreements (PCAs) that legally protect “tax stability” and cap tax rates. Their position is: if Super Tax under Sections 4B/4C pushes taxation beyond what the PCA allows, companies may invoke international arbitration clauses. The concern isn’t just tax cost—it's credibility: investors put money in long-term, high-risk projects because fiscal terms are promised to remain stable. If the state is seen as changing the deal after the fact, the dispute can become international, expensive, and reputation-damaging.

---

### 4) **Section 7E Property Tax Turns into a Fairness Issue: “Not Everyone Is Being Treated the Same”**
**Explanation:**  
Pakistan Tax Bar Association says enforcement of Section 7E is happening aggressively in Punjab and Sindh (notices, forced compliance), but not in Islamabad, KP and Balochistan because High Court judgments there have declared Section 7E unconstitutional—and those orders have not been suspended. So taxpayers in some regions are effectively not paying, while others are being chased. This has become a constitutional fairness question (equal treatment, due process), not just a tax dispute.

---

### 5) **Section 7E Is Still in Legal “Limbo”: Different High Courts, One Federal Tax, No Final Verdict Yet**
**Explanation:**  
The file highlights that various High Courts have taken different positions on whether Section 7E is valid. Appeals were taken to the Supreme Court and later shifted to the Federal Constitutional Court after constitutional changes, but there is no final nationwide outcome yet. That creates uncertainty for taxpayers: in some places, enforcement continues; in others, it is practically frozen due to court protection. For the market, this uncertainty matters because Section 7E impacts property holding cost and can affect transactions and valuations.

---

### 6) **PRA Enforcement Gets Real: Businesses Sealed for Not Issuing E-Bills and Manipulating Sales**
**Explanation:**  
Punjab Revenue Authority sealed outlets (including a well-known food chain) for failure to issue e-bills and for alleged tampering with sales records. PRA is also monitoring POS systems more closely to ensure real-time reporting and recoveries where businesses charged sales tax from customers but didn’t deposit it into the treasury. Practically, this shows enforcement is shifting from “paper checks” to “live monitoring,” and businesses with weak POS discipline face immediate operational consequences.

---

### 7) **FBR Cracks Down at Airports: Dismissals Over Illegal Clearances and Baggage Misuse**
**Explanation:**  
FBR imposed major penalties, including dismissals, on customs officials for allowing non-duty paid goods to be cleared under baggage schemes and for procedural violations (including suspicious handling of currency declaration processes). The broader signal is internal accountability: FBR is trying to cut “leakage points” at airports by taking disciplinary action and considering transfers/rotation of officials to reduce misuse of authority.

---

### 8) **LHC Takes Notice of FBR Reward Schemes: “Are Public Funds Being Distributed Lawfully?”**
**Explanation:**  
The Lahore High Court issued notices to senior government stakeholders over allegations that FBR reward schemes (including IT-based reward systems) enabled large payouts to senior officers beyond lawful authorization and proper oversight. The petition raises issues like whether the correct statutory approvals existed, whether the governance structure was valid, and whether public money was distributed transparently. If this case moves forward strongly, it can reshape how incentive/reward frameworks operate across revenue departments.

---

## The Full Picture (One-Paragraph Wrap)
Across these updates, the direction is consistent: **enforcement is intensifying** (customs, airports, PRA), **courts are shaping how deductions and tax powers are applied** (intangibles), and **constitutional fairness and investor protections are becoming central battlegrounds** (Section 7E and Super Tax under PCAs). For businesses and professionals, the practical takeaway is: strengthen documentation, tighten POS/e-billing compliance, and watch litigation trends closely because the “rules in action” are being defined through enforcement and court outcomes, not just through statutes.

Below are **positive findings**, framed in the tone, structure, and judicial discipline ordinarily adopted by a **Division Bench of the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue**, strictly confined to the facts on record and the settled legal position, and **in favour of the taxpayer**:

---

### Positive Findings of the Tribunal

We have carefully examined the facts of the case, the impugned orders, the submissions of the learned Authorized Representative, and the statutory provisions along with the binding judicial precedents cited before us.

At the outset, it is an admitted and undisputed position that the appellant is not engaged in the business of trading or commercial sale of imported goods. The imports under consideration comprise specialized kitchen equipment, restaurant fittings, machinery, and raw materials, all of which are either capitalized as fixed assets or consumed in the appellant’s own restaurant operations. No material has been brought on record by the Department to establish that the appellant derived any income from the sale of such imported goods.

Section 148(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 provides for collection of advance tax at the import stage. However, the character of such tax—whether adjustable or attaining finality—is governed by subsection (7) thereof. The language employed by the legislature in section 148(7), namely *“on the income of the importer arising from the imports”*, is deliberate and cannot be rendered otiose. It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that no word used by the legislature is redundant or without purpose, particularly in a fiscal statute.

The contention of the tax authorities that tax collected under section 148 automatically assumes the character of final or minimum tax merely because the importer does not fall within the definition of an “industrial undertaking” under section 2(29C) is legally misconceived. The determination under section 148(7) is not contingent solely upon the status of the importer, but primarily upon the nature of income, if any, arising from the imports themselves.

The judicial consensus on this issue now stands conclusively settled. It has consistently been held that imports, by themselves, do not constitute income; rather, they represent expenditure or acquisition of assets. Income arises only when such imported goods are sold or otherwise exploited commercially so as to generate profit. Where imported goods are consumed for self-use in rendering services, no income can be said to “arise from imports” within the meaning of section 148(7).

We find that this precise question has been exhaustively examined and authoritatively settled by the superior courts. The interpretation adopted by the Islamabad High Court—subsequently affirmed by the Honourable Supreme Court by dismissal of the civil petitions—lays down that the Department must first determine, as a matter of fact, whether income has arisen from the imports against which tax has been collected. In the absence of such income, the tax collected under section 148 retains the character of adjustable advance tax by virtue of section 168(2) of the Ordinance.

The same legal position has thereafter been reaffirmed by the Sindh High Court, which expressly held that tax collected on imports made for self-use, including plant, machinery, and operational inputs, cannot be treated as final tax unless income directly arises from the import transaction itself. These pronouncements, having attained finality, are binding under Article 189 of the Constitution and leave no room for a contrary interpretation.

Applying the above settled principles to the facts before us, we find that:
- The appellant did not sell the imported goods;
- No income arose to the appellant from the imports per se;
- The appellant’s income arises from provision of restaurant and related services, which are independently subjected to tax under the normal regime; and
- The tax liability of the appellant under the normal provisions exceeds the tax collected at the import stage.

In these circumstances, treating the tax collected under section 148 as final or minimum tax leads to manifest absurdity and results in taxation of expenditure rather than income, which is neither contemplated nor permitted under the scheme of the Ordinance.

We further observe that the impugned treatment has been upheld by the learned CIR(A) without undertaking the mandatory factual inquiry required under section 148(7), namely whether any income arose from the imports. Such an approach is contrary to law and inconsistent with the binding judicial precedents discussed above.

Accordingly, we hold that the tax collected from the appellant under section 148 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 on the import of raw materials and fixed assets, having been imported for self-consumption and not for sale, does **not** constitute final or minimum tax. The same is to be treated as **adjustable advance tax** and allowed as credit against the appellant’s normal tax liability for the relevant tax year.

The orders passed by the learned ACIR and maintained by the learned CIR(A) on this issue are therefore **unsustainable in law**, suffer from misapplication of section 148(7), and are hereby **set aside**.

---

Below is a **refined, legally structured contention**, drafted **as Authorized Representative of the appellant**, in **polished appellate style**, and suitable for oral and written submissions before the ATIR:

---

### Contention of the Authorized Representative

Without prejudice to the preceding grounds, it is respectfully submitted that the learned Commissioner (Appeals) has failed to adjudicate a vital and material plea raised by the appellant, namely that the learned ACIR has subjected the same stream of income to tax twice—once by treating the tax collected under section 148 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 as final tax, and again by taxing the appellant’s income under the Normal Tax Regime.

It is submitted that such treatment is wholly alien to the scheme of the Ordinance. Where tax collected under section 148 is treated as final or minimum tax, the corresponding income stands discharged to that extent and cannot again be brought to tax under the normal provisions. Conversely, where income is assessed under the normal regime, tax collected under section 148 necessarily assumes the character of adjustable advance tax under section 168(2). The Ordinance does not permit a hybrid approach whereby tax collected under section 148 is accorded finality while the same income is simultaneously subjected to normal taxation.

The appellant had specifically raised this issue before the learned CIR(A); however, the impugned appellate order is conspicuously silent on this plea. Non-adjudication of a substantive ground, going to the very root of the assessment, vitiates the appellate order and renders it legally unsustainable. It is a settled principle of law that an appellate authority is duty-bound to deal with and return findings on every material ground raised before it, particularly where failure to do so results in manifest illegality such as double taxation.

It is further submitted that double taxation of the same income, in the absence of express statutory sanction, is impermissible and has consistently been disapproved by the superior courts. The impugned treatment not only lacks support from the Ordinance but also runs contrary to the settled judicial principle that fiscal statutes must be interpreted so as to avoid absurdity and inequitable results.

In these circumstances, the failure of the learned CIR(A) to address and decide this specific plea, coupled with the continuation of an assessment resulting in double taxation, renders the impugned order liable to be set aside on this ground alone.

---

If you want, I can:
- tighten this into a **short oral argument note** for the Bench, or  
- cross-link it explicitly with **section 148(7) and section 168(2)** for maximum impact.

As a member of the Division Bench of ATIR, please read the content below and prepare positive findings (in favour of the taxpayer): 

The learned ACIR treated the tax collected under section 148 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Ordinance), on the import of raw materials and fixed assets, as final tax rather than as adjustable advance tax. The said decision of the ACIR has been maintained by CIR(A) on the grounds that the tax deducted under the said section is adjustable only for the taxpayers who are “Industrial Undertaking” as defined u/s 2(29C) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. 

The Authorized Representative (AR) of the appellant challenged this treatment, contending that the imported goods were acquired solely for the appellant’s own business use and did not generate any income “arising from imports” within the meaning of section 148(7) of the Ordinance. It was therefore argued that the tax collected at the import stage could not attain finality and must, by operation of section 168(2) of the Ordinance, be treated as advance tax adjustable against the appellant’s normal tax liability for the relevant tax year.

AR of the appellant also highlight that the same issue had recently decided by the Chairmen Bench, Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Islamabad bearing ITA No. 309/IB/25 dated November 05, 2025 in case of Weatherford Oil Tool Middle East Limited, whereby it was held that tax collected under section 148 is not minimum tax for taxpayers engaged in rendering services and do not have income arising from sale of imported goods. The relevant extracts from the decision are as follows:

"…………..
61. The relevant provisions of section 148(7), as applicable for tax year 2021, are reproduced hereunder:

"The tax required to be collected under this section shall be minimum Tax on the income of the importer arising from the imports subject to sub-section (1) and this subsection shall not apply in the case of import of goods on which tax is required to be collected under this section at the rate of 1% or 2% by an industrial undertaking for its own use."

62. In our opinion, the use of words "on the income of the importer arising from the Imports" Is significant here. The tax collected under section 148 is minimum tax in respect of income arising from imports and if there is no income arising from imports then such tax cannot be considered as minimum tax. Previously, the tax collected under section 148 was final tax and this bench held as follows in ITA No. 1236/18/23 dated
September 15, 2025:

71. The use of words “on the income of the importer arising from the imports” is significant as to finality of tax collected under section 148 of the Ordinance. The tax department has maintained that tax collected under section 148 is the final tax for everyone except for the exceptions carved out under clauses “a” to “e” of sub-section (7) of section 148 or elsewhere in the Ordinance. Whereas the taxpayers assert that tax collected under section 148 is final tax only in case of those importers who sell such imported goods, and the income generated from sale of such imported goods is therefore not subjected to any further taxation.

72. The taxpayer argues that tax paid under section 148 on goads which are Imported and not sold but rather used by the taxpayers, particularly the service sector taxpayers, shall not be considered as final tax because they are not earning income from sale of such goods. So, the question in this case is "Whether tax collected under section 148 Is final tax for the
taxpayers in the service sector who do not sell the imported goods but rather use them for their own business?"

73. No text of law can be redundant as it is a settled principle that 0redundancy cannot be attributable the law". If the contention of the department Is accepted than the words "income arising from imports" become redundant hence prima facie the contention of the department is incorrect.

74. If say for the sake of argument, it is considered that telecommunication income or income from IT services also falls under "income arising from imports" then this argument would be against the tax department itself. Because if the tax collected under section 148 is final on such Income from telecom services or IT services, then department cannot ask for any more tax on the telecom income or income for IT services earned by the taxpayer.

75. It is evident that imports are not income, but only expenditure. If the tax collected on imports by a service provider on imports for own use Is considered final tax on his income, then such service provider does not need to pay normal tax on his income but obviously this is not the intention of law. Therefore, the only appropriate interpretation would be that income arising from sale of imported goods shall be subject to final discharge of tax liability where tax is paid under section 148 of the Ordinance. Any other interpretation would create absurdity which cannot be attributed to the law.

76. The same principle has been very eloquently elaborated by Honorable Tribunal in its decision ITA No.1414/IB/20 dated March 16, 2022:

"The Hon'ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case titled M/s Elahi Cotton Mills Ltd, v. Federation of Pakistan, etc, (PLD 1997SC582), it was held that a presumptive tax can only be imposed on items when it is regarded as citizen's income; if no income is being derived from the imports, there can be no question of final tax and any advance payment shall always remain adjustable. In the instant case, admittedly, no income is generated from the sale of the imparted goods and there is no question of section148(7) being applicable;"

77. The learned Tribunal also noted in the same decision:

"To our mind, the sentence "income of the importer arising from the Imports" used in subsection (7) of section 148 of the Ordinance is of broad significance and cannot be lost sight. It provides inter alia that the tax required to be collected under this section shall be a final tax on the income of the importer arising from the imports. We may a so observe that the expression "income" has been defined in section 2(29) of the Ordinance which itself includes the amount subject to collection of tax under section 148 of the Ordinance but had there been an intention to treat all types of transactions as income, the legislature could have stated that "the tax collected under this section shall be a final tax" rather than using the words "income of the importer arising from imports". This unambiguous selection of the words makes it abundantly clear that only those goods fall in the scope of the final tax regime that is imported far resale to make profits. For the foregoing reasons, the tax collected by the Customs Authorities under section 148(1) of the Ordinance is adjustable against the other tax liability of the appellant."

78. Similar principle was also elaborated by Honorable Tribunal in its decision (para 12(a)) reported as 2004 PTD 125 while interpreting provisions of section 8OC relating to final tax on imports when tax was collected under section 53(5):

"Although section B0-C(2)(ii) does not provide any except from said provision to a commercial importer as claimed by the learned A.R., for the assessee, yet the entire Scheme of Presumptive Tax Regime Is focused on taxing the deemed income which is in the nature of turnover or sales of such goods, which are
subsequently sold and generate profits. Apparently machinery and equipments imported and installed by an assessee in his industries undertaking is a fixed asset and does not generate profit in terms of sales or supplies like any other goods."

79. Similar principle was also elaborated by Honorable Tribunal in its decision (para 9) reported as 103 TAX 383 while interpreting provisions of section 8OC relating to final tax an imports when tax was collected under section 53(5):

"The word "commercial import" does not figure in the law and to this extent the contention of the DR is correct. However, when the provision of the section 148(7) of the Ordinance are minutely examined it transpires that the legislature has used the words .... income of the importer arising from ... ". These words, particularly the word 'arising', make the intention of the legislature manifestly clear. By
reference to these words, in our view, what is brought within the ambit of final tax regime is a transaction which involves an import to make a profit Le. a commercial import or import undertaken for resale with the intention of making profit. No doubt the definition of expression 'income' itself includes the amount subject to collection of tax under section 148 of the Ordinance but had the intention been to treat all types of transactions as 'income' the legislature would have not used the words "income of the importer arising front" rather the wording would have been' ... .the tax collected under this section shall be a final tax ..... This cautious and discreet choice of words makes it amply clear that within the scope of final tax regime only those goods fall which are imported for resale to make a profit. This rationale has already been appreciated in the decision 2004 PTO 1251 referred to supra and following this judgment, we hold that the items which are imported for the purpose of self-use fall outside the ambit of final tax regime. Accordingly, we hold that the tax withheld/collected at the import stage in respect of the vehicles remains an adjustable advance tax."

80. Similar principle was also elaborated by Honorable Tribunal in its decision (para 5) reported as 2013 PTO 1165 while interpreting provisions of section 8OC relating to final tax on imports when tax was collected under section 53(5):

'We have heard the respective submissions of both parties, perused the relevant record. We are of the considered opinion that learned CIT(A) has rightly recorded the finding that Assessing Officer did not bother to understand and appreciate the facts of the case and he should have sought guidance from his senior officers. The assessee Company has various contracts and raw material is imported for usage in these contracts. Thus it cannot be taxed twice, one, at the time of import stage and against at the stage of fulfilling contractual obligation. Full and final discharge of tax liability is to be applied at the final stage i.e. at the time of contractual payments and tax deducted at import stage is to be adjusted. With these findings we fully endorse view of the learned
CIT{A)."

81. The same principle has also been elaborated by Honorable Islamabad High Court in its decision /TR # 63 of 2015 dated October 13, 2022, Telenor Pakistan (Pvt) Limited vs CIR, (upheld by Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan in civil petitions no.4651,4652,2588 to 2616 of 2022) as fallows:

"Section 148(7) states that the advance tax collected shall be a final tax “on the income of the importer arising from the imports.” The legislature has not said that the tax collected under section 148(1) shall be a final tax on the income of the importer. It has explicitly provided that it is the final tax on the income of the Importer "arising from the imports" against the value of which advance tax is calculated and collected. In the event that the legislature meant for the advance tax collected to be a final tax in relation to the income of the importer for the taxpayer, there was no reason to further qualify that the income in question is that
"arising from the imposts"

82. In the light of the principles laid down in the case laws discussed above, it is held that the tax paid by service sector companies under section 148 on import of goods shall not be considered as final tax unless such goods are sold by the service sector companies because no income is arising from such imports for the service sector companies.

83. However, if the service provider sells such imported goods, only then the tax collected at import stage becomes final tax to the extent of income arising from sale of such imported goods. The text used in section 148(7) "on the income of the importer arising from the imports" only refers to the income from “sale of such imported goods” and no other income as already discussed above.

84. This is not the case of tax department that the subject taxpayer has sold the imported goods in the current year therefore the appeal of the taxpayer succeeds, the tax collected under section 148 is allowed as
adjustable tax and the orders of DCIR and learned CIR(A) are hereby annulled."

63. Although the word “final” is replaced by “minimum” in subsection
(7) of section 148 however, in our opinion, the principles discussed in the above judgment issued by this bench shall continue to apply. If the said interpretation is upheld, the words “arising from the imports” mentioned in section 148(7), which qualify the income against which the advance tax collected is to be treated as final tax, would be surplusage. As each and every word used by the legislature in a fiscal statute is to be given meaning, the plain reading of section 148(7) suggests that the first exception to the declaration of finality of the advance tax collected from an importer is that it will be deemed to be final tax against an importer deriving income from the imports against the value of which advance tax has been collected under section 148(1) of the Ordinance.

12. Section 4 is a charging section of the Ordinance. Section 4(4)(b) provides that “certain classes of income may be subject to ... collection of tax under Division II of Part V of Chapter X ...”. 13. Also of relevance is section 168(2) of the Ordinance. ### Refined Findings of the Tribunal

We have carefully considered the facts of the case, the impugned orders, the submissions of the learned Authorized Representative, and the statutory framework governing section 148 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, along with the binding judicial precedents cited before us.

It is an admitted position on record that the appellant is not engaged in the business of trading or commercial sale of imported goods. The appellant operates a nationwide chain of restaurants under a franchise arrangement and derives its income exclusively from the provision of restaurant and allied services. The imported items in question comprise specialized kitchen equipment, restaurant machinery, fittings, and raw materials, which are either capitalized as fixed assets or consumed in the appellant’s own operations. No material has been produced by the Department to establish that the appellant sold any of the imported goods or derived income directly from the imports themselves.

The learned ACIR, however, treated the tax collected under section 148 as final (or minimum) tax merely on the premise that the appellant does not qualify as an “industrial undertaking” within the meaning of section 2(29C) of the Ordinance. This approach reflects a fundamental misreading of section 148(7). The determinative factor under subsection (7) is not the status of the importer alone, but whether income has in fact arisen to the importer from the imports. The legislature has consciously employed the qualifying expression *“on the income of the importer arising from the imports”*, and it is a settled principle of interpretation that no word used in a fiscal statute can be treated as redundant or surplusage.

This precise legal question has now been conclusively settled through a consistent line of judicial authority. The Islamabad High Court, in Telenor Pakistan (Pvt.) Limited, after a detailed examination of sections 4, 148, and 168 of the Ordinance, categorically held that tax collected under section 148(1) can attain finality only where income arises to the importer from the imports themselves. Where no such income arises, the tax collected remains adjustable by operation of section 168(2). This interpretation has since attained finality, having been affirmed by the Honourable Supreme Court through dismissal of the Department’s civil petitions, thereby rendering the principle binding under Article 189 of the Constitution.

More significantly, the identical issue, arising in materially indistinguishable circumstances involving a service sector taxpayer, has very recently been examined and decided by the Chairmen Bench of the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Islamabad. In that case, the Tribunal categorically held that tax collected under section 148 on imports consumed by a service provider for rendering services does not constitute minimum or final tax in the absence of income arising from sale of imported goods. The Chairmen Bench reasoned that imports, by their very nature, represent expenditure or acquisition of assets and cannot be equated with income unless the imported goods are sold to generate profits. The Bench further observed that any other interpretation would lead to absurdity by converting tax on expenditure into final tax on income, a result never intended by the legislature.

The factual matrix in the present appeal is indistinguishable from that considered by the Chairmen Bench. Here too, the appellant is a service provider; the imported goods are consumed in the course of providing services; and no income has arisen from the sale of such imports. Nothing has been brought on record by the Department to rebut these facts or to demonstrate that the appellant earned income “arising from imports” within the meaning of section 148(7). In fact, the normal tax liability of the appellant exceeds the tax collected at the import stage, which by itself reinforces the conclusion that the imports do not represent a presumptive income stream.

We further note that the learned CIR(A) upheld the impugned treatment without undertaking the mandatory factual inquiry envisaged under section 148(7), namely, whether any income accrued to the appellant from the imports. Such omission runs contrary to the law as laid down by the superior courts and repeatedly reaffirmed by this Tribunal, including by the Chairmen Bench.

In view of the foregoing discussion, and respectfully following the binding precedents of the Honourable Supreme Court, the Islamabad High Court, the Sindh High Court, and the recent Chairmen Bench of this Tribunal on identical facts relating to service providers, we hold that the tax collected from the appellant under section 148 of the Ordinance on imports made for self-consumption does not constitute final or minimum tax. The same is liable to be treated as adjustable advance tax and allowed as credit against the appellant’s normal tax liability for the relevant tax year.

Accordingly, the impugned orders passed by the learned ACIR and maintained by the learned CIR(A), being based on an erroneous interpretation of section 148(7) and contrary to settled law, are hereby set aside on this issue.

### Positive Findings of the Tribunal

We have carefully examined the facts on record, the impugned order, the submissions of the learned Authorized Representative, and the relevant statutory provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

The core issue for determination is whether the appellant qualifies as an “industrial undertaking” within the meaning of section 2(29C) of the Ordinance so as to be eligible for tax credit under section 65B. The learned ACIR disallowed the claim solely on the premise that the appellant does not fall within the statutory definition of an industrial undertaking. We find this conclusion to be unsupported by the language of the law and the facts on record.

Section 2(29C)(a)(i) defines an industrial undertaking, inter alia, as an undertaking which is set up in Pakistan and which involves the *subjection of goods or materials to a process which substantially changes their original condition*. It is not disputed that the appellant is established in Pakistan, employs more than ten persons, and carries on its operations through the use of electrical energy. These statutory prerequisites stand satisfied and have not been controverted by the Department.

As regards the nature of activities undertaken by the appellant, it is evident from the record that raw food items are subjected to a series of processes including cooking, preparation, processing, and packaging through the use of mechanical equipment and energy-driven systems. These processes result in finished food products that are materially distinct in character, form, and utility from the raw inputs. Such transformation squarely falls within the statutory expression “substantial change in original condition” as used in section 2(29C)(a)(i) of the Ordinance.

We are unable to subscribe to the narrow interpretation adopted by the learned ACIR, whereby food processing and preparation have been excluded from the ambit of industrial activity. The definition under section 2(29C) does not restrict industrial undertakings to heavy manufacturing alone, nor does it exclude undertakings engaged in processing consumable goods. What the statute requires is a substantial transformation of goods through a process, which requirement stands fully satisfied in the present case.

We further note that the definition of industrial undertaking was introduced by the Finance Act, 2005 and subsequently amended by the Finance Act, 2010. As clarified by FBR Circular No. 10 of 2010, the amendments were editorial in nature and did not alter the substantive scope of the definition. The legislative intent has consistently remained to extend the benefit of investment tax credit to undertakings engaged in manufacturing or processing activities that result in transformation of goods.

It is also relevant to observe that section 65B is an incentive provision and, as such, warrants a purposive and liberal interpretation consistent with its object of encouraging investment in plant and machinery within Pakistan. A restrictive construction, such as the one adopted in the impugned order, defeats the very purpose of the provision and is not supported by the statutory scheme.

In the absence of any finding that the appellant’s activities do not involve processing or transformation of goods, and in view of the fact that all statutory conditions prescribed under section 2(29C) stand fulfilled, the disallowance of tax credit under section 65B is found to be legally unsustainable. The learned ACIR has failed to appreciate the true nature of the appellant’s operations and has misapplied the definition of industrial undertaking.

Accordingly, we hold that the appellant qualifies as an industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 2(29C) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. The tax credit claimed under section 65B has been validly claimed and is allowable. The impugned disallowance is therefore set aside.
