Q1. Who is the withholding agent for digital transactions, the customer or the payment intermediary/courier? Who should not be withholding tax?
Section 6A, read together with the special collection mechanism in section 153(2A), is designed so that the withholding responsibility for digitally ordered goods and services rests primarily on payment intermediaries and courier companies, not on the customer or the seller. Payment intermediaries (banks, gateways, wallets, etc.) are to deduct 1% on digital payments, while courier companies handling COD are to deduct 2% on the gross amount they collect. In this framework, OUP SMC is not a withholding agent on its own receipts, and ordinary customers (schools) are not withholding agents under section 6A as such; their only potential role as withholding agents arises under the general provisions of section 153(1), which were enacted earlier for services and other payments.
Q2. Can there be more than one withholding agent (customer and intermediary)? Which tax is final in such cases?
As the law currently stands, there is a technical risk that two parties could be treated as withholding agents on the same payment:
•	Section 153(2A) begins with a “notwithstanding” clause, creating a special rule for digital transactions through intermediaries and couriers, but it does not expressly state that section 153(1) no longer applies to those payments.
•	The negative list in section 153(5), which sets out payments on which the general withholding under section 153(1) does not apply, has not yet been updated to exclude transactions that fall within section 6A / 153(2A).
On a literal reading, this means that a prescribed buyer could still consider itself obliged to withhold under section 153(1)(b) on payments for digital services, even where the intermediary/courier is already withholding under section 6A via section 153(2A), resulting in double withholding. In such a scenario, the tax collected under section 6A remains the final tax on the digital transaction income, whereas any additional tax deducted under section 153(1)(b) would, in principle, be refundable/adjustable in OUP’s hands rather than altering the “final tax” nature of section 6A.
Q3. How should this double withholding risk be managed in practice?
To mitigate the risk of two separate withholdings on the same payment, it is advisable to make the intended hierarchy explicit in your invoice. ### Withholding Tax Mechanics for Digital Transactions under Section 6A — Roles, Risks, and Practical Safeguards

Section 6A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, read with the special collection mechanism in section 153(2A), establishes a distinct withholding framework for digitally ordered goods and services. Under this regime, the primary withholding responsibility rests with payment intermediaries (such as banks, payment gateways, and digital wallets) and courier companies, rather than with the customer or the seller. Specifically, payment intermediaries are required to deduct tax at 1% on digital payments, while courier companies are required to deduct tax at 2% on cash-on-delivery (COD) collections, both calculated on the gross amount collected. Within this framework, OUP SMC is not a withholding agent on its own receipts under section 6A, and ordinary customers (including schools) are likewise not intended to act as withholding agents for these digital transactions. Any withholding role of customers would arise only, if at all, under the general provisions of section 153(1), which predate the digital tax regime and apply broadly to services and certain other payments.

As the law currently stands, however, there is a technical risk that more than one party could be viewed as a withholding agent in respect of the same payment. While section 153(2A) begins with a “notwithstanding” clause—thereby introducing a special rule for digital transactions routed through intermediaries and couriers—it does not expressly state that section 153(1) ceases to apply to those payments. In addition, the negative list in section 153(5), which specifies payments excluded from general withholding under section 153(1), has not yet been updated to carve out transactions that fall within section 6A read with section 153(2A). On a literal reading, this creates the possibility that a prescribed buyer could still consider itself obliged to withhold tax under section 153(1)(b) on payments for digital services, even where tax has already been withheld by the intermediary or courier under section 6A. In such circumstances, while the tax collected under section 6A would continue to constitute final tax on the digital transaction income, any additional tax deducted under section 153(1)(b) would, in principle, be refundable or adjustable in OUP’s hands and would not alter the final-tax character of section 6A.

From a practical perspective, this risk of double withholding can be mitigated through clear contractual and invoicing safeguards. Given that section 153(2A) expressly overrides subsection (1), the intended legislative hierarchy is that the special digital withholding mechanism should prevail over the general rule for payments that squarely fall within section 6A. To operationalize this intent, invoices may include a clear caveat stating that where a payment intermediary or courier company is acting as the withholding agent under section 6A read with section 153(2A), the buyer should not simultaneously treat itself as a withholding agent under section 153(1) in respect of the same payment. This approach aligns with the policy objective of the digital regime—namely, centralized and streamlined withholding at the intermediary or courier level—and provides OUP SMC with a defensible basis to resist duplicative withholding in routine operations.

Accordingly, for digital transactions that clearly fall within the scope of section 6A and are processed through intermediaries or couriers who are fulfilling their statutory withholding obligations, the recommended position is that no parallel withholding under section 153(1) should be applied by the buyer on the same payment. In such cases, the intermediary or courier withholding under section 6A read with section 153(2A) should be treated as the sole operative mechanism, and any attempt by the buyer to deduct tax again under section 153(1)(b) would merely create double withholding and an avoidable refund position for OUP SMC. Until the law is clarified through a corresponding amendment to the negative list in section 153(5), this contractual and procedural safeguard represents the most practical means of preserving the intended single, final tax collection under section 6A.

It is also important to clarify the position where a payment intermediary or courier fails to fulfill its withholding obligations. In such a situation, the receipts of OUP SMC do not fall outside the scope of section 6A merely because of a procedural lapse by the withholding agent. Section 6A taxes income by reference to its nature—namely, digitally ordered and digitally delivered goods or services supplied from within Pakistan through a locally operated platform—and the applicability of the final tax regime depends on this character, not on the actual act of deduction at source. Where a withholding agent fails to withhold or deposit tax, the primary legal exposure rests with that agent under sections 161 and 205 of the Ordinance, including recovery of tax not withheld, default surcharge, and penalties. OUP SMC does not lose the benefit of the final tax regime solely due to such a failure by the intermediary or courier.

Finally, as regards the tax base on which withholding is to be computed, section 6A is explicit in applying to the “gross amounts of receipts” arising from digitally ordered goods or services. Accordingly, the payment intermediary or courier is required to withhold tax on the full invoice value, including any applicable provincial sales tax, and not on a net-of-tax or net-of-charges basis. This treatment is consistent with the statutory language and with earlier advice that the 1% or 2% withholding under section 6A is to be calculated on gross receipts inclusive of sales tax. For consistency and to avoid disputes, both customers (where section 153 is considered) and intermediaries or couriers (for section 6A) should therefore reference the same full invoice value rather than applying withholding on a reduced net amount.

Users in Pakistan access content through school subscriptions or access codes, and access tokens may also be sold with physical books as a blended offering. The platform is available via an online portal and Android application, supporting secure downloads and online/offline use (as per the workflow previously shared). Commercially, revenue arises from school subscription fees and the sale of access tokens bundled with physical books, while costs comprise (i) royalties’ payable to authors based on net receipts from e-books sold and (ii) annual hosting/licensing and per-user service charges payable to MagicBox through OUP UK, which are recharged to OUP SMC under the group’s central technology recharge mechanism.

(iii)	Oxford Extend is an LMS/CMS platform powered by Knowledge Platform (based in Pakistan) that is white-labelled and customized for OUP SMC, enabling schools to subscribe for access to educational materials mapped to OUP books and Student Learning Outcomes (SLOs). The platform offers interactive tools for teachers, supports hosting of e-books published by OUP SMC, and provides secure offline access through an Android application (as per the workflow previously shared). Commercially, revenue arises from platform subscription fees and the sale of e-books for access through the platform in addition to the subscription. The cost model comprises (i) royalties’ payable to authors based on net receipts from e-books sold along with subscriptions, (ii) e-book hosting charges payable to Knowledge Platform on per-user, slab-wise rates linked to the number of e-books sold per subscription, and (iii) service charges payable to Knowledge Platform for platform usage.

3.	Our opinion has been sought on the implications of income tax and sales tax on the above products of the OUP SMC. 


4.	INCOME TAX IMPLICATION 

4.1	The Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] does not define the term goods. Nevertheless, section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 defines goods to include 'every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money, stocks, shares, and securities.' Likewise, Article 260(1) of the Constitution of Pakistan defines goods to encompass all materials, commodities, and articles. Intangible digital offerings such as online access rights, e-subscriptions, and digital learning content do not fall within the traditional concept of movable property or commodities. 

4.2	On the other hand, services, as defined under provincial sales tax statutes and by the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), broadly include all activities other than the supply of goods, encompassing facilities, advantages, or amenities provided for consideration. Accordingly, where no tangible movable property is transferred, the underlying transaction is regarded as a service for tax purposes.

4.3	In the absence of explicit judicial precedent concerning digital platforms, the most defensible interpretation is that online digital platforms represent the provision of services rather than the sale of goods. These platforms provide users with access to content or functionalities, an advantage, without transferring ownership of a tangible item. Consequently, payments received by OUP SMC for platforms such as Oxford Reading Buddy, My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend represent consideration for services within the meaning of section 153(1)(b) of the Ordinance. Corporate customers making such payments are therefore required to withhold tax at the applicable rate for services.

4.4	Prior to the Finance Act 2025, the Ordinance contained no dedicated framework addressing the taxation of the digital economy. Accordingly, income derived by OUP SMC from its e-learning platforms was treated as ordinary business income, taxable under the normal regime. The Finance Act 2025, however, introduced a significant policy shift through the insertion of section 6A into the Ordinance and the inclusion of new statutory definitions for 'digitally delivered services' and 'e-commerce.' These provisions collectively brought digital transactions within the ambit of a final tax regime. 

4.5	Section 6A imposes tax on the gross receipts arising from the supply of digitally ordered goods or services made from within Pakistan through locally operated online platforms, including websites and digital marketplaces. For ready reference, the relevant statutory definitions and charging provision are reproduced below for ease of understanding:

(17C) “digitally delivered services” means any service delivered over the internet or electronic networks, where the delivery is automated and requires minimal or no human intervention including music, audio and video streaming services, cloud services, online software applications services, services delivered through online inter-personal interaction i.e., tele medicines, e-learning etc., online banking services, architectural design services, research and consultancy reports, accounting services in the form of digital files or any other online facility;

(19AA) “e-commerce” means sale or purchase of goods and services conducted over computer networks by methods specifically designed for the purpose of receiving or placing of orders either through websites, mobile applications or online marketplace having digital ordering features by using either mobile phone, iPad, Tablet or automated computer-to-computer ordering system

6A. Tax on payments for digital transactions in e-commerce platforms.– (1) Subject to this Ordinance, a tax shall be imposed, at the rate specified in Division IVA of Part I of the First Schedule, on every person who receives payment for supply of digitally ordered goods or services which are delivered from within Pakistan using locally operated online platforms including online marketplace or websites: 

Provided that the export proceeds subjected to withholding under section 154 and 154A shall not fall within the ambit of this section. 

(2) The tax imposed under sub-section (1) shall be computed by applying the relevant rate of tax to the gross amounts of receipts mentioned in sub-section (1).

4.6	In this regard, we would like to highlight that section 6A of the Ordinance provides a specific charging mechanism whereby tax is imposed “on every person who receives payment for supply of digitally ordered goods or services which are delivered from within Pakistan using locally operated online platforms including online marketplace or websites,” and is chargeable “on the gross amounts of receipts” at the rates prescribed in Division IVA of the First Schedule (i.e., 1% for digital payments and 2% for cash-on-delivery). A key feature of this regime is therefore that it taxes gross receipts (including sales tax, where applicable) arising from the supply of digitally ordered goods or services made from within Pakistan through locally operated online or digital platforms.

4.7	Based on the commercial understanding, the digital platforms operated by OUP SMC exhibit all essential elements of section 6A of the Ordinance. In each case, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate and Oxford Extend, educational content is digitally ordered and delivered to users located in Pakistan and is accessed electronically through personalized lockers, encrypted applications and/or subscription-based portals, without any transfer of tangible property or a physical software copy.

4.8	Customers, primarily schools (and in some cases individual learners), purchase access tokens or annual subscriptions to use the relevant learning materials, and the substance of these arrangements is therefore the provision of digitally delivered services, namely, access to and use of an online system and content, rather than the sale of a physical good. Correspondingly, the subscription fees, access charges and e-book related receipts derived from ORB, My E-Mate and Extend continue to qualify as receipts from “digitally ordered…services…delivered from within Pakistan” and remain taxable on a gross-receipts basis under section 6A at 1% (for digital modes) or 2% (for COD), consistent with the earlier advice.

4.9	The fact that certain platforms are hosted on servers outside Pakistan does not dislodge this conclusion. Section 6A of the Ordinance looks to where the goods or services are delivered from in a commercial and legal sense and whether they are supplied “using locally operated online platforms,” rather than the physical location of hardware or server infrastructure. Here, contracts with schools are entered into by OUP SMC, user access and licensing rights are provisioned and managed locally, and financial settlements with customers are received and administered by OUP SMC in Pakistan. 

4.10	Revenue arising from access fees, subscriptions and platform-related charges therefore represents gross receipts derived from within Pakistan, particularly since the platforms also involve continuous digital support, maintenance and content management, reinforcing that the income is generated from an ongoing service relationship rather than a one-off sale. While the underlying infrastructure may be globally developed and certain hosting may be offshore, its operation in Pakistan through OUP SMC’s authorized management of rights, payments and delivery constitutes a local digital presence for income-tax purposes. On this basis, the updated hosting details merely confirm that OUP SMC remains the “person who receives payment” for digital supplies within Pakistan that fall squarely within the scope of section 6A of the Ordinance, and is accordingly subject to final tax on the prescribed percentages of its gross receipts.

4.11	Taken together, these features align precisely with the statutory definitions of 'digitally delivered services' and 'e-commerce' introduced through the Finance Act 2025. Accordingly, the income derived by OUP SMC from Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend qualifies as gross receipts chargeable to tax under section 6A which is treated as final discharge of tax liability under section 8 of the Ordinance, with corresponding withholding obligations resting on payment intermediaries or digital platforms that facilitate the transactions.

4.12	Division IVA of the First Schedule prescribes tax at 1 percent on payments made through digital channels (such as bank transfers or credit/debit cards) and 2 percent on cash-on-delivery transactions. The proviso excludes transactions already treated as exports under sections 154 or 154A. Consequently, all domestic digital sales, including subscriptions, digital learning content, and e-books, are now subject to final tax on gross receipts (including sales tax) under section 6A read with section 153(2A) of the Ordinance.

4.13	The new regime also introduces a withholding framework for payment intermediaries and courier service providers facilitating digital transactions. Where payments are processed through an electronic gateway or intermediary, such entities must withhold and deposit tax at 1 percent for digital payments or 2 percent for cash-on-delivery before remitting net proceeds to the seller. By broadening the definitions of 'digitally delivered services', 'e-commerce', and 'online marketplace', the Finance Act 2025 ensures that automated and internet-based offerings, including online courses, subscription portals, and software-access services, are comprehensively covered. Accordingly, OUP SMC’s e-learning and content-delivery platforms clearly fall within the scope of this regime.

4.14	It may also be noted that the initial draft of the Finance Act 2025 had imposed a 5 percent 'digital presence tax' on foreign e-retailers earning income from Pakistan without a physical presence. Nevertheless, subsequent notifications exempted goods and services supplied from outside Pakistan from this levy. As OUP SMC operates as a resident entity providing digital products locally, this provision is not applicable.

4.15	In summary, whether the customer is an individual subscriber or an educational institution, any supply of digital content or access made through an online platform now falls under section 6A of the Ordinance. OUP SMC, as the service provider, is not required to withhold tax on its own receipts; rather, the obligation lies with intermediaries such as banks, payment gateways, or courier companies to collect and deposit the applicable tax. OUP SMC should ensure close coordination with these intermediaries to verify accurate deduction, timely deposit, and reconciliation of taxes withheld under section 6A of the Ordinance. All such transactions are to be reported as income subject to final tax under the newly introduced digital economy regime.

4.16	Please note that after promulgation of new provisions, no explicit exclusion has been provided for non-withholding of income tax under section 153(1)(a) and 153(1)(b) of the Ordinance. It means that buyer (where withholding agent) under section 153 is also required to observe the withholding at the applicable rates. Resultantly, the withholding observed under normal provisions would become refundable to OUP SMC.

5.	WITHHOLDING INCOME TAX IMPLICATION 

5.1	Section 6A of the Ordinance, read with the special collection mechanism in section 153(2A), establishes a distinct withholding framework for digitally ordered goods and services. Under this regime, the primary withholding responsibility rests with payment intermediaries (such as banks, payment gateways, and digital wallets) and courier companies, rather than with the customer or the seller. Specifically, payment intermediaries are required to deduct tax at 1% on digital payments, while courier companies are required to deduct tax at 2% on cash-on-delivery (COD) collections, both calculated on the gross amount collected. 

5.2	Within this framework, OUP SMC is not a withholding agent on its own receipts under section 6A, and ordinary customers (including schools) are likewise not intended to act as withholding agents for these digital transactions. Any withholding role of customers would arise only, if at all, under the general provisions of section 153(1), which predate the digital tax regime and apply broadly to services and certain other payments.

5.3	As the law currently stands, however, there is a technical risk that more than one party could be viewed as a withholding agent in respect of the same payment. While section 153(2A) begins with a “notwithstanding” clause, thereby introducing a special rule for digital transactions routed through intermediaries and couriers, it does not expressly state that section 153(1) ceases to apply to those payments. In addition, the negative list in section 153(5), which specifies payments excluded from general withholding under section 153(1), has not yet been updated to carve out transactions that fall within section 6A read with section 153(2A). 

5.4	On a literal reading, this creates the possibility that a prescribed buyer could still consider itself obliged to withhold tax under section 153(1)(b) on payments for digital services, even where tax has already been withheld by the intermediary or courier under section 6A. In such circumstances, while the tax collected under section 6A would continue to constitute final tax on the digital transaction income, any additional tax deducted under section 153(1)(b) would, in principle, be refundable or adjustable in OUP’s hands and would not alter the final-tax character of section 6A.

5.5	From a practical perspective, this risk of double withholding can be mitigated through clear contractual and invoicing safeguards. Given that section 153(2A) expressly overrides subsection (1), the intended legislative hierarchy is that the special digital withholding mechanism should prevail over the general rule for payments that squarely fall within section 6A. 

5.6	To operationalize this intent, invoices may include a clear caveat stating that where a payment intermediary or courier company is acting as the withholding agent under section 6A read with section 153(2A), the buyer should not simultaneously treat itself as a withholding agent under section 153(1) in respect of the same payment. This approach aligns with the policy objective of the digital regime, namely, centralized and streamlined withholding at the intermediary or courier level, and provides OUP SMC with a defensible basis to resist duplicative withholding in routine operations.

5.7	Accordingly, for digital transactions that clearly fall within the scope of section 6A and are processed through intermediaries or couriers who are fulfilling their statutory withholding obligations, the recommended position is that no parallel withholding under section 153(1) should be applied by the buyer on the same payment. In such cases, the intermediary or courier withholding under section 6A read with section 153(2A) should be treated as the sole operative mechanism, and any attempt by the buyer to deduct tax again under section 153(1)(b) would merely create double withholding and an avoidable refund position for OUP SMC. Until the law is clarified through a corresponding amendment to the negative list in section 153(5), this contractual and procedural safeguard represents the most practical means of preserving the intended single, final tax collection under section 6A.

5.8	It is also important to clarify the position where a payment intermediary or courier fails to fulfill its withholding obligations. In such a situation, the receipts of OUP SMC do not fall outside the scope of section 6A merely because of a procedural lapse by the withholding agent. Section 6A taxes income by reference to its nature—namely, digitally ordered and digitally delivered goods or services supplied from within Pakistan through a locally operated platform, and the applicability of the final tax regime depends on this character, not on the actual act of deduction at source. 

5.9	Where a withholding agent fails to withhold or deposit tax, the primary legal exposure rests with that agent under sections 161 and 205 of the Ordinance, including recovery of tax not withheld, default surcharge, and penalties. OUP SMC does not lose the benefit of the final tax regime solely due to such a failure by the intermediary or courier.

5.10	Finally, as regards the tax base on which withholding is to be computed, section 6A is explicit in applying to the “gross amounts of receipts” arising from digitally ordered goods or services. Accordingly, the payment intermediary or courier is required to withhold tax on the full invoice value, including any applicable provincial sales tax, and not on a net-of-tax or net-of-charges basis. 

5.11	The said treatment is consistent with the statutory language and with earlier advice that the 1% or 2% withholding under section 6A is to be calculated on gross receipts inclusive of sales tax. For consistency and to avoid disputes, both customers (where section 153 is considered) and intermediaries or couriers (for section 6A) should therefore reference the same full invoice value rather than applying withholding on a reduced net amount.

6.	FEDERAL SALES TAX IMPLICATION 

6.1	As discussed above, section 2(12) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 defines goods as ‘every kind of movable property other than actionable claims, money, stocks, shares and securities.’ This definition, focused on tangible movables, has traditionally been interpreted to include physical articles, merchandise, and electricity (which was expressly added by amendment). Intangible products, rights, or digital content are not encompassed. An access code or online subscription represents a contractual right to access, a chose in action, and is not a tangible article. It also lacks classification under the Pakistan Customs tariff, as no Harmonized System (HS) code exists for purely online services. Accordingly, digital platform access does not qualify as goods for purposes of the Sales Tax Act.

6.2	Where OUP SMC sells a physical item (for instance, a printed card or USB containing an access key), a nominal tangible element may be involved. Nevertheless, tax authorities typically assess the substance of the transaction. The intrinsic value of platforms such as Oxford Reading Buddy or Oxford My E-Mate lies in the content or service, not in the medium used to convey access credentials. Thus, even if a code is printed on paper, the transaction would be treated as a service rather than a sale of goods. Although there is no specific ruling on e-learning subscriptions, similar reasoning has been applied to electronically delivered software, which has consistently been classified as a service.

6.3	It is pertinent to highlight here that through the Finance (Supplementary) Act, 2022, the long-standing exemption on the import or supply of books was curtailed to cover only educational textbooks, thereby excluding other categories of books that were previously exempt. Subsequently, the Finance Act, 2022 reinstated the earlier position, restoring exemption for the import and supply of all kinds of books under the Sixth Schedule to the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

6.4	Accordingly, printed books, including educational textbooks, remain exempt from sales tax under the Sixth Schedule. The relevant entry (previously serial 53 and now consolidated at serial 32 pursuant to the Finance Act, 2022) encompasses ‘newsprint and books (excluding directories, brochures, and leaflets)’. It is important to note that this exemption is confined to printed material falling within the specified HS codes and does not extend to electronic or digital publications. Consequently, digital subscriptions, e-books, and similar electronic formats, lacking a defined tariff classification, lie outside the scope of the statutory exemption.

6.5	Moreover, legislative reforms have explicitly confined the exemption to printed books and newsprint, as digital books and equivalents do not fall under the ambit of ‘goods’. Consequently, access to OUP SMC’s digital platforms does not come under the scope of Sales Tax Act, 1990. Even if digital books are treated as ‘service’, it falls outside the purview of federal sales tax altogether.

6.6	Accordingly, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend do not qualify as goods under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Revenue derived from these platforms is not subject to the federal sales tax regime, except to the extent of any ancillary supply of physical media. OUP SMC should, however, ensure that invoices for digital access are segregated from those for printed books to preserve the exemption applicable to printed textbooks and prevent inadvertent mixing of taxable and exempt supplies.


7.	PROVINCIAL SALES TAX IMPLICATION 

7.1	Sindh 

7.1.1	Following the Finance Act 2025 Sindh’s adoption of CPC Version 2.1 for classification, the specific category for Oxford SMC’s digital learning products is now clearly identifiable under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SST Act).

7.1.2	Under section 2(79) of SST Act, ‘service’ now encompasses anything that is not good, including facilities, advantages, and rights supplied for consideration. The Second Schedule, updated through the Finance Act, 2025, links every taxable service to its CPC heading. Among these, CPC 843 - On-line content, particularly sub-class 84311 On-line books, newspapers and periodicals supplied electronically, specifically targets digital publishing and e-content distribution. The explanatory notes confirm that 84311 covers books, newspapers and periodicals supplied electronically through the internet. For ready reference, the relevant explanation is reproduced below for ease of understanding:

843 On-line content 

8431 On-line text based information 

84311 On-line books 

This sub-class includes: 
-on-line books, including school textbooks, general reference books, such as atlases and other books of maps or charts, dictionaries and encyclopedias

7.1.3	In substance, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate and Oxford Extend provide controlled access to digital publications and educational materials hosted on secure servers. The user purchases electronic rights to read, interact with, and store those materials on-line. No tangible property or software copy is transferred; the value lies in the delivery of information content. This business model precisely matches the statutory language of CPC 843, sub-class 84311. 

7.1.4	Having concluded that the services primarily fall under CPC 84311 (a subclass of CPC 843), reference is invited to Serial No. 20 of Part-II of the Second Schedule to the SST Act. Under this entry, services classified under CPC 843 are subject to a reduced rate of 3% SST, provided that OUP SMC exercises the option for such reduced rate in accordance with Rule 42I of the SST on Services Rules, 2011. If the option is not filed, these services will attract the standard SST rate of 15%. It is further noted that Serial No. 20 of the First Schedule provides an exemption for ‘library and archive services’ falling under CPC 845. Nevertheless, based on the nature of activities, the services rendered by OUP SMC do not fall within this exempt category.

7.2	Punjab 

7.2.1	Following the Finance Act, 2025, the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012 (PST Act) retained its PSIC-based classification framework, which is functionally mapped to the UN Central Product Classification (CPC) Version 2.1. Each service listed in the Schedule continues to carry numeric classification headings (for example, 98.12, 9857.0000, 9858.0000) derived from the Pakistan Standard Industrial Classification (PSIC), which in turn draws from the international CPC structure. Thus, while the Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) has not expressly cited CPC Version 2.1 in its legislation, it operates on the same classification logic and coding principles.

7.2.2	Section 2(38) defines service to include anything which is not good, including facilities, utilities, and advantages provided for consideration. Section 3, as amended, imposes tax on all services unless specifically exempted in the First Schedule. Oxford SMC’s digital learning platforms, Oxford Reading Buddy, Oxford My E-Mate, and Oxford Extend, constitute the provision of an electronic facility granting access to digital content, rather than the supply of goods. The user acquires an intangible right to view and interact with online publications, not ownership of any physical or downloadable copy.

7.2.3	Consequently, such transactions fall within Punjab’s corresponding to CPC 84311 (On-line books, newspapers and periodicals supplied electronically). Please note that S. No. 8 of First Schedule to PST Act inter alia provides exemption for services relating to libraries, which we understand is not relevant in the instant case as specific online content is being provided by OUP SMC and hence it is not a library in general meaning. Therefore, in absence of a specific exemption for educational e-publications, these supplies attract Punjab sales tax at 16 percent. 

7.3	Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 

7.3.1	Through the Finance Act, 2025, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa formally codified the adoption of CPC and HS Codes by inserting express language in section 3(4) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act, 2022. The Act empowers the Management Committee to specify or amend CPC Codes, HS Codes, or any other code for classification of services, while clarifying that inclusion or exclusion of a code does not affect the underlying taxability.

7.3.2	This amendment aligns KPK’s framework with the UN CPC Version 2.1 structure adopted by Sindh, ensuring that all digital, online, or electronically delivered services can be consistently classified. The broad definition of service under section 2(aaa) includes any advantage or facility provided electronically, making digital platforms taxable by their very nature.

7.3.3	Applying the CPC classification, Oxford SMC’s subscription-based access to digital learning materials squarely falls within CPC 84311 – On-line books and periodicals supplied electronically. Since KPK explicitly recognizes CPC Codes for classification, the receipts from these platforms are taxable as online content services at the general 15 percent KPK sales tax rate. 

7.4	Balochistan 

7.4.1	The Finance Act, 2025 introduced a structural reform in the Balochistan Sales Tax on Services Act, 2015 through the insertion of section 78B - Classification of services. This new provision authorizes the Balochistan Revenue Authority (BRA) to specify, by notification, classification codes for services including CPC Codes, HS Codes, or any other international classification system, and clarifies that such codes are adopted for purposes of administration, analysis, and facilitation. This reform brings Balochistan in line with Sindh and KPK, both of which have formally incorporated CPC systems into their provincial tax laws.

7.4.2	Section 78B therefore establishes a clear legal foundation for the use of CPC Version 2.1 within Balochistan’s service-tax framework. When read together with section 2(147), which defines service as anything that is not goods and includes facilities, advantages, and rights rendered for consideration, it is evident that access to online educational material qualifies as a taxable service.

7.4.3	Oxford SMC’s digital platforms, providing interactive reading, electronic content, and access rights to e-publications, fall squarely under CPC 84311, covering online books and digital periodicals supplied electronically. Accordingly, under BRA’s CPC-linked classification, these supplies constitute taxable online content services at the standard 15 percent rate unless an educational exemption is later notified. 

7.5	Other Consideration

7.5.1	From a provincial sales tax perspective, the choice between applying a reduced rate (e.g., 3% on gross value) and the standard rate (e.g., 15%/16%) materially affects both pricing economics and input tax efficiency. The principal advantage of the reduced-rate approach is that it substantially lowers the output tax burden compared to the standard rate, which is particularly relevant where the customer base, such as schools, may not be in a position to fully recover input tax. 

7.5.2	A lower output tax incidence generally enables the supplier to keep subscription prices competitive in a price-sensitive education market and reduces pressure on net margins relative to a standard-rate regime. Conversely, reduced-rate schemes are commonly accompanied by constraints on input tax recovery, either through partial restrictions on claiming input tax, limitations on carry-forward, or treatment akin to a turnover-based levy, meaning that provincial sales tax incurred on the supplier’s own costs (for example, local service providers, technology support, or other operational inputs) may not be fully offset, potentially increasing the embedded tax cost within the overall operating model.

7.5.3	On the question of jurisdiction for provincial sales tax authorities, and taking a practical and risk-managed view, a defensible approach remains to treat Sindh as the primary place of taxation for the digital platform supplies, principally because the relevant supplying establishment and commercial administration are situated in Karachi. In particular, OUP SMC’s registered office, management oversight, contract administration, billing systems, invoicing, and website/platform administration are operated from Sindh, which supports the characterization of Sindh as the “place of business from which the service is supplied,” notwithstanding that customers may access the platforms from other provinces. 

7.5.4	On this footing, charging and reporting Sindh sales tax on digital platform invoices aligns the tax treatment with the location of the supplying establishment and the jurisdiction exercising administrative control over the business, thereby simplifying compliance and reducing the likelihood of overlapping claims across multiple provinces. That said, it should be recognized that other provincial jurisdictions may still seek to challenge this approach by asserting a consumption-based nexus, particularly where access and use occurs outside Sindh.
With appropriate heading.

## Written Arguments for Tax Year 2022  
### K-Electric Limited — Consolidated submissions based on Grounds of Appeal and replies filed during section 122(5A) proceedings

---

## 1) Unlawful assumption of jurisdiction under section 122(5A)

The impugned order passed under section 122(5A) is liable to be annulled at the very outset because the statutory pre-conditions for assuming jurisdiction were not satisfied. The scope of section 122(5A) is confined to cases where, **from the record**, the deemed assessment is shown to be both **“erroneous”** and **“prejudicial to the interest of revenue.”** In the present case, the notices and subsequent order reflect a roving verification exercise—raising wide-ranging queries, demanding explanations and supporting documents, and challenging accounting and tax positions already disclosed in the return and audited financial statements—without identifying any specific “error” in the deemed order that could justify invocation of section 122(5A). The replies filed by the appellant consistently objected that section 122(5A) cannot be used as a substitute for audit, nor can it be invoked merely because the tax officer forms a different view subsequently. fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file0

In addition, the appellant specifically raised the legal objection that the Additional Commissioner could not lawfully exercise the jurisdiction assumed, relying upon binding judicial precedent (including the Supreme Court’s decision in *Prime Commercial Bank* and the line of decisions following it). This objection goes to the root of jurisdiction and, once accepted, renders the entire proceedings void ab initio. The impugned order does not meaningfully adjudicate this fundamental plea and therefore stands vitiated on jurisdiction alone. fileciteturn0file5

---

## 2) Violation of natural justice and non-speaking adjudication

Without prejudice to the jurisdictional objections, the impugned order is vitiated by violation of natural justice and non-application of mind. Several additions have been made without confronting the appellant with a clear legal basis, without identifying the specific statutory provision allegedly violated, and without dealing with detailed explanations already provided in the replies. It is settled that where an assessee has placed record-based explanations, the tax authority must give a reasoned finding addressing such submissions; mechanical additions based on assumptions or superficial reading of accounts cannot be sustained. The record shows repeated instances where the appellant explained the nature of items (including their accounting treatment, disclosures in notes, and tax computations), yet the impugned order proceeds as if no explanation was given. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 3) Tariff Differential Subsidy (TDS) — exemption under Clause 102A wrongly denied

The disallowance of exemption under Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule, in respect of Tariff Differential Subsidy, is wholly misconceived. The appellant’s replies demonstrated that the subsidy is granted by the Federal Government pursuant to federal policy decisions and directions, with the objective of bridging the gap between the NEPRA tariff and the consumer tariff mandated by Government; K-Electric merely implements this policy mechanism and receives the subsidy as a compensatory transfer to enable compliance. The exemption squarely covers “income…as represents a subsidy granted…by the Federal Government for implementation of any orders of the Federal Government in this behalf.” The impugned order does not rebut this statutory fit through any coherent finding.

More importantly, the appellant placed on record that this identical Clause 102A claim was examined and accepted by the department itself in concluded proceedings for earlier tax years (including proceedings under section 122(5A)), where the department expressly held that there was no legal infirmity in claiming such exemption. In the absence of any change in law, change in material facts, or binding contrary precedent on the same question, the departure from an accepted and settled position violates the principle of consistency and certainty in tax administration. The impugned order’s reliance on unrelated High Court proceedings—where the exemption issue was neither raised nor decided—amounts to misapplication of precedent and cannot override the express statutory exemption and the department’s own accepted history. fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 4) Bad debts / reversal from gross receipts — addition unjustified and revenue-neutral

The addition on account of “bad debts” or alleged deduction from gross receipts is unsustainable on law and facts. The appellant explained that this represents reversal of revenue in respect of chronic defaulters in accordance with IFRS-15, which requires recognition of revenue only where collection is probable. This is not a discretionary reduction to depress income; it is correct measurement of revenue under consistently applied and disclosed accounting policy. Further, and decisively, the appellant demonstrated that the same amount was included in “turnover” for purposes of minimum tax under section 113, thereby negating the allegation of prejudice to revenue. The impugned order neither deals with the IFRS-15 collectability principle nor addresses the revenue-neutrality established through minimum tax inclusion, and therefore cannot be sustained. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 5) Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) — taxation of hypothetical accruals is impermissible

The addition relating to LPS is based on a misunderstanding of accrual under both accounting and tax law. While the appellant follows the mercantile system, accrual still requires enforceable entitlement and reasonable certainty of collection. The appellant placed on record the established policy of recognizing LPS from Government and semi-Government entities only upon receipt, due to chronic non-recovery and settlement uncertainties within the circular debt framework. This approach aligns with IFRS-15 collectability discipline and prevents recognition of illusory income. Taxing such hypothetical accruals would amount to taxation of unreal income, which is not sanctioned by law. The further step of inserting such alleged accruals into turnover for minimum tax purposes aggravates the illegality. fileciteturn0file3

---

## 6) Consumer recoveries / deferred revenue — incorrect taxation of liability as income and denial of matching costs

The treatment of recoveries from consumers for new connections as taxable income in the year of receipt is erroneous. The appellant explained, with record-based detail, that such receipts are initially recognized as liabilities and then amortized to income over the period during which the services are rendered, consistent with IFRS-15 and the economic reality of an ongoing service obligation. Under the Ordinance as well, income is taxable when it becomes “due” and the taxpayer becomes entitled to it; receipts that represent a service obligation cannot be taxed as upfront income merely because cash is received.

Even assuming, without admitting, the department’s contrary approach, the impugned order remains internally inconsistent because it taxes gross receipts without allowing corresponding costs (assets/equipment installed) in full, thereby violating the matching principle and overstating taxable income. This one-sided computation cannot be sustained. fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 7) Foreign exchange loss — allowable under section 71 and settled accounting; alternative depreciation relief ignored

The disallowance of foreign exchange loss as “notional” is contrary to the Ordinance. The appellant explained that section 71 itself mandates translation of foreign currency items at prescribed rates, and exchange differences arising from such translation necessarily feed into profit and loss under mercantile accounting. The appellant also demonstrated consistency: exchange gains arising from the same methodology were offered to tax in prior years, and the department has accepted the treatment in the appellant’s own appellate history. Selectively disallowing losses while accepting gains is legally and equitably untenable.

In any event, the appellant specifically pleaded, without prejudice, that if the loss is treated as capital in nature, then capitalization and depreciation must be allowed. The impugned order fails to deal with this alternative plea, which independently renders the findings defective. fileciteturn0file4 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 8) NEPRA payment treated as “fine” under section 21(g) — characterization and quantum not established

The disallowance of NEPRA-related payments under section 21(g) is procedurally and substantively flawed. The appellant sought clarification of the figure adopted by the department and demonstrated non-reconciliation with actual payments, including the fact that a payment traceable on record was Rs 20 million pursuant to NEPRA Appellate Tribunal order, whereas the department adopted a higher figure without evidentiary basis. Moreover, section 21(g) applies to fines/penalties for breach of law; the burden to establish that a payment is penal (and not compensatory, regulatory, or settlement-based) lies on the department. In the absence of such finding and evidence, the disallowance is arbitrary. fileciteturn0file3

---

## 9) Minimum tax / turnover inflation under section 113 — inclusion of pass-through collections and non-turnover items

A substantial part of the impugned demand arises from artificial inflation of “turnover” for minimum tax purposes under section 113 by including items that are not business receipts. The appellant demonstrated that electricity duty, amounts under sections 235 and 235A, PTV license fee, and similar collections are statutory pass-through amounts collected from consumers on behalf of Government; these do not constitute turnover from K-Electric’s business. The statutory definition of turnover itself excludes sales tax and federal excise duty, and settled principles require that amounts collected for and payable to Government or third parties cannot be treated as the taxpayer’s gross receipts. The impugned order disregards these principles and leads to double counting and taxation of non-income items. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0

The appellant also addressed specific misclassifications such as treating purchases from KANUPP as turnover (despite being disclosed under “purchase of electricity expense”), including tariff differential subsidy as turnover (despite being a Government policy transfer and separately exempt under Clause 102A), inserting liquidated damages from suppliers into turnover (despite being compensatory), and treating balance-sheet recoveries as business receipts. Each of these inclusions stretches section 113 beyond its statutory intent and must be deleted. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 10) Section 148 import tax wrongly treated as minimum tax; “income arising from imports” test ignored; double taxation

The treatment of tax collected under section 148 on imports as minimum tax is untenable because the appellant is not a commercial importer earning “income arising from imports.” The appellant imports plant, machinery and equipment for its own use as a regulated utility, and therefore the qualifying statutory phrase in section 148(7)—“income of the importer arising from imports”—is not satisfied. The appellant relied upon the interpretive principle that no statutory word is redundant; therefore, the department must first determine whether the importer earns income arising from imports, and only then can it examine any exclusions or rate implications. The appellant further highlighted that the Finance Act, 2022 amendment was remedial in nature, intended to remove anomalies and ensure that own-use imports of industrial undertakings do not get trapped into minimum tax due to rate categorization. The impugned order ignores both statutory language and legislative intent, and results in impermissible double taxation where the same economic stream is taxed under presumptive/minimum mechanism and again under the Normal Tax Regime. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 11) Section 7E demand — statutory exclusions and factual record ignored

The demand raised under section 7E is unsustainable because the appellant provided detailed property-wise reconciliations showing that several assets fall within statutory exclusions, include business premises, or relate to plots not in possession due to litigation and other legal constraints. The impugned order fails to meaningfully deal with this record and proceeds to create demand mechanically, thereby rendering the findings arbitrary and non-speaking. Even without entering into constitutional questions, the demand cannot survive on a plain application of section 7E to the facts already placed on record. fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file0

---

## 12) Refund adjustment and short allowance of credits — computational illegality

The impugned order also suffers from computational illegality as it fails to give effect to refund adjustments and curtails credits (including section 236K) without confronting the appellant with the basis of such curtailment or reconciling the figures with record. These are mechanical errors that independently warrant deletion/recomputation of demand and grant of consequential relief. fileciteturn0file0

---

## 13) Prayer for relief

For the foregoing reasons, the impugned order deserves to be annulled in its entirety for want of lawful jurisdiction under section 122(5A), violation of natural justice, and misapplication of law. Without prejudice, even on merits, each addition/disallowance discussed above is independently unsustainable and liable to be deleted. Consequential relief by way of correct recomputation of taxable income, turnover under section 113, minimum tax, refunds and admissible credits must follow as a matter of course.

parts:
I have read the Grounds of Appeal and the sequence of replies filed during 122(5A) proceedings for TY 2022. Below is a consolidated, **issue-wise set of detailed arguments** that you can lift into (i) the written synopsis before ATIR, (ii) “arguments” portion of the appeal, and/or (iii) additional grounds / rejoinder. I’ve aligned each argument to the **specific grounds** and the **record already created** through your replies. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file4 fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file2

---

## A. Jurisdictional / legal defects in invoking section 122(5A)

### 1) Twin conditions not established: “erroneous” + “prejudicial to the interest of revenue”
**Core proposition:** Section 122(5A) is not a general audit power. It can only be invoked when *from the record itself* the deemed order is (i) erroneous, and (ii) prejudicial to revenue. Mere suspicion, audit-style queries, or a desire to re-check accounting treatment does not satisfy the statutory threshold.

**How to argue it (record-based):**
- The show cause is framed as a set of “discrepancies” requiring explanations and documents—this is the hallmark of a **fishing and roving inquiry**, not identification of an error apparent from record. fileciteturn0file0  
- Where the department’s premise itself is incorrect (e.g., misreading notes / alleging “other expenses” from a note that actually relates to contingencies/commitments; or confusing taxes collected as expenses), it demonstrates **non-application of mind**, and the resulting order cannot be said to meet the “record-based” jurisdictional condition. fileciteturn0file5  
- You can emphasize: the ACIR must show **what specific error existed in the deemed order**, and **how it caused prejudice** (quantified or at least legally demonstrable), *before* calling for further evidence.

### 2) Lack of lawful assumption of jurisdiction by an Additional Commissioner (Prime Commercial Bank line)
**Core proposition:** Where the original deemed assessment under section 120(1) is made in a manner that (per binding precedent) restricts who may invoke 122(5A), assumption of jurisdiction by an Additional Commissioner is unlawful.

**How to argue it:**
- The reply DT-4002 expressly relies on Supreme Court decision in *Prime Commercial Bank* (and ATIR’s following) to state that 122(5A) could not be exercised by an Additional Commissioner in those circumstances. This is a **pure legal bar**, and if accepted, the entire impugned order collapses without going into merits. fileciteturn0file5  
- Frame this as a **threshold issue**: once jurisdiction is absent, everything done on merits is void ab initio.

### 3) Violation of confrontation / natural justice (notice did not confront relevant provisions or basis)
**Core proposition:** Additions/disallowances cannot be sustained where the taxpayer was not confronted with (i) the specific legal provision, (ii) the precise factual basis, and (iii) a reasonable opportunity.

**Use it especially for:**
- Bad debts / deduction from gross receipts (notice omission / no proper confrontation) (Ground 5). fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  
- NEPRA “fatal accidents” payment being treated as fine without proper identification and characterization (Ground 12) (you already requested basis details as the notice figure didn’t reconcile). fileciteturn0file3  
- Turnover additions that treat pass-through collections as KE’s receipts without identifying how they meet the definition of turnover (Grounds 13–23). fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file5  

---

## B. Clause 102A Tariff Differential Subsidy (TDS) exemption disallowance (Ground 4)

### 4) Clause 102A squarely covers the subsidy; department already accepted it in prior years
**Statutory fit (build it as a 3-limb test):**
Clause 102A exempts “income…as represents a subsidy granted…by the Federal Government for implementation of any orders of the Federal Government in this behalf.”  
You can argue each limb is met:
1) **Subsidy granted by Federal Government** – TDS is paid/credited under GoP/Federal Finance Division communications. fileciteturn0file5  
2) **Purpose: implementation of GoP orders** – the Implementation Agreement / Subsidy Order mechanism shows KE is directed to charge a consumer tariff different from NEPRA tariff, and GoP funds the differential. fileciteturn0file5  
3) **KE is an implementing conduit; real relief is for the public** – subsidy exists to keep consumer price low; KE’s receipt is cost recovery to implement GoP’s price policy. fileciteturn0file5  

### 5) Principle of consistency / certainty in tax administration
- You have on record that the department concluded 122(5A) proceedings for TY 2016 and 2018–2021 and **accepted** KE’s Clause 102A entitlement with an explicit finding (“no legal infirmity”). fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file5  
- Argue that departing from a settled position requires **cogent reasons** showing (i) change in law, or (ii) change in facts, or (iii) binding superior precedent directly on point. None is shown.

### 6) Reliance on SHC orders (Sept 30, 2024) is misplaced if exemption not adjudicated
- Ground already captures: the SHC orders were relied upon though the exemption issue was neither raised nor decided therein. Frame it as **misapplication of precedent**: a judgment is authority for what it decides, not for what is assumed. fileciteturn0file0  

---

## C. Bad debts / “deduction from gross receipts” Rs 1.644bn (Ground 5)

### 7) The item is a revenue reversal driven by IFRS-15 collectability, not an “extra deduction”
- Your reply explains it is reversal of billing to customers with chronic defaults; under IFRS-15 (para 9(e)), revenue is recognized only when it is probable that consideration will be collected. fileciteturn0file3  
- Therefore, it is not a discretionary write-off to depress income; it is **correct measurement of revenue** under the applicable accounting framework consistently used.

### 8) No prejudice even on the department’s own minimum tax narrative
- You have already included the amount in **turnover for minimum tax computation under section 113**, ensuring it was taxed on a gross basis even if not recognized in P&L. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  
- That fact kills the “prejudice” limb and also supports deletion on merits.

### 9) Natural justice: show-cause did not properly invoke the legal basis
- Ground specifically states the show-cause did not cite the relevant section for disallowance. You can argue the addition is void for lack of proper confrontation, especially when the accounting and tax treatment is technical and record-heavy. fileciteturn0file0  

---

## D. Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) not accrued: Rs 492m addition to income + turnover (Grounds 6–7)

### 10) Accrual requires “due / entitlement”; IFRS-15 requires probability of collection
- Under the Ordinance, income on accrual arises when it is **due/entitled** and can be determined with reasonable accuracy; the company is mandatorily on accrual (section 32(2)), but accrual still depends on enforceable entitlement and realistic collectability. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  
- Your reply establishes a consistent policy: LPS from Government/Semi-Government/local bodies is recognized **on receipt** due to chronic low recovery and uncertainty; this is aligned with IFRS-15 collectability discipline. fileciteturn0file3  

### 11) Department cannot tax “hypothetical” accruals while ignoring the matching / settlement reality
- You have recorded the context of circular debt and the concept that LPS among government entities is often subject to holistic settlement arrangements. This supports that the claimed “accrual” is not unconditional nor reliably measurable. fileciteturn0file3  

### 12) Turnover under section 113 is not a dumping ground for non-recognized, non-earned items
- Even if the department insists on minimum tax logic, “turnover” still requires nexus with business receipts as defined—LPS that is not due/recognized due to collectability constraints is not a “receipt” and cannot be artificially inserted into turnover. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  

---

## E. Deferred revenue / recoveries from consumers for new connections: Rs 2.882bn taxed as income; and matching cost ignored (Grounds 8–9)

### 13) The receipt is a liability first; income only over the service period (IFRS-15 para 69) + sections 32/34 “due” test
- Your DT-1407 reply gives a clean factual model: consumer deposit → short-term liability → reclassification to deferred revenue once assets installed → **income recognized over useful life** as utility is provided. fileciteturn0file2  
- Under section 34, income is “due” when the taxpayer is entitled to receive it. KE is not entitled to “keep” the entire amount as income upfront; it represents an obligation to provide utility over time. fileciteturn0file2  

### 14) Matching principle: if department taxes gross receipts upfront, it must allow corresponding cost
- Ground 9 is powerful: the ACIR taxed recoveries as income but did not allow the corresponding asset/equipment cost in entirety—this violates matching and produces a distorted “income” figure. fileciteturn0file0  
- Frame it as: even on the department’s alternative theory, they must compute **real income**, not one-sided gross inflows.

---

## F. Exchange loss Rs 8.971bn disallowed as “notional”; alternatively depreciation route ignored (Grounds 10–11)

### 15) Exchange loss is allowable on accrual under mercantile accounting + section 71 currency conversion makes recognition mandatory
- Your DT-4327 reply anchors this: section 71 requires foreign currency amounts to be converted at SBP rate when taken into account; the resulting exchange difference is consequential and cannot be dismissed as “notional” without rendering section 71 redundant. fileciteturn0file4  
- The claim is supported by consistent accounting policy and earlier favorable appellate history in KE’s own case (CIR(A) TY 2016). fileciteturn0file4  

### 16) Consistency: exchange gains have been voluntarily offered in prior years
- You have a table showing exchange gains offered in TY 2007–2011. This supports the fairness argument: **uniformity** demands that losses are allowed if gains were taxed. fileciteturn0file4  

### 17) Without prejudice: capitalization/depreciation approach (section 76(5)) must be allowed if revenue’s stance is “capital”
- Ground 11: even if they treat exchange loss as not allowable as revenue, then it must be capitalized and depreciation allowed. This is a strong alternative relief prayer. fileciteturn0file0  

---

## G. NEPRA payment Rs 33.5m treated as “fine” u/s 21(g) (Ground 12)

### 18) Characterization failure + lack of confrontation
- Your record indicates KE could trace a payment of Rs 20m pursuant to NEPRA Appellate Tribunal order and asked the department to provide details/source for Rs 33.5m. This is a procedural and factual gap—an addition cannot be sustained on an unverified number. fileciteturn0file3  
- Legal argument: section 21(g) applies to fines/penalties for breach of law; the onus is on the department to establish the nature of payment as “fine” (as opposed to compensatory, regulatory charge, or settlement). Without that, disallowance is arbitrary.

---

## H. Minimum tax / turnover disputes under section 113 (Grounds 13–23)

This is where the order appears to have inflated “turnover” by adding pass-through taxes, subsidies, netting adjustments, and non-core items. Use a consistent spine:

### Spine: Section 113 “turnover” must be confined to gross receipts derived from business activity, and excludes sales tax/FED; pass-through collections are not KE’s receipts
- Your reply already notes that “turnover” is **exclusive of sales tax and FED** (per definition) and that other taxes collected (electricity duty, 235/235A, TVL fee) are not receipts from sale of electricity but collections on behalf of government. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file5  

Now apply it issue-wise:

### 19) Electricity duty, 235, 235A, PTV license fee wrongly included in turnover (Grounds 13–14)
- These are **statutory collections / advance tax / duties** billed via consumers; KE is a collecting agent/conduit. They are neither consideration for electricity supply nor KE’s income. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file5  

### 20) Purchases from KANUPP added to turnover (Ground 15)
- Purchases are already separately disclosed as “Purchase of Electricity Expenses” (Note reference in GOA). Adding purchases to turnover is conceptually wrong and results in double counting. fileciteturn0file0  

### 21) Tariff differential subsidy treated as turnover (Grounds 16–18)
- Subsidy is not “sale to GoP”; there is no sale of electricity to GoP. It is a compensatory fiscal transfer under GoP policy; it cannot be re-characterized as turnover. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file5  
- Plus: the ATIR has decided the issue in KE’s favor in multiple years; departmental officers are bound (you have cited binding effect). fileciteturn0file3  

### 22) Scrap sales subjected to minimum tax despite finality in KE’s own case + Supreme Court (Ground 19)
- Strong res judicata / finality narrative: already decided in KE’s own case; later upheld by Supreme Court (as pleaded). fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  

### 23) TV license fee collection charges included as turnover (Ground 20)
- Collection charges do not constitute KE’s core business receipts; they are incidental to acting as collection agent for PTV; not turnover from sale of electricity. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  

### 24) Reversal of accrued interest on consumer deposits wrongly treated as receipts; plus arithmetical excess (Ground 21)
- It’s a reversal driven by NEPRA directive / tariff adjustment mechanics, not a business receipt. Also, ACIR added an excess amount beyond actual figure. This is both **legal misclassification** and **factual/arithmetical error**. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  

### 25) “Recoveries from customers” Rs 5.289bn included in turnover (Ground 22)
- Your reply clarifies it is a **balance sheet item** (recoveries during the year, linked to service connection / mains extension / streetlights), and the corresponding revenue is separately disclosed (service connection charges) and was already offered for minimum tax. fileciteturn0file3  

### 26) Liquidated damages from suppliers included in turnover (Ground 23)
- Damages for breach of contract are not receipts from sale of goods/services; they are compensatory in nature. Including them stretches “turnover” beyond its intended scope. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3  

---

## I. Section 148 import tax treated as minimum tax; own-use industrial undertaking; “income arising from imports” test; double taxation (Grounds 24–27)

### 27) Finance Act 2022 amendment is remedial/curative: makes own-use imports adjustable regardless of rate (5.5% included)
- Your DT-1150 reply is already a full legal note: it cites the explanatory circular and explains the anomaly created earlier, and why the 2022 change is remedial/curative and should be applied to remove absurdity. fileciteturn0file3  
- Frame it for ATIR: legislative intent is explicit—**own-use industrial imports are not meant to be stuck as minimum tax** merely because they fall under a higher rate category.

### 28) Independent and stronger: section 148(7) applies only to “income of importer arising from imports”
- This is your best textual argument: KE does not earn “income arising from imports” because it is not a commercial importer; it imports plant/machinery for operations (generation/transmission/distribution), not for resale. Therefore, the first qualifying phrase itself knocks the case out of minimum tax. fileciteturn0file3  
- You have already built the interpretive logic (no surplusage; every word must be given meaning; strict construction of taxing statutes). fileciteturn0file3  

### 29) Binding judicial guidance: IHC answer (Oct 13, 2022) remanded logic
- Your reply quotes the IHC operating para: first determine whether income arises from imports; only then test exclusions. This supports KE’s stance that the department must first identify import-linked income—which it has not. fileciteturn0file3  

### 30) Double taxation (Ground 27)
- If import tax is treated as minimum tax and, simultaneously, the profits generated using the imported assets are taxed under NTR, the same economic stream is effectively taxed twice—once presumptively (as minimum) and again under normal regime—without statutory warrant. fileciteturn0file0  

---

## J. Section 7E demand Rs 183.525m; exclusions ignored; constitutional / sub-judice points (Ground 28)

### 31) On facts: property-wise exclusions and non-possession were provided but not considered
- Your DT-1407 reply provides asset-wise reconciliation showing: (i) self-owned business premises exclusion, (ii) open plots not in possession due to litigation, and (iii) “one capital asset” exclusion narrative (coal plant plots etc.). The ACIR’s demand without properly considering these details is a classic **non-speaking / non-consideration of record** defect. fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file0  

### 32) On law: reserve constitutional points + keep it pragmatic at Tribunal
- You have taken constitutional grounds (federal competence; Articles 23/25; double taxation; sub judice). Keep these as “without prejudice” grounds and emphasize the Tribunal can still grant relief by applying the **statutory exclusions** correctly on facts. fileciteturn0file2  

---

## K. Refund adjustment not allowed; 236K credit short allowed (Grounds 29–30)

### 33) Refund adjustment Rs 2.812bn: failure to give effect to admitted records
- Argue as a computation/legal effect issue: once refunds are available/adjustable per record, demand computation is arithmetically and legally wrong. This is a straightforward relief prayer. fileciteturn0file0  

### 34) 236K credit short allowed without hearing
- A tax credit cannot be curtailed without confronting the basis and allowing hearing, particularly where the variance is mechanical (difference between claimed and allowed). This is another “lack of confrontation + wrong computation” ground. fileciteturn0file0  

---

## Suggested “Reliefs / prayers” you can add at the end of arguments (ready-to-use)

1) **Annulment for lack of jurisdiction**: impugned order under section 122(5A) be declared void ab initio for failure to satisfy statutory preconditions and/or lack of lawful assumption of powers, with deemed assessment restored. fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file0  
2) **Alternatively**, on merits, delete each addition/disallowance as per issue-wise findings requested above. fileciteturn0file0  
3) **Without prejudice**, where an alternative tax treatment is adopted by the department (e.g., exchange loss capital), grant consequential relief (depreciation; matching cost allowance). fileciteturn0file0  
4) **Consequential relief**: recompute demand after giving full effect to refund adjustments and correct credits. fileciteturn0file0  

---

If you want to convert the above into a **formal “Written Arguments / Synopsis”** (tribunal-ready) with headings, concise propositions, and prayer clauses, I can reshape it into that format while keeping every point anchored to the existing record you’ve already built.
