Below is a **fully developed, paragraph-form set of arguments**, deliberately written as a **Tribunal-ready legal narrative**, drawing **directly and substantively from the grounds of appeal and all replies already filed**. I have not introduced new theories unless they naturally flow from the record. The structure mirrors how ATIR Members usually read: jurisdiction first, then substantive issues, then computational / consequential reliefs.

---

The impugned order passed under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 is legally unsustainable at the very threshold, as the mandatory jurisdictional pre-conditions prescribed by law have not been satisfied. It is well settled that the power under section 122(5A) is not an open-ended power to revisit or re-examine a deemed assessment on the basis of suspicion, audit objections, or a desire for further verification. The statute requires the tax authority to first demonstrate, from the record itself, that the deemed assessment is both “erroneous” and “prejudicial to the interest of revenue.” In the present case, the notices issued and the subsequent order reveal that the learned ACIR embarked upon a roving and fishing inquiry, raising wide-ranging questions, seeking explanations and documents, and challenging settled accounting treatments without identifying any specific error apparent from the record at the time the return was processed under section 120. Such an approach fundamentally misconceives the scope of section 122(5A) and vitiates the assumption of jurisdiction.

The replies filed by the appellant consistently highlighted that none of the alleged issues represented an “error” in the return or accompanying audited accounts. Rather, they involved differences of opinion on accounting treatment, re-characterization of receipts already disclosed, or reinterpretation of statutory exemptions and judicially settled matters. Jurisdiction under section 122(5A) cannot be assumed merely because the tax officer forms a different view at a later stage. In the absence of a demonstrable and identifiable mistake in the deemed assessment order itself, the entire exercise becomes void ab initio.

Further compounding this jurisdictional defect is the unlawful assumption of powers by an Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue. The appellant specifically raised, during proceedings, that in light of binding judicial precedent, including the Supreme Court’s decision in Prime Commercial Bank, the power to amend a deemed assessment under section 122(5A) could not be exercised by an Additional Commissioner in the manner adopted. This objection goes to the root of the matter and was never judicially addressed in the impugned order. Once the assumption of jurisdiction itself is shown to be defective, all subsequent findings on merits become irrelevant and unenforceable.

Without prejudice to the above, the impugned order is also vitiated by gross violations of natural justice. Several additions have been made without proper confrontation of the legal basis, without identifying the precise statutory provision allegedly violated, and without addressing the detailed explanations already placed on record. The law is settled that an assessee must be confronted not only with figures but with the precise legal and factual grounds on which adverse action is proposed. Mere narration of amounts followed by mechanical additions cannot substitute for a lawful adjudicatory process.

Turning to the substantive issues, the disallowance of exemption claimed under Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule in respect of Tariff Differential Subsidy is wholly misconceived. The appellant demonstrated, through detailed replies, that the subsidy in question is granted by the Federal Government pursuant to express governmental policy decisions, implemented through NEPRA-approved tariffs and federal notifications, with the sole objective of bridging the gap between the cost-reflective tariff and the consumer tariff mandated by the Government. The appellant merely acts as an implementing conduit for Government policy; the subsidy does not represent income arising from a commercial transaction but a compensatory fiscal transfer to enable compliance with federal directives.

Crucially, the appellant placed on record that identical claims under Clause 102A were examined and accepted by the tax department itself in earlier tax years, including through concluded proceedings under section 122(5A). In those proceedings, the department categorically held that there was no legal infirmity in the appellant’s claim of exemption. No change in law, no change in material facts, and no binding contrary judgment has been identified to justify a departure from this settled position. The principle of consistency and certainty in tax administration, repeatedly affirmed by superior courts, squarely applies. The impugned order’s reliance on unrelated High Court proceedings, where the exemption issue was neither raised nor adjudicated, amounts to misapplication of precedent and cannot override the express statutory exemption or the department’s own past conduct.

The addition relating to alleged “bad debts” or deduction from gross receipts is equally untenable. The appellant clearly explained that the amount represents reversal of revenue in respect of chronic defaulters, in accordance with IFRS-15, which mandates that revenue can only be recognized when collection of consideration is probable. This is not a discretionary write-off or an after-the-fact tax adjustment; it is the correct measurement of revenue under the applicable accounting framework consistently applied by the appellant and accepted by the department in prior years. Importantly, the appellant demonstrated that, notwithstanding such accounting treatment, the amounts in question were included in turnover for the purposes of minimum tax under section 113, thereby fully negating any allegation of prejudice to revenue. The impugned order fails to deal with this critical aspect and proceeds on an erroneous assumption that any reduction in accounting revenue automatically results in tax loss.

Similarly, the addition on account of alleged non-accrual of late payment surcharge (LPS) reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of accrual principles. While the appellant follows the mercantile system of accounting, accrual under tax law still requires enforceable entitlement and reasonable certainty of collection. The appellant placed on record the pervasive issue of circular debt and the established policy of recognizing LPS from government and semi-government entities only upon receipt, due to chronic non-recovery and settlement uncertainties. This approach is fully aligned with IFRS-15 and has been consistently applied. Taxing hypothetical, non-realizable accruals not only violates accounting principles but also results in taxation of illusory income, which the law does not permit. The further inclusion of such notional accruals in turnover for minimum tax purposes compounds the error.

The treatment of recoveries from consumers for new connections as taxable income in the year of receipt is another glaring legal error. The appellant demonstrated, with reference to accounting standards and the nature of the transaction, that such amounts are initially recognized as liabilities and subsequently amortized as income over the period during which services are rendered. This treatment reflects the economic reality that the appellant is under an obligation to provide utility services over time, and the entire receipt does not represent income “due” at the time of collection. Even assuming, without admitting, the department’s contrary position, the impugned order is internally inconsistent as it taxes the gross receipt while completely ignoring the corresponding cost of assets installed, thereby violating the matching principle and overstating income.

The disallowance of foreign exchange loss on the ground that it is “notional” is equally unsustainable. The appellant explained that section 71 of the Ordinance itself mandates conversion of foreign currency items at prescribed rates, and the resulting exchange differences necessarily flow into profit or loss under the mercantile system. Exchange losses recognized in accordance with consistent accounting policy cannot be selectively disallowed when exchange gains arising from the same methodology have been offered to tax in earlier years. The department’s own appellate history in the appellant’s case supports this position. In any event, the appellant specifically pleaded, without prejudice, that if the loss is to be treated as capital in nature, then capitalization and depreciation must be allowed. The impugned order ignores this alternative plea altogether.

The disallowance of payments made pursuant to NEPRA proceedings by characterizing them as “fines” under section 21(g) is also procedurally and substantively flawed. The appellant repeatedly sought clarification of the basis and quantum of the alleged payment, demonstrating that the figure adopted by the department did not reconcile with actual payments made under NEPRA orders. More importantly, no finding has been recorded establishing that the payment was penal in nature rather than compensatory or regulatory. The burden to establish that an expense falls within the mischief of section 21(g) squarely lies on the department, which has not been discharged.

A substantial portion of the impugned demand arises from artificial inflation of “turnover” for minimum tax purposes under section 113. The appellant demonstrated, issue by issue, that several items included by the department—such as electricity duty, withholding taxes under sections 235 and 235A, PTV license fee collections, tariff differential subsidy, recoveries, and liquidated damages—are either statutory pass-through collections, balance-sheet items, or compensatory receipts that do not constitute turnover from business operations. The statutory definition of turnover expressly excludes sales tax and federal excise duty, and settled jurisprudence holds that amounts collected on behalf of government or third parties cannot be treated as business receipts. The impugned order disregards these principles and results in double counting and taxation of non-income items.

The treatment of tax collected under section 148 on imports as minimum tax further demonstrates legal infirmity. The appellant is not a commercial importer earning income from imports; it imports plant, machinery, and equipment for its own use in regulated utility operations. The very language of section 148(7) restricts its application to “income of the importer arising from imports,” a condition that is not satisfied in the appellant’s case. Moreover, the amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2022 were expressly intended to cure anomalies and clarify that own-use imports of industrial undertakings should not be trapped into minimum tax merely due to rate classifications. The impugned order ignores both the statutory language and the legislative intent, resulting in unjustified double taxation.

The levy under section 7E suffers from similar defects. The appellant provided detailed, property-wise information demonstrating that several assets fell within statutory exclusions, were not in possession, or constituted business premises. These submissions were either ignored or cursorily brushed aside, leading to an arbitrary demand. Constitutional and jurisdictional challenges aside, even on a plain application of section 7E, the demand is unsustainable on facts already on record.

Finally, the impugned order fails to give proper effect to refund adjustments and statutory tax credits, including credit under section 236K, without confronting the appellant or reconciling the figures. Such mechanical curtailment of credits further underscores the non-speaking and arbitrary nature of the order.

In view of the foregoing, the impugned order deserves to be annulled in its entirety for want of lawful jurisdiction, violation of natural justice, and patent misapplication of law. Without prejudice, even on merits, each of the additions and disallowances is independently unsustainable and liable to be deleted. Consequential relief by way of correct computation of income, turnover, minimum tax, refunds, and credits must also follow as a matter of course.

### BEFORE THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL INLAND REVENUE, KARACHI  
**KARACHI BENCH**

**ITA No. 239/KB/2024**  
**Tax Year: 2022**  
**Filed vide DT No. 2072 dated November 29, 2024**

---

### APPLICATION FOR TRANSFER OF APPEAL  
*(From Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue to Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals))*

---

**Respectfully Sheweth:**

1. That the above-captioned appeal has been filed by the Appellant before this Hon’ble Tribunal against the impugned order passed by the learned Commissioner Inland Revenue for Tax Year 2022, and the same is presently pending adjudication.

2. That subsequent to the filing of the present appeal, significant **procedural amendments** have been introduced through the **Finance Act, 2025**, whereby **section 126A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 has been omitted**, thereby restoring the legal position as it stood prior to the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024.

3. That as a consequence of the said omission, the **first appellate forum** against an assessment or appellate order of the tax authorities once again stands restored as the **Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals)**, without any pecuniary jurisdictional restriction.

4. That the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Karachi Bench, in its detailed order (inter alia in the case of *Crescent Star Insurance Co. Ltd.*), has already held that:
   - the omission of section 126A is **procedural in nature**;
   - procedural amendments operate **retrospectively** and apply to **pending proceedings**; and  
   - where a taxpayer opts to first avail the forum of Commissioner (Appeals), such request deserves to be allowed and appeals pending before the Tribunal may be **transferred accordingly** fileciteturn0file0.

5. That the said view is further fortified by the judgments of the **Lahore High Court** and the **Islamabad High Court**, wherein it has consistently been held that amendments restoring an appellate forum confer a **beneficial right**, do not impair vested rights, and therefore apply to all pending matters.

6. That in addition, the **proviso to section 127(1)** and the substituted **section 131(1)** of the Ordinance (as amended by the Finance Act, 2025) now expressly provide an **option to the taxpayer** either:
   - to file or continue appeal before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals), or  
   - to surrender that right and approach the Appellate Tribunal directly.

7. That the Appellant, in the present case, **intends to avail the statutory remedy before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) as the first appellate forum**, and therefore seeks transfer of the present appeal accordingly.

---

### **PRAYER**

In view of the foregoing facts and legal position, it is most respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Tribunal may graciously be pleased to:

a) **Allow this application**;  
b) **Direct the transfer** of the present appeal bearing ITA No. 239/KB/2024 for Tax Year 2022, filed vide DT No. 2072 dated November 29, 2024, to the **concerned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals)** for decision in accordance with law; and  
c) Grant any other relief deemed just and proper in the circumstances of the case.

---

**Karachi**

**For and on behalf of the Appellant**

## APPLICATION FOR TRANSFER OF APPEAL  
*(Transfer to Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals))*

**Respectfully Sheweth:**  
That the appellant has filed the above-captioned appeal before this Hon’ble Tribunal in respect of Tax Year 2022, filed vide DT No. 2072 dated 29 November 2024, which is presently pending adjudication. Subsequent to the institution of the appeal, the legal position governing the appellate fora has materially changed through the Finance Act, 2025, whereby section 126A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 has been omitted, restoring the position as it stood prior to the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024. Consequently, the first appellate forum again stands as the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals), and the earlier pecuniary-based routing of appeals to the Tribunal has ceased to operate in the manner previously introduced.

That the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Karachi Bench, in its order (including in the matter of *Crescent Star Insurance Co. Ltd.*), has already taken the view that the omission of section 126A and the restoration of the original appellate regime is procedural in nature and, therefore, applies to pending matters. The Tribunal has further recognized that where a taxpayer opts to first avail the forum of Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals), such request merits acceptance, and the pending appeal may be transmitted accordingly for decision in accordance with law fileciteturn0file0. The said position also finds support from the approach adopted by the superior courts, as noticed in the same order, to the effect that beneficial procedural amendments restoring an appellate forum operate retrospectively for pending proceedings and do not prejudice any party.

That, additionally, the Finance Act, 2025 has introduced an express statutory option through the proviso to section 127(1), read with the corresponding framework under section 131(1), enabling an aggrieved person to either pursue the appeal before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) or, by surrendering that right, approach the Appellate Tribunal directly. The appellant, in the present case, seeks to avail the remedy before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) as the first appellate forum and, therefore, prays that the present appeal may be transferred to the concerned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) for adjudication in accordance with law.

## PRAYER

### BEFORE THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL INLAND REVENUE, KARACHI  
**KARACHI BENCH**

**ITA No. 239/KB/2024 (Tax Year 2022)**  
**Filed vide DT No. 2072 dated 29 November 2024**

## APPLICATION FOR TRANSFER OF APPEAL  
*(Transfer to Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals))*

**Respectfully Sheweth:**  

That the appellant has filed the above-captioned appeal before this Hon’ble Tribunal against the impugned order relating to Tax Year 2022, which appeal is presently pending adjudication. At the time of filing, the appeal was routed directly to this Hon’ble Tribunal in view of the then-prevailing statutory framework introduced through the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024, whereby section 126A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 prescribed pecuniary limits and altered the ordinary appellate hierarchy.

That subsequent to the filing of the present appeal, the legal position governing appellate forums has undergone a fundamental change through the **Finance Act, 2025**, whereby **section 126A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 has been omitted**, thereby restoring the appellate regime as it existed prior to the 2024 amendment. As a result, the **Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals)** once again stands restored as the first appellate forum, irrespective of the quantum of tax demand, and the earlier pecuniary-based bifurcation between the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Appellate Tribunal no longer subsists.

That the Hon’ble **Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Karachi Bench**, in its recent and detailed order (inter alia in the case of *Crescent Star Insurance Co. Ltd.*), has exhaustively examined the impact of the omission of section 126A and the corresponding amendments made through the Finance Act, 2025. The Tribunal has categorically held that the said amendments are **procedural in nature**, that procedural law is ordinarily retrospective, and that such amendments apply to **all pending proceedings**. The Tribunal has further held that where a taxpayer expresses its intention to first avail the forum of the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals), such request ought to be allowed and the appeal pending before the Tribunal may be **transmitted to the concerned Commissioner (Appeals)** for decision in accordance with law fileciteturn0file0.

That while arriving at the above conclusion, the Karachi Tribunal has relied upon and aligned itself with authoritative pronouncements of the **Lahore High Court** and the **Islamabad High Court**. In this regard, the Lahore High Court, in *Haris Hasan Syed v. Commissioner Inland Revenue* (ITR No. 21137/2025, judgment dated 29-09-2025), held that the amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2025 are procedural and beneficial in nature, that they do not infringe upon any vested rights, and that pending matters must be governed by the restored appellate framework. The Lahore High Court further directed that proceedings instituted before an incorrect forum due to an intervening statutory change should be transmitted to the proper forum, rather than being dismissed on technical grounds.

That the Lahore High Court, in another judgment dated 09-09-2026, has reiterated the same principle by holding that upon omission of section 126A and consequential amendments to section 133 of the Ordinance, the original appellate position stands revived, and matters must proceed before the appropriate statutory forum as restored by the Finance Act, 2025. The Court emphasized that such procedural restoration must govern pending cases, as the legislature clearly intended to re-establish the ordinary appellate hierarchy.

That the **Islamabad High Court**, in its judgment dated 16-11-2025, has also taken a consistent view, holding that amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2025—being procedural and restoring an additional appellate forum—must be applied **retrospectively to all pending cases**. Relying upon long-standing jurisprudence of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, the Islamabad High Court reaffirmed that procedural changes, particularly those conferring a beneficial right such as an additional level of appeal, operate retrospectively unless they reopen past and closed transactions or disturb vested rights. The Court further observed that no prejudice is caused to any party by allowing an additional stage of adjudication, and accordingly directed that pending matters be transmitted to the appropriate appellate forum.

That, in addition to the above judicial pronouncements, the statutory scheme itself now expressly recognizes the taxpayer’s **right of choice**. The proviso to **section 127(1)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, grants an aggrieved person the option either to file an appeal before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) or to surrender that right and directly approach the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue. This option is further reinforced by the substituted **section 131(1)**, which permits a direct appeal to the Tribunal only where the taxpayer consciously exercises such option in the manner prescribed.

That the Hon’ble Karachi Tribunal, in *Crescent Star Insurance Co. Ltd.*, has harmoniously read the above statutory provisions with the judgments of the Lahore and Islamabad High Courts and has concluded that where the appellant opts to first avail the forum of the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals), the Tribunal ought to facilitate such choice by transferring the pending appeal to the said forum. The Tribunal has also directed that the appeal so transferred be treated as an appeal against the impugned order and be decided strictly in accordance with law fileciteturn0file0.

That, in the present case, the appellant **consciously elects to avail the remedy before the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) as the first appellate forum**, in line with the restored statutory scheme, binding judicial precedents, and the settled position adopted by this Hon’ble Tribunal. The present appeal, therefore, deserves to be transferred to the concerned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) for adjudication on merits.

## PRAYER  

In view of the foregoing facts, statutory provisions, and binding judicial precedents, it is most respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Tribunal may graciously be pleased to allow this application and **direct the transfer of Appeal bearing ITA No. 239/KB/2024 for Tax Year 2022, filed vide DT No. 2072 dated 29 November 2024, to the concerned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals)** for disposal in accordance with law, along with any other relief deemed just and proper in the circumstances.

**Karachi**  
**Dated:** _____________  

**For and on behalf of the Appellant**  
__________________________  
Authorized Representative

Please read it and suggest heading: 

The impugned order passed by the CIR(A) is bad in law and on facts as it has been issued in violation of the principles of natural justice and without proper application of mind. The CIR(A), being a quasi‑judicial authority under Section 129 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, was legally bound to consider all submissions, documents and legal arguments placed on record, including those filed with the stay application, and to give a reasoned order. Instead, the appeal has been disposed of through a cryptic and non‑speaking order, without addressing the specific factual and legal issues raised by the appellant, thereby infringing the appellant’s right to fair trial and due process.

Further, the CIR(A) erred in law in upholding the action of the ACIR under Section 122(5A), as the jurisdictional preconditions for invoking this provision were not fulfilled. Section 122(5A) can be exercised only where the original assessment is both erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of revenue, on the basis of material already on record. In the present case, no specific error in the original assessment was identified, no independent inquiry was conducted by the department, and the proceedings were used as a tool for fishing and roving enquiries, which is impermissible and tantamount to conducting an audit under the garb of amendment. The show‑cause notice itself is defective, being vague, general, and issued without definite information and, in any event, beyond the prescribed limitation, rendering the entire exercise without lawful authority. The CIR(A) failed to examine these jurisdictional defects, including limitation and absence of “erroneous and prejudicial” findings, and simply endorsed the ACIR’s action without dealing with the appellant’s detailed objections.

It is therefore prayed that the appeal be allowed, the impugned order of the CIR(A) and the amendment proceedings under Section 122(5A) along with the consequential notice/order be declared illegal, without jurisdiction and void ab initio, and the original assessment under Section 120 be restored, along with such other relief, including costs, as may be deemed just and proper in the circumstances.

**Suggested heading (best-fit, single line):**  
**“Non-Speaking Order and Unlawful Assumption of Jurisdiction under Section 122(5A) (Violation of Natural Justice, Limitation, and Defective SCN)”**

Here are heading options that actually *fit what this ground is doing* (i.e., “profit on debt” is **business-linked, project-finance-mandated**, so Section 39 can’t be used as a residuary bucket):

### Best “tribunal-ready” heading (single-line, complete)
**Misclassification of Project-Finance Linked Profit on Debt: Taxable as Business Income under Section 18, Not ‘Other Sources’ under Section 39**

### Slightly more aggressive (high impact)
**Section 39 Wrongly Invoked: Profit on Security Accounts Is an Incidental Business Receipt of the LNG Terminal Project (Section 18 Applies)**

### If you want it to scream the core factual hook
**Profit on Debt Earned on Mandatory Project Security Accounts Is Inseparable from LNG Terminal Operations—Not Passive Investment Income**

### If you want a clean legal framing

Pakistan Branch as Security Trustee. The recitals to the Accounts Agreement unambiguously state that "the Company has been established to design, develop, finance, construct, install, equip, commission, operate and maintain a 4.5 MTPA liquefied natural gas receiving, storage and regasification terminal, and the associated pipeline infrastructure, to be located at Port Qasim near Karachi in Pakistan (the Project)" and that "the Project is being financed in part by financing provided to the Company by the Financiers pursuant to the Facility Agreements". The Accounts Agreement further provides in Clause 3.7 that "the procedures for release of funds from the Security Accounts contained in this Agreement will not affect the obligations of the Company to make all payments required to be made to the Finance Parties on the respective due dates for payment in accordance with the Finance Documents", confirming that the security accounts are an integral part of the debt service and payment mechanism for the project financing. In law, Section 18 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 provides that income chargeable to tax under the head "Income from Business" includes profits and gains of any business or profession carried on by the taxpayer. The fundamental principle underlying the taxation of business income is that all receipts, benefits and gains arising from or in the course of business operations, including incidental income earned as a necessary incident of carrying on such business, are chargeable as business income. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has consistently held that the characterization of income must be determined based on the actual facts, circumstances and source of such income. In a landmark judgment summarized in the "Summary of Supreme Court Judgements" released by the Federal Board of Revenue, the Supreme Court held that where a foundation or entity is established for a specific business purpose and earns surplus income including interest from bank deposits in the course of such business activity aligned with the entity's objectives, such income is to be treated as "business income" rather than "income from other sources". The Court emphasized that income arising from a business relationship and linked to the taxpayer's business operations is chargeable as business income.[2][3]

Similarly, the Islamabad High Court in ITR No. 06 of 2003 examined the question of whether interest income on bank deposits is chargeable to tax as income from business or profession, or as income from other sources, and held in favor of the taxpayer that such interest income, where it arises in the course of business operations and is linked to the business financing structure, is chargeable as business income and not as income from other sources. The Court distinguished the case of Lucky Cement Limited on the ground that Lucky Cement turned on the specific fact that the constituent documents of that company did not empower it to engage in the business of investment, and it was only in view of the explicit prohibition in the constituent documents that the Supreme Court held that income or interest from investment could not be treated as income from business. The Islamabad High Court further observed that up until tax year 1998, the department itself had continued to treat interest income on bank deposits as income from business, demonstrating the department's own consistent historical position that such income, where arising in the course of business operations, is chargeable as business income. The High Court of Sindh has also confirmed that interest income arising from a business relationship and linked to the taxpayer's business operations is chargeable to tax under Section 18 as business income, not under Section 39 as income from other sources.[4][5]

Section 39 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 is a residuary provision that applies only to income which does not fall under any other head of income specified in Section 15 of the Ordinance. Section 39(1) expressly provides that income chargeable under Section 39 is "other than income exempt from tax under this Ordinance or income chargeable to tax under any other provision of this Ordinance", thereby making it clear that income chargeable under Section 18 as business income cannot simultaneously be brought to tax under Section 39. The legislative intent underlying Section 39 is to tax passive, investment-type income that has no nexus with the taxpayer's business activities. Where income arises as a direct, necessary and inseparable incident of conducting business operations and is inextricably linked to the business financing structure and contractual obligations of the business, such income cannot be artificially divorced from the business and treated as income from other sources merely because it takes the form of interest or profit on deposits.[6][7]

In the present case, the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 did not arise from any voluntary, discretionary or passive investment of surplus funds by the appellant for purposes unconnected with its business. On the contrary, the profit arose exclusively and automatically from the mandatory maintenance of project-specific security accounts that the appellant was contractually obligated to establish and operate as a condition precedent to receiving project financing from IFC, ADB and the local banking syndicate for the development and operation of its LNG terminal. The security accounts are not general bank accounts or discretionary treasury investments; they are ring-fenced project accounts governed by detailed contractual covenants under the Accounts Agreement dated 7 January 2016 and the Common Terms Agreement, with strict and binding restrictions on deposits, withdrawals and utilization of funds. Clause 3.12 of the Accounts Agreement mandates that these accounts will automatically bear profit/interest at prevailing rates, and such profit/interest will be added to the account balance. The earning of this profit is therefore not an independent business activity or investment decision; it is a mandatory, automatic and contractual consequence of complying with the project financing structure imposed by the lenders as an integral part of funding the LNG terminal business.[1]

The funds in these security accounts are not freely deployable surplus funds of a general nature available for any purpose; they are balance funds from loan disbursements and project revenues that are tightly ring-fenced by lender covenants exclusively for the terminal's development, operation, debt service, maintenance and credit support mechanisms as set out in the detailed waterfall provisions of Clauses 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the Accounts Agreement. The FSRU SBLC Account, in particular, is maintained solely to comply with credit support requirements under the Time Charter Party agreement with Excelerate Energy Middle East, LLC, which is an essential project contract for the operation of the FSRU that is the core infrastructure of the LNG terminal business. The profit earned on these accounts is therefore functionally, operationally, contractually and legally part of the LNG terminal business operations, arising from and incidental to such operations, rather than a separate stream of passive investment income. To characterize such profit as "income from other sources" under Section 39 would be to artificially sever it from its business source and ignore the commercial, contractual and legal reality that the profit is an inseparable incident of the business financing structure and operations mandated as a condition precedent to the Financiers making financing available to the Company.[1]

The principle established by the superior courts is clear: income that arises from a business relationship and is linked to the taxpayer's business operations must be treated as business income. In the present case, the profit on debt arises directly from security accounts that are mandated, governed and restricted by project financing agreements that are the lifeblood of the LNG terminal business. The accounts exist only because of the business, are maintained only to comply with business financing obligations as a condition precedent to obtaining project loans, and the profit thereon is earned only as an automatic incident of such compliance mandated by Clause 3.12 of the Accounts Agreement. The profit is therefore inextricably linked to, and arises from, the LNG terminal business operations, and is properly chargeable to tax under Section 18 as business income, not under Section 39 as income from other sources. Both the Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue and the learned CIR(A) have manifestly failed to apply the correct legal test, have ignored the binding judicial precedents, and have disregarded the actual factual and contractual matrix as evidenced by the Accounts Agreement, Common Terms Agreement, balance sheet, financial statements and project financing documents. The impugned order of the CIR(A) upholding the characterization of the profit on debt as income from other sources is therefore perverse, contrary to law, unsupported by evidence, and liable to be set aside. It is therefore most respectfully prayed that this Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal may be pleased to allow this ground of appeal, set aside the impugned order of the CIR(A) to the extent it relates to the characterization and taxation of the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000, and hold that such profit on debt is chargeable to tax under Section 18 as business income and not under Section 39 as income from other sources.[3][5][4][1]

Below is a **refined and legally focused articulation of the grounds**, with **clear emphasis on the customer agreement**, the **cost-to-cost reimbursement nature**, and the **volume/throughput-based recovery mechanism**. The language is deliberately tightened to expose the **contractual misreading** and **factual disconnect** in the Impugned Order.

---

**Re-emphasized and Strengthened Grounds of Appeal**

1. The Impugned Order is bad in law and on facts, as it proceeds on a fundamentally erroneous appreciation of the contractual arrangement governing the recovery of royalty and related port charges. The learned Commissioner (Appeals) has failed to properly read, interpret, and apply the express terms of the customer agreement, which unequivocally characterizes such amounts as recoverable strictly on a cost-to-cost, reimbursement basis.

2. The learned Commissioner (Appeals) has erred in maintaining the action taken under section 23 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, read with sections 43(3) and 44 thereof, without first establishing that the impugned amounts constitute “consideration for taxable services.” The statutory pre-condition for levy of sales tax—namely, the existence of value attributable to a service—has not been satisfied.

3. The learned Commissioner (Appeals) has gravely erred in treating Rs. 514,894,529 as taxable value and upholding Sindh sales tax of Rs. 72,085,234 by wrongly including royalty and related port charges within the value of taxable services. Under the Act, only the value of services rendered is subject to tax. The customer agreement explicitly provides that royalty and port charges are recoverable on a **pure pass-through basis**, without any mark-up, margin, or value addition. These amounts merely reimburse statutory and contractual costs incurred by the Appellant on behalf of the customer and therefore fall entirely outside the taxable base.

4. Without prejudice to the above, the learned Commissioner (Appeals) has erred in holding that royalty is “embedded” in the tariff for terminal services. This conclusion is factually incorrect and contractually unsustainable. The Terminal Services Agreement clearly distinguishes between (i) the agreed tariff for handling, storage, and custody transfer services, and (ii) royalty and related port charges, which are recoverable separately on actual basis. Crucially, these charges are **not fixed or lump-sum in nature**; rather, they are **directly linked to the customer’s actual volumes and throughput**, reinforcing their character as variable, reimbursable costs rather than consideration for services. Treating such volume-based reimbursements as part of service value reflects a fundamental misreading of the agreement.

5. Without prejudice to Grounds Nos. 3 and 4, the learned Commissioner (Appeals) failed to consider and apply binding judicial precedent relied upon by the Appellant, particularly the Sindh High Court judgment reported as *IMS Health Pakistan (2022 PTD 576)*. The said judgment squarely holds that amounts recovered on actual, reimbursement basis—where no value addition is involved—do not form part of taxable service value. The non-discussion and non-application of this precedent renders the Impugned Order legally unsustainable.

6. Without prejudice to the foregoing, the learned Commissioner (Appeals) has wrongly concluded that the reimbursement arrangement is non-genuine, merely on the basis of descriptions appearing in the financial statements and billing nomenclature. This approach is legally flawed. Taxability must be determined on the basis of **substance and contractual rights and obligations**, not accounting captions. The customer agreement expressly provides that royalty and related port charges are recoverable strictly on actual basis, as reimbursement of expenses incurred, and are entirely distinct from consideration for terminal services. Ignoring the governing contract and substituting it with assumptions drawn from financial disclosures reflects a serious error of law and fact.

7. Consequently, the levy of penalty and default surcharge under sections 43 and 44 of the Act is also unlawful, as the very foundation of the demand—i.e., inclusion of reimbursable, pass-through costs within taxable value—is erroneous. In the absence of a valid tax demand, no penal consequences can legally survive.

---

This framing keeps the argument **anchored in the customer agreement**, exposes the **incorrect “embedded tariff” assumption**, and clearly demonstrates that **volume-linked recovery is incompatible with the concept of service consideration**. It also subtly positions the issue as one of **jurisdictional overreach**, not merely valuation.

4.	Without prejudice to ground of appeal No. 3, the learned Commissioner (Appeals) has erred in holding that royalty is “embedded” in the tariff for terminal services under the Terminal Services Agreement. This finding is contrary to the express contractual terms, which clearly distinguish between (i) the agreed tariff for handling, storage and custody transfer services, and (ii) royalty charges recoverable separately on actual basis. Moreover, royalty is recovered strictly in proportion to the customer’s actual volume/throughput (and not on a fixed basis), demonstrating that it is a variable, pass-through reimbursement and not part of the consideration for taxable services. By ignoring this contractual and commercial reality, the learned Commissioner (Appeals) has misread the agreement and wrongly included reimbursements in taxable service value.

(2) The books of accounts, documents and records required to be maintained by a company in accordance with this Chapter shall be maintained in accordance with international accounting standards and as required under the Companies Ordinance, 1984.

3.9	Keeping in view of the above provisions of the Ordinance, business income must be computed using the method of accounting regularly employed, and a company shall account on an accrual basis. Under this regime, income is derived when it is due and expenditure is incurred when it is payable, that is, when all events fixing liability have occurred and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy. Disallowing an accrued, definite levy on the premise of non payment would fracture the statutory proportion. The Department would be taxing revenue on accrual while allowing expenses only on payment, producing an unbalanced approach that sections 32 and 34 of the Ordinance do not countenance and that undermines the “clear reflection of income” principle embedded in section 32 of the Ordinance.

3.10	Please note that the Legislature has already installed a protection for unpaid accruals under section 34(5) of the Ordinance. If a deduction is allowed for an accrued liability and it remains unpaid for three years, the unpaid amount is brought back to tax, with a fresh deduction when actually paid thereafter. This recapture and re allowance mechanism confirms that current year accrual is the rule, and cash settlement is not a precondition to deduction. To insist on payment first would render section 34(5) of the Ordinance futile, such redundancy cannot be imputed to the Legislature, which is presumed to avoid surplusage and to legislate effectively rather than ineffectually. In short, if non payment alone justified disallowance, section 34(5) would have no work to do, an outcome established principle of structure reject.

3.11	The windfall levy arises by operation of law and contract once qualifying production and pricing thresholds are met under the Petroleum Policy 2012 and the PCA/supplemental agreement. At year end, all events fixing liability have occurred (production has taken place; reference prices are known) and the amount is mechanically determinable under the prescribed formula. That is the very definition of “payable” under section 34, and it also meets IAS 37 criteria for recognizing a present obligation measured with reliable estimation, hence a proper accrual, not a tentative set aside. The label “provisional” cannot displace the legal character of a definite, enforceable statutory impost that has already attached to the year’s production. 

3.12	Higher appellate forums have long accepted accrual basis deductions where the liability is ascertained and legally enforceable, notwithstanding later payment. The Sindh High Court held that an ascertained liability recognized under the mercantile system is actual, not notional, and thus allowable on accrual. Likewise, the ATIR has acknowledged that a statutory cess computed by rule is appropriately recognized on accrual, even if cash remittance follows, reflecting the very logic of sections 32 and 34 of the Ordinance. These authorities reinforce that timing of payment does not control where the liability has crystallized. 

3.13	Taxing revenue on accrual while allowing expenses only on payment creates a basis mismatch that distorts the true income of the period and contradicts the statutory design of sections 32 and 34 of the Ordinance. The Ordinance requires a consistent method (and even conditions any change on the Commissioner’s approval to “clearly reflect income”), which inherently demands symmetry: where income is recognized when due, expenses arising from the same period and fixed by all events must be recognized when payable. Denying the levy until payment would overstate taxable income and defeat the matching principle embedded in the accrual mandate. 

3.14	Because the windfall levy is a present, definite liability that has accrued under the Policy/PCA formula during the year, and because section 34(5) already protects the revenue against non payment, the claim is properly allowable in the year of provision. Treating it as disallowable until payment would nullify section 34(5) and destabilize the mandatory accrual framework by taxing income on accrual while deferring its associated costs, an untenable, asymmetric approach under the Ordinance.

## Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1 to 3  
### **Scope, Preconditions, and Jurisdiction under Section 122(5A)**

At the outset, it is submitted that section 122(5A) is an **exceptional and narrowly tailored provision**, designed to address situations of *definite escapement of income* arising from a *clear and demonstrable misapplication of law or facts*. It does not confer unfettered powers to revisit concluded assessments merely because a different view is subsequently formed by the Department.

The jurisdiction under section 122(5A) can only be validly assumed where the Commissioner is able to **identify a specific mistake apparent from record**, resulting in under-assessment, which mistake must be **self-evident, objective, and not debatable**. It is a settled principle that **issues involving interpretation of contracts, statutory regimes, fiscal concessions, or long-standing departmental practice fall outside the scope of section 122(5A)**.

In the present case, the matters sought to be re-opened—namely, the applicable tax rate under PCAs and the allowability of windfall levy—are **neither arithmetical errors nor patent mistakes**. These are **substantive legal issues**, governed by a specialized statutory framework comprising the Regulation of Mines and Oilfields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948, the Fifth Schedule to the Ordinance, and binding PCAs executed by the President of Pakistan on behalf of the State.

It is further submitted that **section 122(5A) cannot be used to disturb a position that has consistently been accepted by the Department itself in earlier years**, including under scrutiny assessments. The power under section 122(5A) is **corrective, not review-based**, and cannot be invoked to re-litigate debatable issues or to substitute one legal interpretation with another.

Accordingly, the assumption of jurisdiction under section 122(5A) in the present case is **without lawful authority** and the impugned assessment is liable to be annulled on this ground alone.

---

## Ground of Appeal No. 4  
### **Applicable Tax Rate under PCAs – Issue Pending before the Supreme Court**

The impugned assessment applies a tax computation methodology which has recently been upheld by the Hon’ble Sindh High Court; however, the matter is **sub judice before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan** through a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal filed by the Appellant.

The High Court judgment has proceeded on the assumption that the expression *“before deduction of payments to the Government”* applies uniformly to both the **minimum (50%) and maximum (55%) tax limits**, an interpretation which is **contrary to the plain language of the PCAs, Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979, and decades of settled departmental practice**.

The Appellant has demonstrated before the Hon’ble Supreme Court that:

- The phrase *“before deduction of payments to the Government”* is **deliberately confined to the minimum threshold** and does not extend to the maximum ceiling;

## Grounds of Appeal Nos. 6 to 7  
### **Allowability of Windfall Levy – Statutory, Contractual, and Accrual-Based Deduction**

The disallowance of windfall levy in the impugned assessment is legally untenable and factually misconceived.

It is a settled principle that **section 122(5A) cannot be used as a substitute for original assessment, audit proceedings, or inquiry under section 177**. ## Grounds of Appeal Nos. 6 and 7  
### **Windfall Levy – Disallowance Based on Alleged Non-Furnishing of Documents Is Itself Beyond Section 122(5A)**

The disallowance of windfall levy in the impugned assessment is not only substantively incorrect but is also **procedurally illegal**, as it is founded entirely on an allegation that the taxpayer did not furnish documentary evidence during the proceedings.

A perusal of the assessment order reveals that the Assessing Officer has categorically recorded that the claim of windfall levy is being disallowed because **“documentary evidence was not furnished by the taxpayer”**. This finding, on the face of it, exposes the fatal jurisdictional defect in the proceedings. If documentary evidence was required to examine the claim, the matter could not, by definition, fall within the scope of section 122(5A).

Section 122(5A) does not permit the Assessing Officer to demand evidence, test explanations, or evaluate documentation. The provision operates only where the alleged escapement is **discernible from the existing record**. Once the officer proceeds to seek documents and then disallows a claim for non-submission, the proceedings unmistakably transform into a **fact-finding inquiry**, which is alien to section 122(5A).

Moreover, the windfall levy is not a discretionary or contingent expense requiring evidentiary substantiation beyond the record. It is a **statutory levy**, imposed pursuant to the Petroleum Exploration and Production Policy, 2012, and expressly incorporated into the Petroleum Concession Agreements. Its computation is formula-based, its incidence automatic, and its allowability contractually recognized. The Appellant has consistently claimed the levy on accrual basis in accordance with section 32 of the Ordinance, and the Department itself has accepted this position in earlier years.

The assessment order for Tax Year 2024, instead of identifying any mistake apparent from record, proceeds on the impermissible premise that the taxpayer was required to *prove* the claim afresh through documents. Such an approach is **diametrically opposed to the spirit, purpose, and limitations of section 122(5A)** and renders the impugned disallowance legally unsustainable.

The impugned order, however, disregards this material and substitutes lawful analysis with an impermissible inquiry-based disallowance.

---

## Concluding Submissions

In view of the foregoing submissions:

- The invocation of section 122(5A) is vitiated by fishing inquiry and document-seeking, which the provision does not permit;
- The tax-rate issue is pending adjudication before the Hon’ble Supreme Court and cannot be conclusively determined at this stage;
- The disallowance of windfall levy based on alleged non-furnishing of documents is itself proof of jurisdictional overreach under section 122(5A).

The impugned amended assessment is therefore **void, unlawful, and unsustainable**, and is liable to be annulled in its entirety. In the alternative, the additions challenged herein deserve to be deleted.

- The windfall levy is a statutory, accrued, and deductible business expense.

The impugned amended assessment is therefore **unsustainable in law and on facts** and is liable to be annulled in toto. In the alternative, the additions challenged in the present appeal deserve to be deleted.

Ground No. 4: Provide a more detailed argument based on the previously attached documents. In the first paragraph, refer to the Sindh High Court decision against the taxpayer, and then explain the contentions and highlight that the matter is pending before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. 

Grounds of 6 and 7, please find the attached assessment order. In the said assessment, the officer stated that documentary evidence was not furnished by the taxpayer, which is itself against the spirit of section 122(5A) of the Ordinance.

Below is a **concise, tightened, and submission-ready version**, preserving the legal force while removing repetition and surplus explanation. Numbering is retained for ease of substitution.

---

**3.7**  
With respect to the contention that the impugned expense is a mere “provisional” claim, it is submitted that the appellant maintains its books of account under the mercantile (accrual) system. Under this method, a definite and ascertained liability is allowable as a deduction on accrual, irrespective of actual payment. Section 32 of the Ordinance mandatorily requires a company to compute its business income on an accrual basis, and the Department is therefore bound to accept expenses claimed in accordance with this method.

**3.8**  
Further, Rule 32 of the Income Tax Rules requires companies to maintain books of account in accordance with International Accounting Standards. Accordingly, liabilities recognized in the financial statements in compliance with IAS constitute valid accruals for tax purposes.

**3.9**  
Under the accrual regime, income is recognized when it becomes due and expenditure when the liability to pay has crystallized and can be determined with reasonable certainty. Disallowing a definite accrued levy merely on the ground of non-payment would result in taxing income on accrual while allowing expenses only on payment—an approach not contemplated by sections 32 and 34 of the Ordinance and contrary to the principle of clear reflection of income.

**3.10**  
The Legislature has itself addressed the issue of unpaid accrued liabilities through section 34(5) of the Ordinance, which provides for recapture of deductions remaining unpaid for three years, with re-allowance upon actual payment. This statutory mechanism confirms that accrual, not payment, is the governing rule. Any interpretation requiring payment as a precondition would render section 34(5) redundant, which is impermissible in law.

**3.11**  
The windfall levy arises by operation of law and contract once the prescribed production and pricing thresholds under the Petroleum Policy 2012 and the PCA are met. By year-end, all events fixing liability have occurred and the amount is determinable through a prescribed formula. The levy therefore constitutes a present and enforceable obligation, fully meeting the criteria of an accrued liability under section 34 of the Ordinance and IAS 37. The description of the levy as “provisional” is legally misconceived.

**3.12**  
It is well settled that an ascertained and enforceable statutory liability is allowable on accrual notwithstanding subsequent payment. Appellate fora, including the High Courts and the Appellate Tribunal, have consistently held that timing of payment does not govern deductibility once liability has crystallized.

**3.13**  
Allowing revenue on accrual while deferring related expenses until payment creates a mismatch that distorts taxable income and defeats the matching principle inherent in the accrual system mandated by the Ordinance.

**3.14**  
Accordingly, as the windfall levy is a definite liability accrued during the year under the Policy and PCA, and section 34(5) adequately safeguards the revenue in case of non-payment, the deduction is correctly allowable in the year of provision. Any contrary treatment would undermine the statutory accrual framework and result in an impermissible asymmetry in taxation.

---

Below is a **polished, self-contained secondary argument**, drafted to sit seamlessly after your primary contention, and framed **strictly without prejudice**. It is aligned with the facts of the instant case, the statutory scheme of **section 40**, and—critically—the **department’s own accepted position** in the attached order.

---

## **Without Prejudice: Allowability of Related Finance Cost under Section 40 if Profit on Debt is Treated as Income from Other Sources**

1. **Without prejudice** to the appellant’s primary and substantive contention that the impugned profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 is chargeable to tax as **business income under section 18**, it is respectfully submitted that **even if**, for the sake of argument, such income is classified under the head **“Income from Other Sources” under section 39**, then the **corresponding and directly related finance costs are mandatorily allowable as a deduction under section 40** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

2. Section 40 embodies a clear and unambiguous statutory principle: **any expenditure paid by a person in the year is deductible to the extent to which it is incurred in deriving income chargeable under the head “Income from Other Sources.”** Once income is assessed under section 39, the Ordinance itself requires that **all expenditures having a direct and proximate nexus with the earning of such income must be allowed**. The provision does not permit a selective or fragmented approach whereby income is taxed gross while the directly related costs are ignored.

3. In the instant case, the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 did not arise in isolation. It arose **exclusively from funds sourced through subordinated loans and foreign borrowings**, on which substantial finance costs were incurred during the same tax year. As disclosed in **Note 27 to the audited financial statements**, the total finance cost directly relatable to such borrowings aggregates to **Rs 483,401,279**, comprising:
   - Interest/markup on subordinated loan: **Rs 157,750,000**  
   - Interest/markup on foreign loans: **Rs 239,026,279**  
   - Amortisation of transaction costs: **Rs 86,625,000**

4. These costs were not general or unrelated business expenses. They represent the **very cost of funds** from which the deposits and balances giving rise to the profit on debt were generated. Absent these borrowings—and the attendant finance cost—the profit on debt could not, and would not, have arisen. The relationship between the income and the expenditure is therefore **direct, immediate, and inseparable**, satisfying the statutory test under section 40 in its entirety.

5. Consistent with this legal position, the appellant, in its return of income, adopted a **netting approach**, whereby the mark-up income of Rs 139,985,000 was set off against the related finance costs. Consequently, the return reflects **net finance costs of Rs 649,405,000**, being the balance after adjustment of total finance costs of Rs 794,882,000 against the said mark-up income. This treatment is not only commercially rational but is also fully supported by the express language of section 40.

6. Significantly, this position is **not merely a taxpayer assertion**. The attached order passed under section 122(5A) for **Tax Year 2024** demonstrates that the **tax department itself has accepted, on identical legal principles**, that where profit on debt is assessed under section 39, the **corresponding finance cost incurred to earn such income is allowable under section 40**. In the said order, the learned Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue, after examining the facts, statutory provisions, and judicial precedents, expressly held that:
   - interest income earned from borrowed funds kept in bank accounts constitutes income from other sources; and  
   - **finance cost paid on such borrowings is deductible under section 40**, being expenditure incurred in deriving that income.  

   The proceedings were accordingly **closed with no adverse inference**, thereby affirming the department’s own settled understanding of section 40 in cases of this nature. fileciteturn1file0

7. The attached order further reinforces this conclusion by relying upon and reaffirming binding judicial precedents, including **Lahore High Court judgment in *Pioneer Cement* (2005 PTD 2086)** and multiple decisions of the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue in the cases of **Lalpir (Pvt.) Ltd., Nishat Power Ltd., Kohinoor Energy Ltd.**, and others, all of which consistently hold that **interest or finance cost incurred to earn interest income is deductible under the relevant “other sources” provision**.

8. Applying these principles to the present case, it would be legally impermissible and contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance to:
   - assess the profit on debt under section 39; yet  
   - deny deduction of the finance costs that are demonstrably and directly attributable to earning that very income.  

   Such an approach would amount to taxing a **notional gross receipt**, ignoring the economic and legal reality recognised by section 40 and settled judicial law.

9. Accordingly, **without prejudice** to the appellant’s primary case under section 18, it is respectfully submitted that **if the impugned profit on debt is upheld as income from other sources**, then the learned authorities are **bound in law** to allow deduction of the corresponding finance costs under section 40, resulting in taxation—if any—only on the **net amount**, as already reflected in the return.

10. The failure to allow such deduction would not only violate the express mandate of section 40 but would also be **inconsistent with the department’s own accepted position on identical facts**, rendering any such action arbitrary, discriminatory, and unsustainable in law.

---
