During the last hearing, reliance was placed by the tax department on the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in case of UCH Powers (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Income Tax Appellate Tribunal reported as 2010 PTD 1809. With utmost respect, it is submitted that the said judgment operates in an entirely different factual and legal field and does not govern the controversy involved in the present appeal. A careful reading of the judgment itself demonstrates that the ratio laid down therein is confined to the interpretation of a specific tax exemption provision and not to the head-wise characterization of income under the Ordinance.
In UCH Powers, the central and determinative issue before the Hon’ble Supreme Court was whether interest/profit earned on bank deposits by private sector power generation companies could be treated as part of the “profits and gains derived from an electric power generation project” so as to qualify for exemption under Clause 176 of Part-I of the Second Schedule to the repealed Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 (corresponding to Clause 132 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001). The controversy, therefore, arose squarely in the context of exemption law, where strict construction is the governing principle.
The Supreme Court, after a review of the statutory scheme, held that the exemption under Clause 176 was limited to business income chargeable under section 22 of the repealed Ordinance and could not be extended to interest income falling under section 30, even if such interest was earned on bank accounts maintained in connection with the power project. The Court emphasized that exemption provisions cannot be enlarged by implication and that interest income, for exemption purposes, retained its separate statutory character.
Crucially, the present case does not involve any claim for exemption under the Second Schedule or under any other provision of the Ordinance. The appellant is not seeking immunity from tax on the profit on debt. The sole question in issue is the correct head of income under which such profit is to be assessed, whether as income from business under section 18 or as income from other sources under section 39. This distinction is fundamental, because the legal principles applicable to exemption provisions are materially different from those applicable to classification of income under different heads.
The factual matrix in UCH Powers is also materially distinguishable. In that case, the interest income was earned on bank deposits of share capital or surplus funds, which, although related to the project, were not shown to be subject to a rigid, lender-controlled financing and security framework. The Supreme Court repeatedly noted that such interest income constituted a separate stream of income for the purposes of applying the exemption clause.
In the present case, by contrast, the profit on debt has arisen exclusively and automatically from mandatory security accounts established under binding project finance documents. These accounts were required to be opened, funded, and maintained as a condition precedent to the disbursement of loans by international financial institutions and the local banking syndicate. The appellant had no discretion whatsoever in opening these accounts, choosing their nature, determining their operation, or deciding whether the funds should earn profit. The earning of profit is an inevitable contractual consequence of compliance with lender-imposed covenants forming the backbone of the LNG terminal’s financing and operations.
It is respectfully submitted that the Supreme Court in UCH Powers did not lay down any absolute or universal proposition that interest or profit on bank accounts can never constitute business income. Rather, the Court’s findings are expressly anchored to the limited question of exemption and to the statutory language of Clause 176 read with the scheme of heads of income under the repealed Ordinance. Indeed, the judgment itself acknowledges that characterization of income depends upon the statutory context, factual source, and purpose for which the inquiry is undertaken.
The present inquiry is of a fundamentally different nature. Here, the Tribunal is required to determine whether the profit on debt is inextricably linked to and arises in the course of the appellant’s LNG terminal business operations, including its project financing, debt service structure, and mandatory reserve mechanisms. The profit in question is not earned by parking idle or surplus funds for treasury or investment purposes; it arises from ring-fenced, lender-controlled project accounts, the existence of which is inseparable from the conduct and financing of the business itself.
Applying the ratio of UCH Powers to the present case would therefore amount to transposing a rule evolved for strict interpretation of tax exemptions into an entirely different field of income characterization, something the Supreme Court itself did not intend or hold. The judgment does not address, nor does it decide, whether income arising as an automatic incident of mandatory project financing arrangements constitutes business income under section 18.
For these reasons, it is respectfully submitted that the decision in UCH Powers (Pvt.) Ltd. v. ITAT is clearly distinguishable on facts, on law, and on the statutory issue involved, and does not detract from the appellant’s contention that the impugned profit on debt, arising from mandatory LNG project security accounts, is chargeable as income from business under section 18, and not as income from other sources under section 39.

Please only read below content: 

PROFIT ON DEBT EARNED ON MANDATORY PROJECT SECURITY ACCOUNTS IS INSEPARABLE FROM LNG TERMINAL OPERATIONS, NOT PASSIVE INVESTMENT INCOME

5.	It is respectfully submitted that the learned CIR(A) has erred fundamentally in law and on facts in classifying and treating the profit on debt amounting to Rs 139,985,000 as taxable under section 39 as "Income from Other Sources" instead of correctly characterizing the same as business income chargeable under section 18 as "Income from Business". 

6.	Both the learned officers below have manifestly failed to appreciate the actual nature, source, character and genesis of the profit on debt, which arose not from any independent investment activity or passive deployment of surplus funds, but exclusively from mandatory contractual obligations imposed upon the appellant as an integral and inseparable component of its core LNG terminal business operations and project financing structure.

7.	During the relevant tax year, the appellant, obtained long-term and short-term borrowings specifically to design, develop, finance, construct, operate and maintain a 4.5 million tons per annum LNG receiving, storage and regasification terminal at Port Qasim, Karachi. These loans, disclosed in the audited financial statements as "Long term borrowings", "Current portion of long term borrowings" and "Short term borrowings", were provided by international financial institutions including the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and a local banking syndicate under detailed and restrictive project finance arrangements documented in a Common Terms Agreement (CTA) and related Finance Documents. 

8.	The balance sheet of the appellant for the relevant period, together with Notes 16 and 18 to the Financial Statements, clearly evidences that all these borrowings were raised exclusively for the establishment, operation and financing of the LNG terminal operations, not for any extraneous investment purpose.

9.	The profits earned on bank deposits and term deposit receipts represent income earned on balance funds arising from the project loan disbursements and maintained in specific security accounts as mandated by the project financing structure. These funds were not discretionary surplus or idle funds available for general investment; rather, they represent balance funds from the loan disbursements that were contractually required to be kept with the bank in designated security accounts to satisfy the financing covenants and manage the finance cost structure under the project loan arrangements. 

10.	Critically, the long-term foreign borrowing from IFC, ADB and the local syndicate is explicitly and specifically in relation to the LNG operations of the appellant, as is conclusively established by the Accounts Agreement executed pursuant to the Common Terms Agreement.

11.	The Accounts Agreement, dated January 7, 2016, is executed between appellant, NIB Bank Limited as Account Bank, National Bank of Pakistan as the FSRU SBLC Facility Bank and Performance Bond Facility Bank, NIB Bank Limited as Intercreditor Agent, and Citibank N.A. Pakistan Branch as Security Trustee. The recitals to the Accounts Agreement unambiguously state that "the Appellant has been established to design, develop, finance, construct, install, equip, commission, operate and maintain a 4.5 MTPA liquefied natural gas receiving, storage and regasification terminal, and the associated pipeline infrastructure, to be located at Port Qasim near Karachi in Pakistan (the Project)" and that "the Project is being financed in part by financing provided to the Appellant by the Financiers pursuant to the Facility Agreements". 

12.	The recitals further record that "the Parties desire to record their agreement as to, inter alia, the establishment and operation of the Appellant's bank accounts relating to the Project" and that "it is a condition precedent to the Financiers making financing available to the Appellant and entering into the other Finance Documents that the Parties enter into this Agreement". These recitals establish beyond any doubt that the entire purpose and genesis of the Accounts Agreement, and the security accounts established thereunder, is intrinsically and inextricably tied to the LNG terminal project and its financing, and not to any separate or independent investment activity.

13.	Clause 3.1 of the Accounts Agreement mandates that "the Appellant shall, subject to the terms of this Agreement, open, fund, maintain and operate during the period from the date not later than six (6) Business Days prior to Financial Close until the Senior Release Date, unless otherwise set forth in this Agreement, the Security Accounts in its name at the Designated Branch of the Account Bank". Clause 3.2 further provides that save with the consent of the Intercreditor Agent, the Appellant shall not open or maintain any bank, deposit, savings or other type of account except for the specified Security Accounts and certain other limited accounts permitted under the Common Terms Agreement, and any other account opened with the consent of the Intercreditor Agent shall be secured in favour of the Security Trustee. 

14.	This demonstrates that the security accounts are not voluntary or discretionary accounts opened by the appellant for treasury management or investment purposes; they are mandatory, restricted and tightly controlled accounts that the appellant is contractually obligated to establish, fund, maintain and operate as a condition precedent to receiving project financing. The appellant cannot open or operate any other accounts without lender consent, and all such accounts are secured and ring-fenced for project purposes.

15.	Clause 3.3 provides that if the Appellant receives any sum which it is obliged to ensure is paid to a Security Account, the Appellant shall promptly deposit that sum into the relevant Security Account and in the intervening period shall hold that sum on trust for the Security Trustee, thereby confirming that the funds in these accounts are not beneficially owned by the appellant for general purposes but are held in trust for the secured creditors and subject to the project financing covenants. 

16.	Clause 3.5 provides that each Security Account will be a separate account at the Account Bank, and Schedule 1 to the Accounts Agreement lists the Security Accounts as including the USD Proceeds Account, Rupee Proceeds Account, Revenue Account, Debt Payment Account, Financiers Debt Service Reserve Account, Local Debt Service Reserve Account, Insurance and Compensation Account, Operations and Maintenance Account, PB Account, and FSRU SBLC Account, all maintained at NIB Bank Limited Main Branch Gul Tower, Karachi. These accounts are specifically designed and structured to receive loan proceeds, project revenues, debt service reserves, insurance proceeds, operating funds and credit support funds, and to make payments strictly in accordance with the waterfall and priority provisions set out in the Accounts Agreement and Common Terms Agreement.

17.	Clause 3.12 of the Accounts Agreement, titled "Interest on Balance", expressly and unambiguously provides that "each sum credited to a Security Account will, from the time it is credited until the time it is withdrawn, bear profit/interest at the prevailing rate for such account as from time to time offered by the Account Bank to the Appellant. Except where this Agreement provides otherwise, such profit/interest will be added to the balance of the relevant Security Account". This provision establishes beyond any doubt that the earning of profit/interest is an automatic, mandatory and contractual incident of maintaining the project security accounts mandated by the Financiers as a condition precedent to the disbursement of project loans, and is not an independent, discretionary or profit-seeking deployment of funds by the appellant for investment purposes unrelated to its business. 

18.	The appellant has no choice or discretion in the matter: once funds are credited to a security account (whether loan proceeds, project revenues, or balance funds from loan disbursements), they automatically and mandatorily bear profit/interest at prevailing rates, and such profit/interest is automatically added to the account balance. This is not an investment decision by the appellant; it is a contractual consequence of the project financing structure imposed by the lenders as an integral part of funding and securing the LNG terminal business. The relevant provision 3.12 of the Accounts Agreement is depicted below for your perusal:

 


19.	Clause 4.1 governs "Payments into Proceeds Accounts and Revenue Account" and provides detailed provisions requiring the appellant to deposit all loan proceeds, equity contributions, project revenues, and other specified funds into the designated security accounts. Clause 4.2 governs "Withdrawals from Proceeds Accounts" and permits the appellant to withdraw amounts from the Proceeds Accounts only to repay Sponsor Facilities and to pay Project Costs as and when they fall due, prior to the Project Physical Completion Date. Clause 4.3 governs "Withdrawals from Revenue Account" and sets out a detailed waterfall requiring the appellant to withdraw and apply monies from the Revenue Account strictly in accordance with a specified order of priority, including payment of taxes, transfer to Operations and Maintenance Account for Operating Costs, payment of fees and expenses to the Security Trustee and Administrative Parties, reimbursement of Performance Bond Facility Bank and FSRU SBLC Facility Bank, transfer to Debt Payment Account for debt service, payment of financing costs, prepayments, transfer to Debt Service Reserve Accounts to maintain required balances, and finally transfer to Distribution Account only if the Distribution Test is satisfied. 

20.	These provisions demonstrate that the balance funds from loan disbursements maintained in the security accounts are not freely available for any purpose chosen by the appellant; they are tightly ring-fenced and can only be withdrawn and applied in strict accordance with the contractual waterfall and priority provisions of the project financing documents, exclusively for purposes related to the LNG terminal project, its construction, operation, debt service and related obligations. For the sake of ready reference “Accounts Agreement” executed with “Common Terms Agreement” [CTA] is enclosed as Annexure ‘A’.

21.	Moreover, among the accounts so mandated to be maintained are the FSRU SBLC Account and the PB (Performance Bond) Account. Clause 6 of the Accounts Agreement governs the FSRU SBLC Account and provides that the Appellant shall procure that certain amounts are promptly credited into the FSRU SBLC Account, and that the appellant may withdraw monies from this account for specified purposes related to the FSRU. 

22.	The FSRU (Floating Storage Regasification Unit) is the core operational infrastructure of the LNG terminal, and the FSRU SBLC Account is specifically tied to credit support obligations for the FSRU under the Time Charter Party agreement with Excelerate Energy Middle East, LLC (EE), a non-resident entity. The Accounts Agreement confirms that the FSRU SBLC Facility Bank (National Bank of Pakistan) is a party to the Agreement specifically in its capacity as provider of the FSRU SBLC facility, and that the balances in the FSRU SBLC Account (up to the FSRU SBLC Account Cap) are maintained to secure and support the FSRU operations, which are the heart of the LNG terminal business. 

23.	Similarly, Clause 5 governs the PB Account, which is used to secure Performance Bonds issued for the benefit of the project and to reimburse the Performance Bond Facility Bank in respect of drawings under the Performance Bonds, with balances held as cash collateral until expiry of the Performance Bonds. The balances in these accounts, and the incidental profit earned thereon, are therefore functionally and operationally part of fulfilling LNG terminal contractual obligations, including SBLC and performance bond requirements imposed by the project lenders, the FSRU operator and other project counterparties, rather than any separate, passive investment portfolio maintained for purposes unrelated to business operations.

24.	The Accounts Agreement further provides in Clause 3.7 that "the procedures for release of funds from the Security Accounts contained in this Agreement will not affect the obligations of the Appellant to make all payments required to be made to the Finance Parties on the respective due dates for payment in accordance with the Finance Documents", confirming that the security accounts are an integral part of the debt service and payment mechanism for the project financing. Clause 3.8 sets out detailed Operating Procedures governing how withdrawals and payments from security accounts are to be made, including that the Account Bank shall comply with Payment Instructions of the Appellant or, after service of a notice of an Account Block Event or occurrence of the FSRU Enforcement Date or PB Enforcement Date, with Payment Instructions of the Security Trustee or any Receiver. 

25.	Clause 3.9 provides that "neither the ability of the Appellant to make any withdrawal from a Security Account in accordance with this Agreement nor any such withdrawal will be construed as a waiver by any Secured Creditor of any Security Interest over the Security Accounts or the Authorised Investments", thereby confirming that the security accounts and their balances (including profit earned thereon) are subject to security interests in favour of the project lenders and are not free, unencumbered funds of the appellant. Clause 3.10 provides that the Security Accounts can only be closed and balances transferred to the appellant's order upon expiry of the Security Period and notice from the Intercreditor Agent, further demonstrating that the accounts and their balances are not freely available to the appellant during the project financing period.

26.	The recitals to the Accounts Agreement explicitly record that "it is a condition precedent to the Financiers making financing available to the Appellant and entering into the other Finance Documents that the Parties enter into this Agreement", confirming that the establishment and operation of these security accounts (and the automatic earning of profit/interest thereon as mandated by Clause 3.12) is not a voluntary investment decision by the appellant but a mandatory condition imposed by the lenders without which the LNG terminal project could not have been financed or constructed. 

27.	The profit/interest accruing on these security accounts is therefore an automatic consequence of fulfilling mandatory contractual and financing obligations imposed upon the appellant as part of its LNG terminal business operations, and cannot be divorced or severed from such operations for tax characterization purposes. The balance funds from the loan disbursements that are maintained in these accounts pending application for project costs, debt service, operating expenses and other project-related payments are not discretionary surplus funds deployed for investment purposes; they are working balances and reserve balances required to be maintained under the project financing structure, and the profit earned thereon is an automatic and inseparable incident of such maintenance.

28.	As per Ordinance, section 18 provides that income chargeable to tax under the head "Income from Business" includes profits and gains of any business or profession carried on by the taxpayer. The fundamental principle underlying the taxation of business income is that all receipts, benefits and gains arising from or in the course of business operations, including incidental income earned as a necessary incident of carrying on such business, are chargeable as business income. 

29.	The Supreme Court of Pakistan (SCP) has consistently held that the characterization of income must be determined based on the actual facts, circumstances and source of such income. In the case of Fauji Foundation, the Hon'ble SCP held that the respondent operates as a welfare trust whose core activity is generating income through business ventures to fund welfare projects for its beneficiaries. The Court recognized that investing in industrial undertakings and earning surplus income, including interest from bank deposits, constitutes business activity aligned with the Foundation's objectives. Therefore, such income is treated as "business income" rather than "income from other sources." The Court emphasized that income arising from a business relationship and linked to the taxpayer's business operations is chargeable as business income.

30.	Section 39 of the Ordinance is a residuary provision that applies only to income which does not fall under any other head of income specified in section 15 of the Ordinance. Section 39(1) expressly provides that income chargeable under section 39 is "other than income exempt from tax under this Ordinance or income chargeable to tax under any other provision of this Ordinance", thereby making it clear that income chargeable under section 18 as business income cannot simultaneously be brought to tax under Section 39. 

31.	The legislative intent underlying section 39 is to tax passive, investment-type income that has no nexus with the taxpayer's business activities. Where income arises as a direct, necessary and inseparable incident of conducting business operations and is inextricably linked to the business financing structure and contractual obligations of the business, such income cannot be artificially divorced from the business and treated as income from other sources merely because it takes the form of interest or profit on deposits.

32.	Moreover, the accounts so maintained include the FSRU standby letter of credit [SBLC] account; the facility being availed from the bank for purposes of compliance with credit support requirements under Time Charter Party agreement with Excelerate Energy Middle East, LLC [EE]. We give below a picture of the relevant extracts of the contract for clarity: 



           






	



33.	In the present case, the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 did not arise from any voluntary, discretionary or passive investment of surplus funds by the appellant for purposes unconnected with its business. On the contrary, the profit arose exclusively and automatically from the mandatory maintenance of project-specific security accounts that the appellant was contractually obligated to establish and operate as a condition precedent to receiving project financing from IFC, ADB and the local banking syndicate for the development and operation of its LNG terminal. 

34.	The security accounts are not general bank accounts or discretionary treasury investments; they are ring-fenced project accounts governed by detailed contractual covenants under the Accounts Agreement dated 7 January 2016 and the Common Terms Agreement, with strict and binding restrictions on deposits, withdrawals and utilization of funds. 
Clause 3.12 of the Accounts Agreement mandates that these accounts will automatically bear profit/interest at prevailing rates, and such profit/interest will be added to the account balance. The earning of this profit is therefore not an independent business activity or investment decision; it is a mandatory, automatic and contractual consequence of complying with the project financing structure imposed by the lenders as an integral part of funding the LNG terminal business.

35.	The funds in these security accounts are not freely deployable surplus funds of a general nature available for any purpose; they are balance funds from loan disbursements and project revenues that are tightly ring-fenced by lender covenants exclusively for the terminal's development, operation, debt service, maintenance and credit support mechanisms as set out in the detailed waterfall provisions of Clauses 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the Accounts Agreement. 

36.	The FSRU SBLC Account, in particular, is maintained solely to comply with credit support requirements under the Time Charter Party agreement with Excelerate Energy Middle East, LLC, which is an essential project contract for the operation of the FSRU that is the core infrastructure of the LNG terminal business. The profit earned on these accounts is therefore functionally, operationally, contractually and legally part of the LNG terminal business operations, arising from and incidental to such operations, rather than a separate stream of passive investment income. To characterize such profit as "income from other sources" under Section 39 would be to artificially sever it from its business source and ignore the commercial, contractual and legal reality that the profit is an inseparable incident of the business financing structure and operations mandated as a condition precedent to the Financiers making financing available to the Appellant.

37.	The principle established by the superior courts is clear: income that arises from a business relationship and is linked to the taxpayer's business operations must be treated as business income. In the present case, the profit on debt arises directly from security accounts that are mandated, governed and restricted by project financing agreements that are the lifeblood of the LNG terminal business. The accounts exist only because of the business, are maintained only to comply with business financing obligations as a condition precedent to obtaining project loans, and the profit thereon is earned only as an automatic incident of such compliance mandated by Clause 3.12 of the Accounts Agreement. 

38.	The profit is therefore inextricably linked to, and arises from, the LNG terminal business operations, and is properly chargeable to tax under section 18 as business income, not under section 39 as income from other sources. Both the Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue and the learned CIR(A) have manifestly failed to apply the correct legal test, have ignored the binding judicial precedents, and have disregarded the actual factual and contractual matrix as evidenced by the Accounts Agreement, Common Terms Agreement, balance sheet, financial statements and project financing documents. 

39.	The impugned order of the CIR(A) upholding the characterization of the profit on debt as income from other sources is therefore perverse, contrary to law, unsupported by evidence, and liable to be set aside. It is therefore most respectfully prayed that this Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal may be pleased to allow this ground of appeal, set aside the impugned order of the CIR(A) to the extent it relates to the characterization and taxation of the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000, and hold that such profit on debt is chargeable to tax under Section 18 as business income and not under Section 39 as income from other sources.

### **Additional Note on Distinction from the Judgment in *UCH Powers (Pvt.) Ltd. v. ITAT* (2010 PTD 1809)**

1. The reliance placed by the Revenue on the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in *UCH Powers (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Income Tax Appellate Tribunal* (2010 PTD 1809) is wholly misplaced, as the factual matrix, statutory context, and nature of income involved in that case are materially and fundamentally distinguishable from the facts of the present appeal. A close reading of the judgment itself demonstrates that the Supreme Court decided the controversy in the context of **tax exemption under Clause 176 of Part-I of the Second Schedule** to the repealed Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 (now Clause 132 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001), and **not** in the context of characterization of income as business income versus income from other sources under sections 18 and 39 of the Ordinance.

2. In *UCH Powers*, the assessees were private sector power generation companies claiming that **interest/profit earned on bank deposits** should be treated as part of “profits and gains of the electric power generation project” and hence **exempt from tax** under Clause 176. The core issue before the Supreme Court was whether such interest income, admittedly earned on bank deposits, could be brought within the scope of a **specific statutory tax exemption** meant for “profits and gains derived from an electric power generation project”.

3. The Supreme Court, after an exhaustive examination, held that the exemption under Clause 176 was confined strictly to **business income covered under section 22** (now section 18) and could not be extended to **interest income falling under section 30** (now section 39), even if such interest was earned on deposits maintained in connection with the project. Crucially, the Court emphasized the **limited and strict construction of exemption provisions**, holding that interest income retained its separate character for exemption purposes.

4. In contrast, the present case **does not involve any claim of exemption whatsoever**. The appellant is not seeking immunity from tax under any provision of the Second Schedule. The sole and narrow controversy here is **under which head of income the profit on debt should be taxed**—whether as **business income under section 18** or as **income from other sources under section 39**. This distinction is critical, as the legal tests governing exemption provisions and those governing head-wise classification of income are entirely different.

5. More importantly, the factual foundation in *UCH Powers* was that the interest income arose from **bank deposits of share capital or surplus funds**, which, although connected with the project, were treated by the Court as a **separate income stream** for the purposes of exemption analysis. In the instant case, however, the profit on debt has arisen **exclusively from mandatory, lender-controlled security accounts**, which the appellant was contractually bound to establish and maintain as a **condition precedent to project financing**. The appellant had **no discretion** to deploy or invest these funds, and the earning of profit was an **automatic and contractual incident** of compliance with the project finance structure.

6. The Supreme Court itself, in *UCH Powers*, repeatedly recognized that the characterization of income depends on the **source, nature, and governing statutory context**. The Court did not lay down a universal proposition that interest or profit on bank accounts can never constitute business income. Rather, its conclusions were expressly tied to the interpretation of **Clause 176 and exemption law**, read with the specific scheme of the repealed Ordinance.

7. By contrast, the present case squarely falls within the well-settled principle that **income arising as a necessary and inseparable incident of carrying on business**, particularly where such income is generated through **mandatory project financing arrangements**, forms part of business income. The profit on debt in the present case is not earned by placing idle or surplus funds in banks, but is inseparably linked to the LNG terminal’s financing, debt service, security structure, and operational covenants imposed by IFC, ADB, and the banking syndicate.

8. It is therefore respectfully submitted that *UCH Powers* does not govern the present controversy. That judgment addresses the **scope of tax exemption for power projects**, whereas the present appeal concerns the **correct head of income for taxation of project-linked profit on debt**. Applying the ratio of *UCH Powers* to the instant case would amount to extending a decision rendered in a **narrow exemption context** to a **classification issue under sections 18 and 39**, which the Supreme Court itself did not contemplate.

9. For these reasons, the facts, legal issue, and ratio of *UCH Powers (Pvt.) Ltd. v. ITAT* are clearly distinguishable, and the said judgment does not prejudice the appellant’s contention that the impugned profit on debt, arising from mandatory LNG project security accounts, is chargeable as **income from business under section 18**, and not as income from other sources.

LIMITED for Tax Years 2022 and 2024**, and **supported by the judicial precedents expressly relied upon and accepted by the tax department in the attached order**. The tone and structure are aligned for filing before the Hon’ble Tribunal.

---

## **Without Prejudice Secondary Argument: Allowability of Related Finance Cost under Section 40 if Profit on Debt is Treated as Income from Other Sources**

1. **Without prejudice** to the appellant’s primary contention that the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 is inextricably linked with the LNG terminal business and is chargeable under section 18 as business income, it is respectfully submitted that **even assuming (arguendo)** that such income is held to fall under the head **“Income from Other Sources” under section 39**, the **corresponding finance cost incurred to earn such income is mandatorily allowable as a deduction under section 40 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**.

2. Section 40 of the Ordinance is explicit and unequivocal in its mandate. It provides that **any expenditure paid by a person in the year shall be deductible to the extent to which such expenditure is paid in deriving income chargeable under the head “Income from Other Sources.”** Once an item of income is brought to tax under section 39, the statute itself requires that the computation must be on a **net basis**, allowing all expenditures that have a **direct, proximate, and real nexus** with the earning of that income. The Ordinance does not permit taxation of gross receipts divorced from the cost incurred to generate them.

3. In the instant case, the profit on debt of Rs 139,985,000 arose exclusively from **borrowed funds**, including subordinated loans and foreign loans, obtained under the project financing structure. The same set of borrowings gave rise to substantial finance costs during the relevant tax year. As disclosed in **Note 27 to the audited financial statements**, the finance cost directly relatable to such borrowings aggregates to **Rs 483,401,279**, comprising:
   - Interest / markup on subordinated loan: **Rs 157,750,000**  
   - Interest / markup on foreign loan: **Rs 239,026,279**  
   - Amortisation of transaction costs: **Rs 86,625,000**

   These costs represent the **cost of funds** from which the deposits and balances earning profit on debt were generated. The nexus between the income and the expenditure is therefore **direct, immediate, and incontrovertible**.

4. Consistent with this statutory framework, the appellant, in its return of income, **netted off the profit on debt against the related finance costs**, resulting in disclosure of **net finance costs of Rs 649,405,000**, after setting off mark-up income of Rs 139,985,000 against total finance costs of Rs 794,882,000. This treatment is not only commercially correct but is **squarely in line with section 40**, which envisages computation of income from other sources after allowing directly related expenditures.

5. Crucially, this legal position has already been **examined, accepted, and affirmed by the tax department itself** in the assessment proceedings of **ENGRO POWERGEN THAR (PVT.) LIMITED**, a similarly placed power generation company operating under a comparable project-finance structure.

6. In the **order passed under section 122(5A) for Tax Year 2024**, the learned Additional Commissioner Inland Revenue, LTO Karachi, after issuing a show-cause notice and examining detailed submissions, **categorically accepted** that:
   - interest / profit on debt earned from bank accounts constitutes income chargeable under section 39; and  
   - **finance cost incurred on the borrowed funds placed in such bank accounts is allowable as a deduction under section 40**, being expenditure incurred in deriving that income.  

   The proceedings were accordingly **closed with no adverse inference**, expressly recording that the taxpayer’s position under section 40 was legally sound and supported by judicial precedent. fileciteturn1file0

7. The same position was also **accepted by the department in the assessment proceedings of ENGRO POWERGEN THAR (PVT.) LIMITED for Tax Year 2022**, where identical treatment—set-off of finance cost against profit on debt under section 40—was examined and allowed. This demonstrates a **consistent departmental understanding and application of section 40** in the case of project-financed energy sector entities, negating any suggestion that such treatment is novel or impermissible.

8. Significantly, while allowing the deduction under section 40 in the said order, the learned Additional Commissioner did not act in isolation but **explicitly relied upon and followed binding judicial precedents**, including:
   - **Lahore High Court judgment in *Commissioner of Income Tax v. Pioneer Cement* (2005 PTD 2086)**, wherein it was held that interest paid on borrowed funds used to earn interest income is deductible against such income, as the expenditure is directly incurred for earning the income;  
   - **ATIR Lahore in *AES Lalpir (Pvt.) Ltd.* (ITA Nos. 624–627/LB/2008)**, holding that where banks require maintenance of deposits from borrowed funds, interest paid on such borrowings is allowable under section 40;  
   - **ATIR Lahore in *Nishat Power Limited* (ITA Nos. 1521 & 1522/LB/2011)**, affirming that profit on debt earned from borrowed funds is not an independent stream of income but effectively a reduction of finance cost, and that corresponding interest expense is allowable; and  
   - subsequent ATIR decisions in **Lalpir (2014 PTD 842)** and **Kohinoor Energy Limited (2021 SLD 908)**, all of which uniformly uphold deduction of finance cost under section 40 against profit on debt earned from borrowed funds.

9. These authorities, as acknowledged in the ENGRO POWERGEN THAR order itself, settle the legal position beyond doubt: **once interest or profit on debt is taxed under section 39, the related finance cost incurred to earn that income must be allowed under section 40**. Any contrary approach would result in taxation of a **fictional gross income**, contrary to both the statutory scheme and binding precedent.

10. Applying the same principles to the present case, it is respectfully submitted that **even if** the Hon’ble Tribunal were to uphold the classification of the impugned profit on debt under section 39, the learned authorities below were **duty-bound** to allow deduction of the corresponding finance costs under section 40. Denial of such deduction would be:
   - contrary to the express language of section 40;  
   - inconsistent with settled judicial law; and  
   - **wholly irreconcilable with the department’s own accepted position in the cases of ENGRO POWERGEN THAR (PVT.) LIMITED for Tax Years 2022 and 2024 on identical facts**.

11. Accordingly, **without prejudice to the appellant’s primary case under section 18**, it is prayed that this Hon’ble Tribunal may hold that **if the profit on debt is assessed under section 39, the related finance cost is allowable under section 40**, and the income, if any, must be computed strictly on a **net basis**, as already reflected in the return of income.

---

The dispute originates from SRB’s attempt to levy Sindh sales tax on certain receipts reflected in the Company’s audited financial statements, namely penalty for delay (idle/overstay charges of vessels), NOC charges, and reimbursement of labour charges, along with imposition of penalty and default surcharge.

---

### **History of Appellate Findings**
At the first appellate stage, the Commissioner (Appeals) examined the contractual framework with Port Qasim Authority and the true nature of the receipts and concluded that penalty for delay did not represent consideration for any taxable service and was compensatory in nature, that NOC charges did not fall within the ambit of franchise services and, in any case, could not be taxed as this issue was never confronted in the show-cause notice, and that penalty and default surcharge were unsustainable due to absence of mens rea. Sales tax was sustained only on reimbursement of labour charges.

SRB’s appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue was dismissed in its entirety. The Tribunal confirmed that there was no legal infirmity in the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) and reiterated the settled principle that issues not raised in the show-cause notice cannot be introduced or expanded at the appellate stage.

---

### **Proceedings before the Sindh High Court**
SRB has now escalated the matter to the Sindh High Court through a reference limited to questions of law. The principal grounds taken by SRB are that the Tribunal wrongly set aside taxability of receipts disclosed in audited financial statements, that the Tribunal had no authority to uphold waiver of penalty and default surcharge, and that the Tribunal failed to enforce the show-cause notice as framed by the department. In substance, SRB seeks to reopen factual findings already concurrently decided in favour of the Company by two appellate forums.

At the time of filing, both the subject matter and the quantum involved unequivocally fell within the statutory and pecuniary jurisdiction of the Commissioner (Appeals) as prescribed under the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

2. Subsequently, owing to amendments introduced in the Sales Tax Act, 1990—whereby the pecuniary limits governing appellate jurisdiction were restructured—the appeal pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) was administratively transferred to the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue. In consequence thereof, the appeal came to be registered before this Hon’ble Tribunal as **STA No. 750/KB/2024**, not on account of any defect or election by the appellant, but purely as a result of a statutory reallocation of jurisdiction.

3. It is respectfully submitted that jurisdiction is a matter of **substantive law**, not merely of procedure, and any forum derives its authority strictly from the statute as it stands at the relevant time. Where the legislature, in its wisdom, modifies or restores jurisdictional thresholds, the forums are required to realign pending matters accordingly, unless the statute expressly provides otherwise.

4. In this regard, the appellant submits that through the **Finance Act, 2025**, the legislature has **restored the earlier appellate framework** under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, whereby appeals involving the present nature and value once again fall within the jurisdiction of the Commissioner (Appeals). The Finance Act, 2025 does not merely introduce a prospective procedural change; rather, it reinstates the previously prevailing scheme of appellate adjudication, thereby reviving the jurisdiction of the Commissioner (Appeals) over such matters.

5. It is a settled principle of law that **no litigant has a vested right in a particular forum**, but equally, no forum can continue to exercise jurisdiction once the statutory basis for such jurisdiction ceases to exist. Jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, convenience, or continuation; it must flow directly from the statute. Accordingly, once the Finance Act, 2025 restored the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Commissioner (Appeals), the continuation of the present appeal before this Hon’ble Tribunal would be inconsistent with the amended law.

6. It is further submitted that appellate forums are creatures of statute, and their jurisdiction must be construed strictly. The Hon’ble superior courts have consistently held that where jurisdiction is wrongly assumed or retained, the resulting proceedings are rendered vulnerable to being declared without lawful authority. The appellant seeks to avoid such an eventuality by requesting realignment of the appeal with the competent forum at this stage.

7. The appellant also submits that the Commissioner (Appeals) is the **statutorily designated first appellate authority**, entrusted with examining both factual and legal controversies arising out of adjudication orders. Denial of adjudication by the correct forum would prejudice the appellant’s statutory right of appeal and disrupt the appellate hierarchy envisaged by the legislature.

8. It is pertinent to note that the transfer of the appeal to this Hon’ble Tribunal was not occasioned by any act or omission of the appellant, but solely due to an intervening legislative change. With the restoration of the earlier position through the Finance Act, 2025, principles of fairness, legal certainty, and orderly administration of justice demand that the appeal be remitted to the forum now legally competent to hear and decide the matter.

9. The appellant further submits that such transfers, upon restoration or alteration of jurisdiction, have consistently been recognized as permissible and necessary to uphold the supremacy of statutory mandate. The Hon’ble Tribunal, being a forum of record and bound by law, is fully empowered to direct such transfer in order to ensure that adjudication takes place strictly in accordance with the governing statute.

10. In these circumstances, retention of the present appeal by this Hon’ble Tribunal, despite the restored pecuniary jurisdiction of the Commissioner (Appeals), would amount to exercising jurisdiction not contemplated by law as presently in force. Such a course would neither advance the cause of justice nor align with legislative intent.

In view of the foregoing facts, statutory developments, and settled legal principles, it is most respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Tribunal may graciously be pleased to:

- **Order the transfer of Appeal bearing STA No. 750/KB/2024, for tax periods July 2019 to December 2019, to the learned Commissioner (Appeals-IV) Inland Revenue**, being the competent appellate authority under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, as amended through the Finance Act, 2025; and

Alright—let’s take this out of the “practice note” zone and into **statutory construction + OECD mechanics + Pakistan-specific enforcement logic**. I’ll keep it dense, but clean.

---

## 1. Statutory architecture under Pakistani law (who actually bears the obligation)

The transfer pricing documentation regime in Pakistan is **not symmetrical**. Each tier of documentation is imposed on a **different legal trigger**.

### (a) Charging provision: Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001  
Section 108 empowers the FBR to prescribe **documentation requirements** for associates in an international group. Importantly, Section 108 **does not itself mandate a Master File**; it delegates rule-making power.

So the real law lives in the **Rules**, not the section.

---

## 2. Rule-by-rule dissection: 27M vs 27N (this is where most confusion arises)

### Rule 27M — *Master File* (group-level document)

Key legal characteristics of Rule 27M:

• It is framed **with reference to the multinational group**, not the Pakistani entity in isolation  
• The Master File content is **group-wide** (global business lines, intangibles, financing, TP policies, etc.)  
• The Rule assumes the existence of a **single, centralized document**, prepared at group level  

Critically, **Rule 27M does not say**:
> “Every Pakistani constituent entity shall independently prepare a Master File.”

Instead, it operates on the premise that:
> *A Master File exists (or is required to exist) at the group level.*

This is not an accident—it mirrors OECD BEPS Action 13 almost verbatim.

---

### Rule 27N — *Local File* (entity-level document)

By contrast, Rule 27N is explicitly **entity-centric**:

• “Every resident taxpayer who has entered into international transactions…”  
• Requires Pakistan-specific functional analysis, benchmarking, and transaction-level substantiation  
• No thresholds based on global revenue exemptions unless notified  

This structural contrast is decisive:  
👉 **Local File = primary compliance obligation**  
👉 **Master File = secondary / derivative obligation**

---

## 3. OECD BEPS Action 13 logic (which Pakistan intentionally adopted)

Pakistan’s rules are aligned with **entity["organization","OECD","intergovernmental org"] BEPS Action 13**, which deliberately designed the Master File as:

• **Prepared once**
• **At the level of the Ultimate Parent Entity**
• **Shared across jurisdictions**

The OECD commentary is explicit on this point:

> Jurisdictions should not require local entities to create a Master File where the group is not otherwise required to prepare one.

Pakistan did **not** introduce any “gold-plating” deviation from this model. No substitute obligation. No fallback requirement.

If Pakistan had intended to impose an **independent Master File obligation**, the Rules would have had to say so expressly. They do not.

---

## 4. Threshold exemptions and their legal effect

In practice, most UPE exemptions arise because:

• The group does not meet **consolidated revenue thresholds**  
• The UPE jurisdiction has not adopted Action 13 Master File rules  
• Transitional or jurisdiction-specific exemptions apply  

Now the crucial legal point:

A **lawful exemption at the UPE level means the obligation never arises**.  
This is not a waiver—it is **absence of charge**.

You cannot transfer a **non-existent obligation** downstream to a constituent entity unless the statute expressly creates a secondary duty. Pakistan’s Rules do not.

---

## 5. Why Pakistan cannot legally require a “locally manufactured” Master File

There are three hard legal barriers:

### (i) Ultra vires risk  
Requiring a Pakistani entity to **create** a Master File independently would exceed the scope of Rule 27M, which presumes centralized group information.

### (ii) Practical impossibility  
A local subsidiary:
• Does not control global IP  
• Does not set group financing policy  
• Does not own consolidated financial data  

Pakistani tax law does not impose **impossible compliance burdens** by implication.

### (iii) International consistency principle  
Pakistan is a signatory to BEPS-aligned standards. Deviating unilaterally would:
• Break information symmetry  
• Undermine exchange-of-information frameworks  
• Create inconsistent group disclosures  

Courts and tribunals generally interpret transfer pricing rules **harmoniously with OECD guidance**, unless explicitly excluded. Pakistan has never excluded it.

---

## 6. FBR audit practice (what actually happens on the ground)

In audits, the FBR typically challenges:

• Absence or weakness of the **Local File**  
• Inadequate benchmarking  
• Inconsistencies between financials and TP positions  

Where Master Files are questioned, the inquiry usually narrows to:
> “Provide evidence that the group is not required to prepare a Master File.”

Once that evidence is furnished, the issue normally **dies quietly**.

There is **no consistent precedent** where:
• A lawful UPE exemption existed, **and**
• The Pakistani entity was penalized for not independently preparing a Master File

That silence matters in tax law.

---

## 7. What *is* expected from the Pakistani entity (this part is non-negotiable)

While a Master File may not be required, the Pakistani entity must still:

• Maintain a **robust Local File** under Rule 27N  
• Retain **written evidence** of UPE exemption (legal basis, thresholds, jurisdictional rules)  
• Be able to **reconcile its TP policy** with group conduct, even without a Master File  

In other words:  
No Master File ≠ No explanation.

---

## 8. Bottom-line legal position (defensible in audit and litigation)

**Legally sustainable conclusion:**

> Where the Ultimate Parent Entity is not required to prepare or maintain a Master File under applicable law, the Pakistani constituent entity is **not independently required** to maintain or prepare a Master File under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 read with Rules 27M and 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002—provided that the Local File is duly maintained and the exemption is properly evidenced.

This position is:
• Textually correct  
• OECD-consistent  
• Administratively aligned  
• Litigation-defensible  

In transfer pricing, obligations do not arise by anxiety. They arise by statute.

If the **ultimate parent entity (UPE)** is **not required to prepare a Master File** under the applicable law of its jurisdiction, the **Pakistani local entity is not independently required to maintain a Master File** under Pakistan’s transfer pricing regime.

Now the reasoning—because tax law lives in the footnotes.

Under the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, read with **Rules 27M and 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002**, Pakistan follows the OECD-aligned three-tiered documentation framework: Local File, Master File, and CbCR. Crucially, the **Master File obligation is group-centric, not entity-centric**.

Here’s how the logic actually works in law:

• The obligation to **prepare and maintain a Master File rests with the multinational group**, typically through its **ultimate parent entity**.  
• A **Pakistani constituent entity’s obligation is derivative**—it arises **only if** a Master File exists or is required to be prepared at the group level.  
• The Rules do **not** impose a standalone duty on a Pakistani entity to *create* a Master File where the UPE itself is **exempt** (for example, due to revenue thresholds or jurisdictional exemptions).

So, if the **UPE is legally exempt** from maintaining a Master File in its home jurisdiction, Pakistan’s rules **do not require the local Pakistani entity to prepare one from scratch**. There is no “substitute Master File” concept hiding between the lines.

What **is** still required, without exception:

• The **Local File** under Rule 27N, fully documenting Pakistan-specific related-party transactions.  
• Adequate contemporaneous evidence to demonstrate that the group falls **outside the Master File applicability thresholds**, should the FBR ask.

Think of it this way:  
Pakistan asks for the **group’s blueprint** only if the group is already required to have one. If the architect never had to draw it, the local office isn’t forced to invent it later.

This interpretation is consistent with:
• The **plain wording** of Rules 27M/27N  
• **OECD BEPS Action 13** design  
• FBR’s practice in audits (where disputes usually arise on *absence of Local File*, not on non-existent Master Files)

The real risk area is not “failure to maintain Master File,” but **failure to justify why it was not applicable**. That’s a documentation discipline issue, not a compliance default.

In transfer pricing, silence isn’t guilt—but unsupported silence can look suspicious.

Let’s answer this **strictly from the statute**, not from practice shortcuts.

---

## 1. Where the penalty comes from (there is no separate “Master File penalty section”)

The **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** does **not** create a stand-alone penalty section titled “penalty for non-furnishing Master File”.

Instead, the penalty flows through **Section 182** (Penalties), read with **Section 108** (Transfer Pricing documentation) and **Rules 27M / 27N**.

So the logic chain is:

**Rule 27M obligation → Section 108 documentation requirement → Section 182 penalty**

---

## 2. The exact penalty provision that applies

### **Section 182(1)(b)** — Failure to maintain or furnish documents

This clause applies where a taxpayer:

> **fails to maintain or furnish any document required under the Ordinance or the Rules**, including documents required under Section 108.

A **Master File** is explicitly a document required under:
• Section 108 (enabling provision), and  
• Rule 27M (prescribed documentation).

Therefore, **non-furnishing or non-maintenance of a Master File squarely attracts Section 182(1)(b)**.

---

## 3. Quantum of penalty (this is the part auditors care about)

Under **Section 182(1)(b)**, the penalty is:

> **PKR 1,000,000 (one million rupees)**

This is a **fixed penalty**, not percentage-based, and **not transaction-linked**.

Key points:

• It is **per default**, not per transaction  
• It applies **even if no TP adjustment is made**  
• Mens rea (intent) is **not required**  
• Revenue loss is **irrelevant**  

In other words, it is a **pure compliance penalty**.

---

## 4. Important distinction: “not maintaining” vs “not furnishing”

Legally, both are covered.

However, in enforcement practice:

• **Not maintaining at all** → strongest case for penalty  
• **Maintained but not furnished on time** → still penalty-exposed, but defensible for mitigation  

The Ordinance **does not differentiate the quantum**—both attract the same PKR 1,000,000 ceiling.

---

## 5. Can FBR impose multiple penalties?

This matters in group audits.

### What FBR **can** do:
• Impose **one penalty per tax year per taxpayer** for Master File non-compliance

### What FBR **cannot legally do**:
• Impose multiple penalties for each missing chapter  
• Impose penalty per transaction  
• Impose separate penalties under both 27M and 27N for the *same* default  

Courts generally treat Master File default as **one composite failure**.

---

## 6. Interaction with Local File penalties (often misunderstood)

If a taxpayer fails to furnish:

• **Master File** → Section 182(1)(b): PKR 1,000,000  
• **Local File** → *same clause*, but **separate default**

So yes, in theory:

👉 **Two penalties can coexist** (one for Rule 27M, one for Rule 27N),  
👉 **but only if both failures are independently established**.

This is why FBR often threatens “multiple penalties” in TP audits.

---

## 7. Mitigation and defense (very important in real cases)

Even though Section 182 is strict, relief is possible:

• Demonstrating **threshold non-applicability** under Rule 27M  
• Showing **partial compliance** (group Master File available but delayed)  
• Proving **reasonable cause** under Section 182(3) (limited but usable)  

Tribunals have repeatedly held that:
> Penalty cannot be automatic; the authority must record **why reasonable cause does not exist**.

That procedural safeguard is often violated.

---

## 8. Final, litigation-safe answer

**Penalty for not furnishing / maintaining Master File in Pakistan:**

> **PKR 1,000,000 per tax year per taxpayer**, imposed under **Section 182(1)(b)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, for failure to comply with documentation requirements prescribed under **Section 108 read with Rule 27M** of the Income Tax Rules, 2002.

No adjustment needed.  
No revenue loss required.  
Pure compliance exposure.

---

### Closing thought  
Transfer pricing penalties in Pakistan are designed less to punish profit shifting and more to **force paperwork discipline**. The Master File penalty is a blunt instrument—but it is very much a real one.

You’re right to challenge it. When the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** and the **Income Tax Rules, 2002** are read **strictly and literally**, the earlier conclusion needs correction.

Let’s walk through the law **as written**, not as “OECD-expected”.

---

## 1. Start with the charging authority: Section 108, Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

Section 108 authorizes the FBR to require **any taxpayer** who has entered into international transactions with associates to:

> “maintain and furnish such information and documents… as may be prescribed.”

Two things matter here:

1. The obligation is **taxpayer-centric**, not group-centric  
2. There is **no carve-out** in the Ordinance for exemptions available to the ultimate parent entity

So the Ordinance itself **does not recognize upstream exemptions**.

---

## 2. Rule 27M — the Master File obligation (this is the decisive provision)

Rule 27M(1) states (paraphrased faithfully):

> **Every resident taxpayer** who is a constituent entity of a multinational enterprise group **shall maintain a master file**, if the multinational enterprise group falls within the prescribed threshold.

Key legal consequences of this wording:

• The obligation is imposed on **“every resident taxpayer”**  
• The trigger is whether the **group falls within the threshold**, not whether the UPE prepares a Master File  
• The Rule does **not** say “where the UPE is required to prepare”  
• The Rule does **not** provide an exemption where the UPE jurisdiction does not mandate a Master File  

This is materially different from the OECD model text.

---

## 3. Threshold test under Pakistani Rules (not foreign law)

Under Rule 27M, the threshold test is based on:

• **Consolidated group revenue**  
• As determined **for the multinational enterprise group as a whole**

Importantly:

👉 The test is **economic**, not **jurisdictional**  
👉 It does **not depend** on whether the parent country has Action 13 legislation  
👉 It does **not depend** on whether the UPE actually prepared a Master File  

If the group **meets the revenue threshold**, Rule 27M is triggered **in Pakistan**, full stop.

---

## 4. No “derivative obligation” concept exists in Pakistani Rules

This is where OECD logic and Pakistani law diverge.

Pakistan’s Rules **do not say**:

• “Master File shall be prepared by the UPE”  
• “Local entity shall furnish a copy prepared by the parent”  
• “If available” or “where prepared”  

Instead, they say:

> **“Every resident taxpayer shall maintain…”**

That language creates a **direct statutory obligation**, not a secondary or derivative one.

From a legal-interpretation standpoint:

• Courts cannot read in a foreign-law exemption  
• Administrative convenience cannot override explicit wording  
• OECD guidance is **persuasive**, not controlling  

---

## 5. Practical impossibility is not a legal exemption

While it is true that a Pakistani subsidiary may not control group-level information, Pakistani tax law:

• Frequently imposes obligations that require coordination with group entities  
• Does not recognize “lack of access” as a statutory defense  
• Places the compliance burden squarely on the resident taxpayer  

In fact, Rule 27M implicitly assumes that the local entity will **obtain** the Master File from the group or cause it to be prepared.

---

## 6. Comparison with Rule 27N (Local File) strengthens this reading

Rule 27N uses similar mandatory language:

> “Every resident taxpayer shall maintain a local file…”

The legislature used **identical drafting discipline** for both tiers.

There is no textual basis to treat Rule 27M as optional while Rule 27N is mandatory.

---

## 7. What the law actually allows (and what it does not)

### ✔ Allowed under Pakistani law
• Claim **threshold-based exemption** if the group does not meet the revenue criteria  
• Furnish a **single group Master File** prepared outside Pakistan  
• Seek reasonable time for compliance where information is delayed  

### ✘ Not allowed under Pakistani law
• Rely solely on the fact that the **UPE jurisdiction grants an exemption**  
• Argue that absence of Action 13 rules abroad nullifies Rule 27M  
• Treat the Master File obligation as purely derivative  

---

## 8. Correct legal conclusion (strict reading)

**Legally correct position under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 read with the Income Tax Rules, 2002:**

> If a multinational enterprise group meets the revenue threshold prescribed under Rule 27M, **every resident constituent entity in Pakistan is required to maintain a Master File**, regardless of whether the ultimate parent entity is exempt from maintaining a Master File under the laws of its home jurisdiction.

This may be **OECD-inconvenient**, but it is **textually accurate**.

---

## 9. Why this distinction matters in audits and litigation

In practice, many taxpayers rely on OECD logic—and often get away with it administratively. But in **litigation**, the FBR’s strongest position is:

> “Show us the Master File or show us the Rule-based exemption.”

Courts in Pakistan tend to side with **plain statutory language** where wording is unambiguous.

---

### Final thought  
OECD guidance explains *why* Master Files exist.  
Pakistani Rules decide *who must maintain them*.  

In Pakistan, the Rules speak louder than Paris.

Receiving two cars from ex-employer. He is asking that instead of purchase from company in his own, evaluate purchasing directly from ex-employer in the name of recently establish SMC. In whole purchase to park some expneses in the new company such vehicle running expenses and insurance. Please check whether proposed tranction in possible, please note that authorized and paid up capital fully utilized.

Please improvise below: 

Please that we assume that expenses are bear by you irrespective of the fact that whether you run a company or not. Therefore, while computing total net cash takeout, we cannel the impact of expenses. Furthermore, clarity, please provide us estimate figure of other expenses.

Let’s treat this as a working theory and walk it carefully, because on paper it looks simple (“buy the cars in the SMC and park expenses”), but the tax, corporate, and banking layers make it more interesting.

### 1. Can the SMC legally purchase the cars directly from the ex-employer?
Yes, **in principle**, an SMC can purchase vehicles directly from a third party (including an ex-employer of the shareholder/director), **provided the transaction is genuine, arm’s length, and properly funded**. There is no prohibition in the Companies Act or the Income Tax Ordinance on an SMC owning vehicles.

However, the devil lives in the funding and documentation.

### 2. The real constraint: paid-up capital already fully utilized
This is the critical red flag in your facts.

If:
- authorized capital is already issued, **and**
- paid-up capital is fully utilized in existing assets/operations,

then the SMC **cannot magically buy cars** unless one of the following happens:

1) **Fresh funding is introduced**, or  
2) **The seller allows credit**, or  
3) **The director injects money in some other legally recognizable form**

Each route has consequences.

### 3. Possible funding structures (and their tax comfort level)

#### (a) Shareholder loan / director loan (most practical)
The shareholder (your client) injects funds as an **interest-free or interest-bearing loan** to the SMC, which then purchases the vehicles.

- Legally acceptable.
- Commonly used in SMCs.
- Must be:
  - Properly documented (loan agreement / board resolution),
  - Routed through banking channels,
  - Reflected in balance sheet as “Loan from Director.”

**Tax angle:**  
No income tax exposure merely on receipt of loan if source is explainable (salary savings, bank balance, etc.). This avoids awkward questions under section 111.

This is the **cleanest route** if capital cannot be increased immediately.

#### (b) Increase in authorized & paid-up capital
The SMC increases authorized capital and issues further shares to the shareholder, who injects funds.

- Corporate-law clean.
- Slightly slower (SECP filings).
- Often preferred if the vehicles are significant and long-term assets.

**Tax angle:**  
Generally safe if banking trail and source of funds are clear.

#### (c) Credit purchase from ex-employer (risky in practice)
If the ex-employer sells the vehicles on deferred payment / credit:

- The SMC records a liability.
- No immediate cash outflow.

**Risk:**  
Tax authorities may question:
- Why credit is given to a newly formed SMC with no financial history,
- Whether this is a disguised benefit to the individual.

This route needs **very strong documentation** and commercial justification.

### 4. Parking running expenses & insurance in the SMC — allowed, but…
Yes, **vehicle running expenses, insurance, repairs, tracking, fuel, etc.** can be claimed by the SMC **only if**:

- The vehicles are **owned by the SMC**, and
- They are **used for business purposes**.

Two important cautions:

1) **Personal use adjustment**  
If the director uses the cars personally (which is common), the tax department may:
- Disallow a portion of running expenses, or
- Treat personal use as a **perquisite**.

Maintaining a **logbook** is boring but powerful.

2) **Depreciation**  
Depreciation is allowable under normal tax rules, but again, proportionate to business use.

### 5. Sales tax & withholding aspects (often overlooked)
- If the ex-employer is a **registered person**, sales tax implications on vehicle sale must be checked.
- Advance tax at registration (section 231B / 231A) will apply in the **name of the SMC**.
- Registration authority records must clearly show the SMC as owner.

### 6. Substance over form: the core risk
If, in substance:
- The cars are for personal convenience, and
- The SMC has limited or no real operational need,

then the arrangement becomes vulnerable. Tax authorities tend to ask:
“Why does a newly incorporated SMC need two vehicles immediately?”

This does not make it illegal—but it raises the audit temperature.

### Bottom line (practical conclusion)
- **Yes**, purchasing directly in the name of the SMC is legally possible.
- **No**, it cannot be done casually when paid-up capital is already fully utilized.
- The transaction should be routed through:
  - Director loan **or**
  - Capital enhancement,
  with full banking trail and documentation.
- Running expenses and insurance are allowable **only to the extent of business use**.

Handled cleanly, this structure is defensible. Handled casually, it becomes a textbook example of “company used as a wallet,” which never ends well.

If you want, the next logical extension is mapping this into a **tax-audit-proof structure** (documents, resolutions, accounting entries) so the story remains consistent from SECP to IRIS to the bank.

Dear [Client Name],

We refer to your query regarding the proposed acquisition of two vehicles from your ex-employer directly in the name of your recently incorporated Single Member Company (SMC), with a view to claiming vehicle-related expenses (such as running costs and insurance) in the company. We have reviewed the matter in light of corporate and income tax considerations and summarize our advice below for clarity.

At the outset, there is no legal restriction on an SMC purchasing vehicles directly from a third party, including an ex-employer, provided the transaction is genuine, conducted at arm’s length, properly documented, and supported through identifiable banking channels. Accordingly, the proposed transaction is permissible in principle. However, a key constraint in your case is that the authorized and paid-up capital of the SMC has already been fully utilized. In this situation, the company cannot acquire additional assets unless fresh funding is introduced or a valid liability is created.

Practically, the most workable and tax-efficient option is for you, as the sole shareholder/director, to inject funds into the SMC by way of a documented director’s loan, which may be interest-free. Such funding should be supported through banking channels and appropriate board resolutions, and reflected in the books as “Loan from Director.” Alternatively, the transaction may be structured through an increase in authorized and paid-up capital, subject to completion of the requisite SECP formalities. A credit purchase arrangement with the ex-employer is theoretically possible; however, given the recent incorporation of the SMC, this route carries higher scrutiny risk and would require strong commercial justification and documentation.

Once the vehicles are validly purchased and registered in the name of the SMC, vehicle-related expenses (including insurance, fuel, maintenance, and repairs) as well as depreciation may be claimed by the company, subject to the condition that the vehicles are used for business purposes. Where the vehicles are also used personally, an appropriate apportionment may be required, and maintenance of basic usage records is advisable to mitigate disallowance risk. Advance tax at the time of registration and any applicable sales tax implications on the transfer will also need to be addressed in the name of the SMC.

In summary, the proposed structure is feasible, but it should be implemented through a clean and defensible funding mechanism (preferably a director loan or capital enhancement), with complete documentation and a clear business rationale for the vehicles at the company level. We would be pleased to assist you further in structuring the transaction, preparing the necessary resolutions and agreements, and aligning the accounting and tax treatment accordingly.

Please let us know if you would like us to proceed with the next steps.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

In **Pakistan**, the **State Bank of Pakistan (SBP)** regulates how much foreign currency an individual can buy from an authorised exchange company and carry for travel or remit. These are the key limits you should know (based on SBP rules and related regulations):

**1. Limits on buying foreign currency from exchange companies (for individuals):**  
• A person may **purchase foreign currency (cash or electronic/ outward remittance)** up to a **maximum of USD 10,000 (or equivalent) per day** from all licensed exchange companies combined.  
• The **annual limit for purchase** from all exchange companies combined is **USD 100,000 (or equivalent)** per calendar year.  
• For any transaction above **USD 1,000 (or equivalent)**, the exchange company must obtain your **CNIC/NICOP/Passport and an undertaking** that you have not exceeded these limits for the day/year.  
These limits apply to documented purchases of foreign exchange and are part of formal SBP foreign exchange regulations. citeturn0search0turn0search33

**2. Cash dollar transaction documentation requirements:**  
• Under recent SBP directions, exchange companies must now require biometric verification and documentation of **purpose** for cash purchases above **around USD 500**. Cash delivery for deposits into foreign currency accounts must be made via **account-to-account transfers or cheque**, not physical cash hand-over in many cases. citeturn0search7turn0search24

**3. Limits on carrying foreign currency out of Pakistan (travel/cross-border cash limit):**  
• For **international travel**, the customs rules (enforced by FBR/Customs) cap how much foreign currency you can carry physically out of Pakistan: generally up to about **USD 5,000 per visit** for adults and **USD 30,000 per calendar year** (equivalents in other currencies) if declared properly. Lower limits apply for minors and certain destinations like Afghanistan. citeturn0search18

**What this means in practice:**  
• If you want to **exchange money (PKR → foreign currency)** with a licensed exchange company, you cannot simply buy an unlimited amount; the SBP’s **purchase ceiling is USD 10,000 per day and USD 100,000 per year** per individual.  
• To **carry foreign cash abroad**, you must stay within **customs limits** (e.g., ~USD 5,000 for travel) and declare larger amounts as required.

These limits and documentation requirements aim to improve oversight, prevent informal/undocumented FX flows, and align with anti-money-laundering standards.

If you need precise current figures in PKR terms (e.g., for rupee-to-dollar conversion), I can help compute those too based on the latest exchange rates.

### **ADR Reinforced — A Faster Way Out of Costly Tax Disputes**

Big shift in Pakistan’s tax dispute landscape. The **Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 2026** has strengthened **Section 134A**, turning Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) into a **real, time-bound alternative** to long court battles. High-value disputes involving **Rs 50 million or more**, refunds, penalty or surcharge waivers, and specific relief can now be routed to ADR—**with an automatic stay on recovery** once the committee is formed. The message is clear: less litigation, faster closure.

The change is even stronger for **state-owned enterprises (SOEs)**. ADR is now **mandatory**, regardless of amount, and once the committee decides, the outcome is **final and binding**—with all pending court cases automatically falling away. Each ADR committee is led by a **retired superior court judge**, alongside a senior tax officer and a taxpayer nominee, and must decide the dispute within **90 days**. No delays, no precedents—just focused, case-specific resolution.  

**Bottom line:** ADR is no longer a backup option. It’s now a powerful tool for resolving serious tax disputes quickly, strategically, and without years of courtroom uncertainty.
Please read it and prepare social media headlines with explanation.

### **ADR Reinforced — A Faster Exit from Tax Disputes**

The **Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 2026** has strengthened **Section 134A**, making Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) a **practical, time-bound alternative** to lengthy tax litigation. - **Chairperson:** A retired judge of the High Court, Federal Constitutional Court, or Supreme Court
