### **Super Tax Fully Upheld — Supreme Constitutional Authority Backs the Levy**
The entity["organization","Federal Constitutional Court","pakistan apex constitutional court"] has conclusively ruled that Super Tax imposed under Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 is **constitutionally valid**. The Court held that Parliament has clear authority to impose income-based taxes through Finance Acts and Money Bills. Importantly, earlier judgments of the Sindh, Lahore, and Islamabad High Courts—where parts of the Super Tax regime were struck down as discriminatory—have now been **overruled to that extent**, bringing legal finality to the issue.

---

### **Sector-Based Super Tax Is Not Discrimination — It’s Lawful Classification**
The Court clarified that taxing specific high-earning sectors under Section 4C does **not violate equality under Article 25** of the Constitution. The classification is based on income thresholds and sectoral profitability, which the Court termed an “intelligible differentia” with a rational link to revenue objectives. In simple terms: treating highly profitable sectors differently is legally acceptable when the basis is objective and income-driven.

---

### **10% Super Tax for Tax Year 2022 Confirmed — No Escape on ‘Closed Accounts’**
A major relief for the tax authorities—and a major clarification for taxpayers—the Court held that Super Tax at **10% for Tax Year 2022** applies even if businesses had already closed their accounts. The reasoning is crucial: **closing of accounts is not a protected event** under tax law. Since income tax returns for TY-2022 were still pending when Super Tax was imposed, the levy does not amount to unlawful retrospective taxation.

---

### **Finance Act 2023 Rates Apply to Tax Year 2023 — Courts Cannot Freeze Tax Policy**
The Court further ruled that Super Tax rates introduced through the **Finance Act 2023** validly apply to **Tax Year 2023**. The Islamabad High Court’s earlier view—restricting the application of amended rates—was set aside. This confirms that Parliament may lawfully adjust tax rates mid-stream, provided they do not disturb already concluded tax matters.

---

### **Super Tax Is a Separate, Standalone Tax — Not Just ‘Extra’ Income Tax**
One of the most important legal clarifications: Super Tax is **not an extension of normal income tax under Section 4**. It is a **self-contained, standalone tax on income**, enacted under Parliament’s constitutional power to tax income. This means Super Tax can apply independently across different income heads, including capital gains, without violating the structure of the Income Tax Ordinance.

---

### **Oil & Gas Companies Get Conditional Protection — Not a Blanket Exemption**
For exploration and production (E&P) companies, the Court struck a balance. Super Tax applies **only to the extent it does not breach the tax caps already agreed** under Petroleum Concession Agreements and the Fifth Schedule. Where Super Tax would push taxation beyond those thresholds, it must give way. However, other income streams of E&P companies—outside concession protections—remain fully exposed to Super Tax.

---

### **Fresh Determination Required Before Recovery from E&P Companies**
The Court directed that tax authorities **cannot jump straight to recovery**. For E&P companies, Commissioners must first reassess Super Tax liability by comparing concession terms with applicable tax laws, issue fresh notices, and provide a proper hearing. This reinforces procedural fairness even while upholding the tax itself.

---

### **Banks Are In, Welfare Funds Are Out**
Banking companies are squarely covered by Super Tax from **Tax Year 2023 onwards**. However, provident funds and benevolent funds holding valid exemption certificates remain **fully protected**. The Court emphasized that taxing welfare funds would defeat the very legislative purpose behind granting exemptions, unless Parliament clearly withdraws those protections.

---

### **High Courts Cannot Order FBR to Apply Judgments Nationwide**
The Court firmly ruled that High Courts **lack jurisdiction** to direct the FBR to issue country-wide implementation circulars based on their judgments. Such directions intrude into executive and legislative functions and have now been explicitly struck down.

---

### **Business Community Alarmed — One-Time Recovery May Paralyze Industry**
Following the verdict, business groups have warned that **forcing immediate, lump-sum recovery** of Super Tax could severely disrupt working capital, payrolls, imports, and debt servicing. With businesses already under pressure from high energy costs and interest rates, they have urged the government to allow **installments or adjustment against pending refunds** to avoid large-scale shutdowns.

---

### **Wider Signal: Courts Back Revenue Measures, Expect Compliance**
The judgment sends a strong message: **courts will not interfere in fiscal policy** merely due to hardship or inconvenience. Unless a tax is clearly unconstitutional, revenue measures will stand. Going forward, disputes are likely to shift from *vires* challenges to **quantification, recovery mechanisms, and sector-specific relief**.

I have carefully reviewed the facts, and I will address this purely from the perspective of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, keeping the advice practical and defensible in case of any future FBR scrutiny.

---

### 1. **Nature of the transaction – what FBR will look at**
From a tax standpoint, the tax authorities will not focus on the family arrangement or hardship factors. Their focus will be on:

- **Source of funds** used to settle the elder brother’s 50% share  
- **Nature of receipt** in the hands of the elder brother  
- **Nature of funding** provided by you (loan vs gift)  
- **Future wealth reconciliation** of the niece (if ownership is given)

If documentation is weak, the transaction can easily be questioned under **section 111 (unexplained income/assets)**.

---

### 2. **Option analysis**

#### **Option 1: Transfer Rs. 7.5 million to the younger brother**
This option carries **higher tax risk**, because:

- The younger brother has **no repayment capacity**
- Any so-called “loan” without repayment evidence may be recharacterized by FBR as **income or gift**
- If treated as a **gift**, it must strictly fall within **section 39** read with **section 85** (gift from relative), otherwise it becomes taxable
- The younger brother will also need to justify **outflow of funds** when paying the elder brother

⚠️ **This option is not advisable** unless there is a genuine loan agreement with repayment capacity, which does not exist here.

---

#### **Option 2: Transfer Rs. 7.5 million directly to the elder brother (Recommended)**
This is the **cleanest and most defensible structure**.

Why this works better:

- Funds move **directly against transfer of property rights**
- No unexplained inflow appears in the younger brother’s bank account
- Elder brother can clearly document that the amount represents **sale consideration of his inherited share**
- Avoids artificial loan/gift characterization

This aligns better with audit practice and reduces exposure under section 111.

---

### 3. **Tax position of each party**

#### **Elder brother (receiving Rs. 7.5 million)**
- Amount received is **sale consideration of inherited property**
- Capital gains tax will apply **only if the property is sold within the holding period** as per **section 37**
- Since the property is inherited, **holding period is counted from the date of acquisition by the mother**, not from succession date
- If held beyond the prescribed period, **no capital gains tax** may arise

Documentation is critical here.

---

#### **You (providing the funds)**
- This is **neither your income nor your asset**
- Funds should be documented as **family financial assistance for settlement of inheritance**
- Your **wealth statement** must show:
  - Reduction in cash/bank
  - Brief narration explaining payment on behalf of cousin towards inherited property settlement

No tax liability arises if properly disclosed.

---

#### **Younger brother**
- No inflow of funds → no section 111 exposure
- He only receives **property title**, not cash
- His ownership should be reflected in his wealth statement as **inheritance/acquired share**

---

#### **Niece (if 50% ownership is given)**
- If ownership is transferred to her **without consideration**, it may constitute a **gift**
- Gift from **maternal uncle** does **not** fall under the “relative” definition for unconditional exemption
- To avoid issues:
  - Either document her share as **inheritance settlement**, or
  - Record **future right/beneficial ownership** instead of immediate legal title, or
  - Ensure consideration is properly documented

This needs careful drafting.

---

### 4. **Essential paperwork to minimise tax exposure**

1. **Succession Certificate / Letter of Administration**
2. **Registered Transfer / Conveyance Deed**
   - Clearly stating consideration and ownership split
3. **Payment evidence**
   - Bank transfer directly from you to elder brother
4. **Family settlement agreement**
   - Explaining why payment is made by you
5. **Affidavit / Declaration**
   - Confirming nature of transaction and source of funds
6. **Wealth statement disclosures**
   - For all relevant parties in the tax year

---

### 5. **Clear recommendation**
From a tax-risk and compliance perspective under the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**:

✅ **Pay Rs. 7.5 million directly into the elder brother’s bank account**  
✅ Link payment explicitly with transfer of his inherited share  
❌ Avoid routing funds through the younger brother  
❌ Avoid labeling the amount as a “loan” where repayment is not realistic  

This approach minimizes exposure under **sections 37, 39, 85, and 111**, and is far easier to defend in assessment proceedings.

If needed, the documentation can be structured in a way that is **audit-ready**, which is crucial given the size of the transaction.

In family arrangements of this nature, FBR’s concern is never the hardship or intent; it is the **movement of funds, ownership trail, and source explanation**.

From a tax-risk perspective, routing Rs. 7.5 million through the younger brother’s bank account—whether termed as a loan or a gift—is the weakest option. Given his age, contractual employment, and lack of repayment capacity, any “loan” structure would be artificial and could easily be challenged as a non-genuine arrangement. Similarly, if treated as a gift, it would still require justification under the law, and the subsequent outflow of funds by the younger brother to the elder brother would again trigger source-of-funds questions. The most realistic and tax-efficient option is for you to **pay Rs. 7.5 million directly into the elder brother’s bank account**, strictly against the transfer of his 50% inherited share in the apartment. This creates a clear audit trail: the elder brother receives funds as **sale consideration of inherited property**, the younger brother does not receive any unexplained cash, and the transaction directly corresponds to a registered transfer of ownership. For capital gains purposes, the elder brother’s holding period will be counted from the date the property was originally acquired by the deceased mother, not from the date of succession, which in many cases results in either no capital gains tax or a significantly reduced exposure under section 37.

A safer approach is to document her share as part of a **family settlement or inheritance arrangement**, or alternatively to defer her legal ownership while recognising her beneficial interest, so that future wealth reconciliation remains clean.

At the outset, it is important to appreciate that FBR will examine this transaction as a **property settlement involving third-party funding**, not merely as a family arrangement. The key tax risks arise from (i) unexplained movement of funds, (ii) mischaracterisation of loans or gifts, and (iii) improper reflection in wealth statements. Any structure that creates artificial inflows or outflows in the hands of a person without financial capacity is almost always questioned in audit and assessment proceedings.

Routing Rs. 7.5 million into the younger brother’s bank account—whether labelled as a loan or a gift—is inherently weak under tax law. A loan requires demonstrable intent and capacity to repay, supported by repayment schedules and actual servicing of the loan. In the absence of such capacity, FBR routinely disregards the nomenclature and treats the amount as income under section 39 or as an unexplained asset under section 111. Similarly, a gift structure does not provide a safe harbour here because the younger brother would still be required to explain the **subsequent application of funds** when paying the elder brother, which again exposes him to section 111 challenges. From a litigation and audit-defence perspective, this option is highly vulnerable and commercially indefensible.

The most robust and legally sustainable approach is for you to **pay Rs. 7.5 million directly to the elder brother**, strictly contemporaneous with the transfer of his 50% inherited share through a registered conveyance or transfer deed. This aligns the flow of funds directly with the transfer of property rights and eliminates any unexplained cash movement in the hands of the younger brother. In such a structure, the elder brother’s receipt is clearly characterised as **sale consideration of inherited immovable property**, bringing the matter squarely within section 37. Importantly, under settled tax principles and audit practice, the **holding period of inherited property is reckoned from the date of acquisition by the deceased**, not from the date of issuance of succession documents. In many cases, this results in either exemption from capital gains tax or a substantially reduced liability, subject to the applicable holding thresholds.

From your perspective as the funding party, the payment does not create any taxable income or asset. However, proper disclosure is critical. In your wealth statement under section 116, the transaction should be reflected as a reduction in cash or bank balance with a clear and specific narration stating that the payment was made **on behalf of a cousin towards settlement of inherited property**. Where source is explained and disclosure is consistent, no adverse inference can be drawn under section 111.

The younger brother’s position remains tax-neutral if no funds pass through his bank account. He will only be required to reflect acquisition of immovable property in his wealth statement, supported by succession documents and the registered transfer deed. This avoids any mismatch between his income profile and asset acquisition, which is often the primary trigger for audit selection.

The proposed allocation of 50% ownership to the niece requires particular care. If legal title is transferred to her without documented consideration, FBR may examine the transaction under section 39 read with section 85 to determine whether it constitutes a taxable receipt. While gifts from specified relatives enjoy exemption, a maternal uncle does not always fall within a completely risk-free category for unconditional exemption. This approach materially reduces exposure under sections 37 and 111 and remains defensible if examined by the tax authorities at any stage in the future.

---

### **Tax Insight 2 – Finance Act, 2025 Amendments Apply to Pending Appeals Only**  
**(Islamabad High Court – ITR No. 205/2024)**  

The Islamabad High Court has provided much-needed clarity on the **retrospective application of appellate forum amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2025**. The Court held that changes restoring or expanding the appellate jurisdiction of ATIR are **beneficial in nature** and therefore apply to *pending cases*, but not to matters that have already attained finality.

As a result, references filed directly before the High Court against CIR(A) orders—where appeals were pending—are liable to be remitted back to the ATIR. This judgment is critical for ongoing litigation strategy and reinforces that forum-related amendments are procedural and remedial, not punitive.

---

### **Tax Insight 3 – Section 111 Additions Require Independent Proceedings, Not Shortcuts**  
**(ATIR Peshawar – ITA No. 169/PB/2025 | Retired PAF Officer Case)**  

In a strong reaffirmation of settled law, the Tribunal held that additions under section 111 cannot be sustained unless **independent and lawful proceedings** are first conducted. The Assessing Officer cannot leapfrog into section 122 and make additions without complying with the mandatory procedural framework.

The Tribunal also found gross violation of **natural justice**, noting that notices were not properly served and hearings were fixed in undue haste, particularly for a salaried individual residing in another city. Both the assessment and appellate orders were declared procedurally defective and remanded for fresh adjudication.

This order is highly relevant for salaried individuals and pensioners facing reopening of assessments on the basis of property purchases.

---

### **Tax Insight 4 – Minimum Tax Cannot Be Built on Presumptions or Withholding Figures Alone**  
**(ATIR Multan – ITA No. 855/MB/2023 | Section 113 & 236G)**  

The Tribunal has categorically ruled that **withholding tax figures cannot be mechanically used to extrapolate turnover** for the purpose of charging minimum tax under section 113. Any enhancement of turnover must be supported by independent material such as suppressed sales, unrecorded supplies, or third-party evidence.

In this case, the Assessing Officer relied on assumed multipliers derived from section 236G certificates, without reconciling them with portal data or MIS reports. The Tribunal held that such an approach amounts to taxation on conjectures and surmises. Once the factual foundation collapsed, the entire minimum tax demand was annulled.

This judgment is particularly useful in audit and minimum tax disputes where turnover is artificially inflated.

---

### **Tax Insight 5 – Customs Valuation Rulings Can Be Withdrawn Ab Initio**  
**(Directorate of Customs Valuation – Rice (All Types), Jan 2026)**  

The Directorate of Customs Valuation has formally **cancelled and withdrawn Valuation Ruling No. 1/2026 ab initio**, underscoring that valuation rulings are not immutable. Where a ruling is found to be flawed or unworkable, the authority retains the power to withdraw it entirely.

For importers, this reinforces the importance of continuously monitoring valuation notifications and challenging them where commercial realities or legal benchmarks are ignored. A withdrawn ruling cannot be used to justify past or ongoing assessments.

---
